current_manifest_record.title: First-order power-source rates in polynomial and exponential spectra
current_manifest_record.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact operator of infinite rank, and write $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, for its positive singular values. Set $Q=\rho>0$ and $\nu=1$. Over the minimum-norm power source ball $X_{1,\rho}(K)$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse model associated with this singular system, if $s_j\asymp j^{-1}$ then the minimax RMS error is of order $\epsilon^{2/5}$; if $s_j\asymp e^{-j}$ then it is of order $\epsilon^{1/2}$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. The constants may depend on $\rho$ and the fixed singular-value comparison constants.
current_manifest_record.strategy: Identify the source ball with the ellipsoid having weights a_j=s_j^{-1}, then apply the polynomial/polynomial and exponential/exponential rows of the minimax-rate corollary.

Assume Countable Choice, $Q>0$, and $p,\kappa>0$. As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, the minimax RMS error over $\Theta_a(Q)$ has the following order-sharp rates: if $s_j\asymp j^{-p}$ and $a_j\asymp j^\kappa$, then $R_*(\epsilon)\asymp\epsilon^{\kappa/(\kappa+p+1/2)}$; if $s_j\asymp e^{-pj}$ and $a_j\asymp j^\kappa$, then $R_*(\epsilon)\asymp[\log(1/\epsilon)]^{-\kappa}$; if $s_j\asymp j^{-p}$ and $a_j\asymp e^{\kappa j}$, then $R_*(\epsilon)\asymp\epsilon[\log(1/\epsilon)]^{p+1/2}$; and if $s_j\asymp e^{-pj}$ and $a_j\asymp e^{\kappa j}$, then $R_*(\epsilon)\asymp\epsilon^{\kappa/(p+\kappa)}$. Here $u_j\asymp v_j$ as $j\to\infty$ or $f(\epsilon)\asymp g(\epsilon)$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$ means the ratio is bounded above and below by positive constants on the indicated tail; the constants may depend on $Q,p,\kappa$ and the axis comparison constants.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

current_manifest_record.title: SOLIT in the mean-zero 2D satellite-gradiometry model
current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume Countable Choice.

For a relative satellite radius $R>1$, identify the mean-zero real Fourier coefficients of a function on the unit circle with $X=\ell^2(\mathbb N;\mathbb R^2)$, where the two coordinates at frequency $n$ are its normalized cosine and sine coefficients, and give this space the canonical inner product $\langle(a_n,b_n),(c_n,d_n)\rangle=\sum_{n\ge1}(a_nc_n+b_nd_n)$. Interleaving the coordinates identifies it isometrically with real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, so $X$ is a real Hilbert space. In these coordinates define the 2D satellite-gradiometry operator by
$$
(T_R(a_n,b_n))_{n\ge1}=(t_n a_n,t_n b_n)_{n\ge1},\qquad t_n=n(n+1)R^{-n-2}.
$$
This is the Fourier-coordinate map for recovering the mean-zero gravitational potential from the radial second derivative measured at relative satellite radius $R$. Take the truth to be the Fourier coefficient sequence of $f^\dagger(x)=\pi/2-|x|$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$. Its constant coefficient is zero, so the omitted zero-frequency component is not part of this mean-zero model. The per-frequency eigenvalue of $T_R^*T_R$ is $\mu_n=n^2(n+1)^2R^{-2n-4}$, each with multiplicity two. For the inverse sequence model, order the cosine–sine modes by nonincreasing multiplier $t_n$, breaking ties by frequency and then placing cosine before sine; write the resulting ordered singular values as $(s_j)$ and their squares as $\lambda_j=s_j^2$. Such an ordering exists because $t_n\to0$ and only finitely many modes exceed any positive threshold. Use the Tikhonov filter $q_\alpha(\lambda)=(\lambda+\alpha)^{-1}$ and its continuous geometric-variance candidate grid in the SOLIT rule with known $\sigma>0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T:X\to Y$ be an injective compact linear operator of infinite rank between separable real Hilbert spaces (each with a countable dense subset), and assume $T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt, meaning that for its positive singular values $s_j$ the sum $\sum_{j\ge1}s_j^2$ is finite. Put $S=T^*T$, $\lambda_j=s_j^2$, and $\lambda_1=\|S\|$, with the positive eigenvalues listed with multiplicity in nonincreasing order. Let $\varphi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous and strictly increasing with $\varphi(0)=0$, and take its inverse on its range. Assume the paper's convexity condition on the spectral range: $x\mapsto x\varphi^{-1}(\sqrt{x})$ is convex for $0\le x\le\varphi(\lambda_1)^2$. Define the source class $\mathcal W_\varphi(\rho):=\{\varphi(S)w:w\in X,\ \|w\|_X\le\rho\}$ for $\rho>0$; equivalently, it is the source ball with singular-value index $\psi(t)=\varphi(t^2)$.

An ordered spectral filter is a family of functions $q_\alpha:[0,\lambda_1]\to[0,\infty)$ indexed by a set $\mathcal A\subset(0,\infty)$ with $0$ as an accumulation point, such that for constants $C_q'<\infty$ and $C_q''=1$,
$$
0\le\alpha q_\alpha(x)\le C_q',\qquad 0\le xq_\alpha(x)\le1,
$$
and $q_\alpha(x)\le q_{\widetilde\alpha}(x)$ whenever $\widetilde\alpha<\alpha$, for every $x\in[0,\lambda_1]$. The index function $\varphi$ is a qualification of this filter if for some $C_\varphi<\infty$,
$$
\sup_{0\le x\le\lambda_1}\varphi(x)(1-xq_\alpha(x))\le C_\varphi\varphi(\alpha)\qquad(\alpha\in\mathcal A).
$$

For $\alpha\in\mathcal A$, define the variance function
$$
V_{T,q}(\alpha):=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_\alpha(\lambda_j)^2.
$$
For $\sigma>0$, a decreasing candidate sequence $(\alpha_m)_{m\in\mathbb N_0}$ in $\mathcal A$ has **geometric variance growth** if $V_{T,q}(\alpha_0)>0$ and there are constants $1<\theta_1\le\theta_2<\infty$ such that
$$
\theta_1\le\frac{V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)}{V_{T,q}(\alpha_{m-1})}\le\theta_2\qquad(m\ge1).
$$
Set $v_m:=\sigma^2V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)$ and
$$
u_m:=\sigma^2\sup_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2,
$$
the operator norm of the estimator-noise covariance in the singular basis. The bound $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$ and $\sum_j\lambda_j<\infty$ make each $u_m$ and $v_m$ finite. The finite candidate set ends at
$$
m_{\max}:=\min\{m\in\mathbb N_0:v_m\ge1\}.
$$
The geometric lower bound $v_m\ge v_0\theta_1^m$ makes this index finite.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T:X\to Y$ be an injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator of infinite rank between separable real Hilbert spaces, let $S=T^*T$, and let $(s_j,v_j,u_j)$ be a fixed positive singular system with $\lambda_j=s_j^2$. Let $Z$ be a real isonormal Gaussian process on $Y$, meaning that $g\mapsto Z(g)$ is linear into $L^2$, is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. In the weak observation experiment $Y_x(g)=\langle Tx,g\rangle_Y+\sigma Z(g)$ with known noise standard deviation $\sigma>0$, use the ordered filter $q_\alpha$, the geometric-variance candidates $\alpha_0>\cdots>\alpha_{m_{\max}}$, and variances $v_m=\sigma^2\sum_j\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2$ from the preceding definition. For each candidate index $m$, the regularized estimator $\widehat x_m$ is the $L^2$ limit of its finite singular-coordinate sums; its $j$th coordinate is $\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\theta_j+\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\xi_j$, where $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$ and $\xi_j=Z(u_j)$.

Take as input the observed sequence $y=(y_j)_{j\ge1}$, where $y_j:=Y_x(u_j)$. For each candidate $m$ and each $N=1,2,\ldots$, compute
$$
\widehat x_{m,N}^{\mathrm{obs}}:=\sum_{j=1}^N s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)y_jv_j.
$$
If these partial sums converge in $X$, define $\widehat x_m(y)$ to be their limit; otherwise set $\widehat x_m(y)=0_X$. This specifies an $X$-valued output for every input sequence. The quantities $v_{m_1,m_2}$ and $z_{m_1,m_2}(x)$ are determined by the known operator, filter, noise level and Gaussian coordinate law.

For $0\le m_1<m_2\le m_{\max}$, set
$$
v_{m_1,m_2}:=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j\bigl(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\bigr)^2
$$
and let $N_{m_1,m_2}$ be the norm of the centered estimator difference divided by $\sigma$. For $x>0$, define its upper quantile by
$$
z_{m_1,m_2}(x):=\inf\{z\ge0:\mathbb P(N_{m_1,m_2}>z)\le e^{-x}\}.
$$
Given fixed $\beta>0$ and $\gamma>0$, for $0\le m<m_{\max}$ put $x_m:=2(1+\gamma)\log(v_{m+1}/v_0)$, and for each pair $m_1<m_2$ put $\eta_{m_1,m_2}:=\sigma z_{m_1,m_2}(x_{m_1})+\beta\sqrt{v_{m_1,m_2}}$. Accept an index $m_1$ exactly when $\|\widehat x_{m_1}(y)-\widehat x_{m_2}(y)\|_X\le\eta_{m_1,m_2}$ for every $m_2$ with $m_1<m_2\le m_{\max}$, and output the smallest accepted index $\widehat m$ and parameter $\widehat\alpha=\alpha_{\widehat m}$. For $m_1=m_{\max}$, accept without comparisons, including when $m_{\max}=0$. This rule uses only the observed sequence, the known operator and filter, the noise level, the fixed candidate grid, and $\beta,\gamma$; it does not use $x$ or its source index $\varphi$.

Write $\lambda_j=s_j^2$ and let $\xi_j$ be the independent standard-normal noise coordinates. $$
X_{m,N}:=\sum_{j=1}^N\bigl(\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\theta_j+\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\xi_j\bigr)v_j.
$$
The conclusion below includes the existence of their limit $\widehat x_m$ in $L^2(\Omega;X)$. Put $f_m:=\mathbb E\widehat x_m$, $B_m:=\|f_m-x\|_X$, and $v_m:=\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-f_m\|_X^2$. Then $\widehat x_m$ is a measurable $X$-valued random element with finite second moment and
$$
\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-x\|_X^2=B_m^2+v_m,\qquad v_m=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2.
$$
If $m_1<m_2$, then $B_{m_2}\le B_{m_1}$, $\|f_{m_2}-f_{m_1}\|_X\le B_{m_1}$, and
$$
v_{m_1,m_2}:=\mathbb E\| (\widehat x_{m_2}-f_{m_2})-(\widehat x_{m_1}-f_{m_1})\|_X^2=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j\bigl(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\bigr)^2\le v_{m_2}.
$$

derivations.claim: Interleaving $(a_n,b_n)_{n\ge1}$ as $(a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2,\ldots)$ is a linear isometry onto real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, so [F7] gives the stated real Hilbert structure. The integral of $f^\dagger$ over $[-\pi,\pi]$ is $\pi^2-\pi^2=0$, so its constant Fourier coefficient vanishes and its real Fourier coefficient sequence lies in the stated mean-zero coefficient space. The real cosine and sine modes are orthonormal because they are the real and imaginary parts of the orthonormal character basis in [F1].

For every $n\ge1$, $t_n>0$ and $t_n\to0$ exponentially since $R>1$. The ratio of consecutive squared multipliers is $((n+1)/n)^2((n+2)/(n+1))^2R^{-2}$, which tends to $R^{-2}<1$; choose $\rho$ strictly between $R^{-2}$ and $1$, then the ratio is at most $\rho$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Thus $\sum_{n\ge1}2t_n^2<\infty$. The operator is injective because all its diagonal multipliers are positive. Its truncation to frequencies $n\le N$ is finite rank and the operator-norm error is $\sup_{n>N}t_n\to0$, so $T_R$ is compact and Hilbert–Schmidt.

The frequency multipliers satisfy $t_{n+1}/t_n=(n+2)/(nR)$, which can exceed $1$ for small $n$; thus the frequency order is not always the singular-value order. The multiset of modes has a nonincreasing enumeration: at every stage a remaining maximum exists because $t_n\to0$ and only finitely many modes lie above any fixed positive threshold, and the fixed tie rule selects one uniquely. Every mode is eventually listed because only finitely many modes have multiplier at least its positive multiplier. The operator is diagonal on the orthonormal cosine–sine basis, so the frequency eigenvalue is $\mu_n=t_n^2=n^2(n+1)^2R^{-2n-4}$ twice at each frequency, and the enumerated singular system has these values in nonincreasing order. Since $(n+1)^2\asymp n^2$, $\mu_n\asymp n^4e^{-2n\log R}$, an exponential spectrum with exponent $\vartheta=1$.

For every $\lambda\ge0$, $q_\alpha(\lambda)=(\lambda+\alpha)^{-1}$ is nonnegative, $\alpha q_\alpha(\lambda)\le1$, and $\lambda q_\alpha(\lambda)\le1$. If $\widetilde\alpha<\alpha$, then $\lambda+\widetilde\alpha<\lambda+\alpha$, so $q_\alpha(\lambda)\le q_{\widetilde\alpha}(\lambda)$. Thus it is an ordered filter with $C_q'=1$ by [F6]. Its trace variance is
$$
V(\alpha):=2\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\mu_n}{(\mu_n+\alpha)^2},\qquad \alpha>0.
$$
On every compact interval $[a,b]\subset(0,\infty)$, each summand is continuous and is bounded above by $2\mu_n/a^2$. Since $\sum_n2\mu_n<\infty$ by step 1.2, the series converges uniformly there, so $V$ is continuous. Each summand strictly decreases as $\alpha$ increases, hence so does $V$. Also $V(\alpha)\le2\alpha^{-2}\sum_n\mu_n\to0$ as $\alpha\to\infty$. For every fixed $n$, $V(\alpha)\ge2\mu_n/(\mu_n+\alpha)^2\to2/\mu_n$ as $\alpha\downarrow0$; because $\mu_n\to0$, these lower bounds imply $V(\alpha)\to\infty$. Fix any $c>0$ and $\theta>1$. Continuity, strict decrease, and these endpoint limits give a unique $\alpha_m>0$ with $V(\alpha_m)=c\theta^m$ for every $m\in\mathbb N_0$. Thus $\alpha_m$ decreases to zero and the variances $v_m=\sigma^2V(\alpha_m)$ have the constant consecutive ratio $\theta$. The resulting infinite grid meets [F2], and the SOLIT rule truncates it at its finite $m_{\max}$.

The truth lies in $L^2$ because it is bounded, and its Fourier coefficients are coordinates in the model by [F1]. The positive diagonal multipliers give the injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator verified in step 1.2; the Tikhonov filter satisfies [F6] and its candidates satisfy [F2], and the positive-noise experiment and finite selector are [F3]–[F4]. The well-definedness and moment properties of its estimators follow from [F5]. This example asserts no rate for the resulting estimator.

current_manifest_record.title: SOLIT for the periodic heat equation (reported simulation)
current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume Countable Choice.

Let the real periodic Fourier coefficient space be $X=Y=\mathbb R\oplus\ell^2(\mathbb N;\mathbb R^2)$, with one constant coordinate and cosine–sine coordinate pairs for each positive frequency, and give it the canonical inner product $\langle(c_0,(a_n,b_n)),(d_0,(c_n,d_n))\rangle=c_0d_0+\sum_{n\ge1}(a_nc_n+b_nd_n)$. The interleaving map $(c_0,(a_n,b_n))\mapsto(c_0,a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2,\ldots)$ is an isometry onto real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, so this is a real Hilbert space. For a heat time $\bar t>0$, define the periodic heat forward operator by
$$
T_{\bar t}(c_0,(a_n,b_n)_{n\ge1})=(c_0,(e^{-n^2\bar t}a_n,e^{-n^2\bar t}b_n)_{n\ge1}).
$$
Its eigenvalues for $T_{\bar t}^*T_{\bar t}$ are $1$ on the constant mode and $e^{-2n^2\bar t}$ on both modes of frequency $n$. The singular system for the sequence model is ordered as the constant mode, then cosine and sine modes in increasing positive frequency; its singular values are nonincreasing. Use the truth whose function is $f^\dagger(x)=\pi/2-|x|$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$, and observe its weak Gaussian white-noise data with known standard deviation $\sigma>0$. Li and Werner report an empirical SOLIT simulation at $\bar t=0.1$ using $10^4$ Monte Carlo runs: SOLIT appears close to the oracle, while the minimax behavior is unclear and the empirical adaptation behavior for spectral cut-off is irregular. These are reported simulation findings, not a theorem or a simulation performed for this library.

For the spectral-cutoff candidate sequence $\alpha_n=e^{-2n^2\bar t}$, indexed by $n\in\mathbb N_0$, the variance sums $V_n=1+2\sum_{k=1}^n e^{2k^2\bar t}$ do not have a uniformly bounded consecutive ratio: $V_n/V_{n-1}\to\infty$. Thus this infinite spectral-cutoff sequence does not meet the uniform geometric-variance-grid condition. A continuous Tikhonov filter $q_\alpha(\lambda)=(\lambda+\alpha)^{-1}$ does admit such a grid because its variance function is continuous, decreases from $+\infty$ to $0$, and can be sampled at successive fixed variance ratios.
current_manifest_record.strategy: Compute the periodic heat spectrum, verify the Tikhonov filter, show the cutoff grid ratio diverges, and report only the cited simulation.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The characters
$(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z}$ form an orthonormal basis of the complex Hilbert space
$L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]): they are
orthonormal and their closed linear span is all of $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T:X\to Y$ be an injective compact linear operator of infinite rank between separable real Hilbert spaces (each with a countable dense subset), and assume $T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt, meaning that for its positive singular values $s_j$ the sum $\sum_{j\ge1}s_j^2$ is finite. Put $S=T^*T$, $\lambda_j=s_j^2$, and $\lambda_1=\|S\|$, with the positive eigenvalues listed with multiplicity in nonincreasing order. Let $\varphi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous and strictly increasing with $\varphi(0)=0$, and take its inverse on its range. Assume the paper's convexity condition on the spectral range: $x\mapsto x\varphi^{-1}(\sqrt{x})$ is convex for $0\le x\le\varphi(\lambda_1)^2$. Define the source class $\mathcal W_\varphi(\rho):=\{\varphi(S)w:w\in X,\ \|w\|_X\le\rho\}$ for $\rho>0$; equivalently, it is the source ball with singular-value index $\psi(t)=\varphi(t^2)$.

An ordered spectral filter is a family of functions $q_\alpha:[0,\lambda_1]\to[0,\infty)$ indexed by a set $\mathcal A\subset(0,\infty)$ with $0$ as an accumulation point, such that for constants $C_q'<\infty$ and $C_q''=1$,
$$
0\le\alpha q_\alpha(x)\le C_q',\qquad 0\le xq_\alpha(x)\le1,
$$
and $q_\alpha(x)\le q_{\widetilde\alpha}(x)$ whenever $\widetilde\alpha<\alpha$, for every $x\in[0,\lambda_1]$. The index function $\varphi$ is a qualification of this filter if for some $C_\varphi<\infty$,
$$
\sup_{0\le x\le\lambda_1}\varphi(x)(1-xq_\alpha(x))\le C_\varphi\varphi(\alpha)\qquad(\alpha\in\mathcal A).
$$

For $\alpha\in\mathcal A$, define the variance function
$$
V_{T,q}(\alpha):=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_\alpha(\lambda_j)^2.
$$
For $\sigma>0$, a decreasing candidate sequence $(\alpha_m)_{m\in\mathbb N_0}$ in $\mathcal A$ has **geometric variance growth** if $V_{T,q}(\alpha_0)>0$ and there are constants $1<\theta_1\le\theta_2<\infty$ such that
$$

$$
Set $v_m:=\sigma^2V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)$ and
$$
u_m:=\sigma^2\sup_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2,
$$
the operator norm of the estimator-noise covariance in the singular basis. The bound $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$ and $\sum_j\lambda_j<\infty$ make each $u_m$ and $v_m$ finite. The finite candidate set ends at
$$
m_{\max}:=\min\{m\in\mathbb N_0:v_m\ge1\}.
$$
The geometric lower bound $v_m\ge v_0\theta_1^m$ makes this index finite.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T:X\to Y$ be an injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator of infinite rank between separable real Hilbert spaces, let $S=T^*T$, and let $(s_j,v_j,u_j)$ be a fixed positive singular system with $\lambda_j=s_j^2$. Let $Z$ be a real isonormal Gaussian process on $Y$, meaning that $g\mapsto Z(g)$ is linear into $L^2$, is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. In the weak observation experiment $Y_x(g)=\langle Tx,g\rangle_Y+\sigma Z(g)$ with known noise standard deviation $\sigma>0$, use the ordered filter $q_\alpha$, the geometric-variance candidates $\alpha_0>\cdots>\alpha_{m_{\max}}$, and variances $v_m=\sigma^2\sum_j\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2$ from the preceding definition. For each candidate index $m$, the regularized estimator $\widehat x_m$ is the $L^2$ limit of its finite singular-coordinate sums; its $j$th coordinate is $\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\theta_j+\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\xi_j$, where $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$ and $\xi_j=Z(u_j)$.

Take as input the observed sequence $y=(y_j)_{j\ge1}$, where $y_j:=Y_x(u_j)$. For each candidate $m$ and each $N=1,2,\ldots$, compute
$$
\widehat x_{m,N}^{\mathrm{obs}}:=\sum_{j=1}^N s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)y_jv_j.
$$
If these partial sums converge in $X$, define $\widehat x_m(y)$ to be their limit; otherwise set $\widehat x_m(y)=0_X$. This specifies an $X$-valued output for every input sequence. The quantities $v_{m_1,m_2}$ and $z_{m_1,m_2}(x)$ are determined by the known operator, filter, noise level and Gaussian coordinate law.

For $0\le m_1<m_2\le m_{\max}$, set
$$
v_{m_1,m_2}:=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j\bigl(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\bigr)^2
$$
and let $N_{m_1,m_2}$ be the norm of the centered estimator difference divided by $\sigma$. For $x>0$, define its upper quantile by
$$
z_{m_1,m_2}(x):=\inf\{z\ge0:\mathbb P(N_{m_1,m_2}>z)\le e^{-x}\}.
$$
Given fixed $\beta>0$ and $\gamma>0$, for $0\le m<m_{\max}$ put $x_m:=2(1+\gamma)\log(v_{m+1}/v_0)$, and for each pair $m_1<m_2$ put $\eta_{m_1,m_2}:=\sigma z_{m_1,m_2}(x_{m_1})+\beta\sqrt{v_{m_1,m_2}}$. Accept an index $m_1$ exactly when $\|\widehat x_{m_1}(y)-\widehat x_{m_2}(y)\|_X\le\eta_{m_1,m_2}$ for every $m_2$ with $m_1<m_2\le m_{\max}$, and output the smallest accepted index $\widehat m$ and parameter $\widehat\alpha=\alpha_{\widehat m}$. For $m_1=m_{\max}$, accept without comparisons, including when $m_{\max}=0$. This rule uses only the observed sequence, the known operator and filter, the noise level, the fixed candidate grid, and $\beta,\gamma$; it does not use $x$ or its source index $\varphi$.

Assume Countable Choice and the positive-noise Gaussian sequence model with $\sigma>0$, a fixed complete positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)$ for an injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator $T:X\to Y$, and a truth with coordinates $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$ in $\ell^2$. Write $\lambda_j=s_j^2$ and let $\xi_j$ be the independent standard-normal noise coordinates. Let $q_\alpha$ be nonnegative and satisfy $0\le\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le1$, $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$, and $q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\le q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)$ whenever $m_1<m_2$. $$

derivations.claim: Interleaving the constant coordinate and cosine–sine pairs is a linear isometry onto real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, so [F7] gives the stated real Hilbert structure. The real Fourier modes are orthonormal by taking real and imaginary parts of the character basis in [F1]. On each positive frequency, $\partial_{xx}\cos(nx)=-n^2\cos(nx)$ and $\partial_{xx}\sin(nx)=-n^2\sin(nx)$, so solving $\partial_tu=\partial_{xx}u$ multiplies both coefficients by $e^{-n^2\bar t}$; the constant mode is unchanged. Therefore the operator in the Example is the periodic heat forward map in Fourier coordinates.

Every multiplier of $T_{\bar t}$ is positive, so $T_{\bar t}$ is injective. The positive-frequency multipliers tend to zero, so finite-frequency truncations converge in operator norm and $T_{\bar t}$ is compact. Moreover, $\sum_{n\ge1}2e^{-2n^2\bar t}<\infty$ by comparison with the geometric series $\sum_{n\ge1}2e^{-2n\bar t}$, so the operator is Hilbert–Schmidt. Squaring the multipliers gives the stated eigenvalues of $T_{\bar t}^*T_{\bar t}$.

Let parameter and data spaces be $X=Y=\mathbb R$ with their Borel sigma-algebras, let the admissible truth set be $U=\mathbb R$, and let $F:U\to Y$ be the identity map. Regard $\theta\in\mathbb R$ as the constant coefficient field $a_\theta(x)=\theta$ on $[0,1]$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

Let $X$ be a specified real separable Banach or Hilbert parameter space with metric $d_X(x,x')=\|x-x'\|_X$ and its norm topology. Let $(Y,d_Y)$ be a metric data space equipped with a sigma-algebra $\Sigma_Y$, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth set, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map. Choose a Borel set $D\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $D\subseteq U$ such that the restriction $G:=F|_D:D\to Y$ is measurable for the trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. A prior on this forward domain is a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ such that $\mu(D)=1$. Its restriction $\mu|_D$, defined by $\mu|_D(A)=\mu(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$, is then a probability measure on $D$, and the induced data law is $G_\#(\mu|_D)$, defined by $G_\#(\mu|_D)(E)=(\mu|_D)(G^{-1}(E))$ for $E\in\Sigma_Y$. A Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu(D)<1$ is not a prior on this declared forward domain.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
(Measurable spaces and measurable sets). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

The density in [F1] is continuous and strictly positive on $[0,\tfrac12]$, so it has a positive minimum there and $\mu((-\infty,1))\ge\int_0^{1/2}\phi(t)\,dt>0$.

current_manifest_record.title: Exact posterior second moment and contraction bound for a Gaussian sequence inverse problem
current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $0<\epsilon$, let $(s_j)_{j\ge1}$ be the positive singular values in the Gaussian sequence inverse model, and let a fixed truth $\theta^\dagger=(\theta^\dagger_j)_{j\ge1}$ belong to $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$. Let $\tau_j>0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\tau_j^2<\infty$, and let the prior be a Borel probability on $\ell^2$ whose coordinates are independent $N(0,\tau_j^2)$ variables, independent of the observation noise. Under the prior-predictive law the observations are $Y_j=s_j\theta_j+\epsilon\xi_j$; under the fixed truth they are $Y_j=s_j\theta^\dagger_j+\epsilon\xi_j$, where the $\xi_j$ are independent $N(0,1)$ variables. Define $v_j=(\tau_j^{-2}+s_j^2/\epsilon^2)^{-1}$ and $\lambda_j=\tau_j^2s_j^2/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)$. For fixed-truth-almost every data sequence, a posterior version on $\ell^2$ is the restriction of $\bigotimes_{j\ge1}N(\lambda_jY_j/s_j,v_j)$. Its expected posterior squared distance from the truth is
$$S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger):=\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}\!\left[\int_{\ell^2}\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2\,\Pi_\epsilon(d\theta\mid Y)\right]=\sum_{j\ge1}\left[(1-\lambda_j)^2(\theta^\dagger_j)^2+\frac{v_j^2s_j^2}{\epsilon^2}+v_j\right].$$
The identity holds in $[0,+\infty]$; under the stated trace condition its right side is finite. For every $R>0$, the expected posterior mass outside the radius-$R$ ball is at most $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)/R^2$. In particular, if $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C r_\epsilon^2$ for a constant $C$ and a positive $r_\epsilon\to0$, then $r_\epsilon$ is a posterior contraction rate in the sense of the preceding definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Assume AC. Let $n,m\ge1$, $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let
$C_0\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with $v^TC_0v\ge0$ for every
$v\in\mathbb R^n$. Let
$A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ and let
$\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite, meaning
$u^T\Gamma u>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^m$. Suppose
$X$ and $\eta$ are independent random vectors with laws
$X\sim N_n(m_0,C_0)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$, and set
$Y=AX+\eta$. Define $\mu_0(E)=\mathbb P(X\in E)$ for Borel
$E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and set
$S=AC_0A^T+\Gamma$. Then $S$ is positive definite. For each
$y\in\mathbb R^m$, define
$$ \Phi_y(x)=\tfrac12(y-Ax)^T\Gamma^{-1}(y-Ax),\qquad Z(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx). $$
For every $y$, $0<Z(y)<\infty$, so the normalized potential update
$$ \Pi^y(E)=\frac{\int_E e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx)}{Z(y)} \quad(E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)) $$
is a probability measure and equals the conditional-law version obtained by
conditioning the observation model at $y$. Its Gaussian formula, defined for
every $y$, is
$$ N_n\!\left( m_0+C_0A^TS^{-1}(y-Am_0),\ C_0-C_0A^TS^{-1}AC_0 \right). $$
Let $P_Y(B)=\mathbb P(Y\in B)$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^m$.
Conditional-law versions are unique only $P_Y$-almost surely. The displayed
mean and covariance formulas invert only $S$, not $C_0$; $C_0$ and the
posterior covariance may be singular. The prior support is
$m_0+\operatorname{Ran}(C_0)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a set, let $m:T\to\mathbb R$, and let
$k:T\times T\to\mathbb R$ be symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning that
for every finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_n\in T$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\sum_{i,j=1}^n a_i a_j k(t_i,t_j)\ge0.$$
There is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the cylinder sigma-algebra
$\mathcal C_T$ of $\mathbb R^T$ whose marginal on each finite-coordinate space
$\mathbb R^F$, for $F\subseteq T$ finite, is the Gaussian law with mean
$(m(t))_{t\in F}$ and covariance matrix $(k(s,t))_{s,t\in F}$. The coordinate
process $X_t(x)=x(t)$ is Gaussian, has mean function $m$, and has covariance
kernel $k$. This construction gives only the cylinder-space process; it
asserts no sample-path continuity, joint measurability in $(t,x)$, or tight
Banach-valued law.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
Independent sigma-algebras and independent events.

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from The sigma-algebra generated by a function.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. For each positive noise level $\epsilon$, let $\Pi_{0,\epsilon}$ be a proper Borel prior on $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse experiment, and let $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}$ be the resulting prior-predictive joint law of parameter and data. A posterior kernel is a data-measurable assignment $y\mapsto\Pi_\epsilon(\cdot\mid y)$ of Borel probability measures on $\ell^2$ satisfying
$$\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}(\theta\in A,\,Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid y)\,\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y(dy)$$
for every Borel $A\subseteq\ell^2$ and every product-Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$, where $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y$ is the prior-predictive data marginal. Fix a truth $\theta^\dagger\in\ell^2$ and write $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ for its data law. Since a conditional-law version is specified only up to a prior-predictive null set, any contraction claim under $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ refers to the stated version. A positive function $r_\epsilon\to0$ is a posterior contraction rate in the $\ell^2$ norm at $\theta^\dagger$ if, for every positive function $M_\epsilon\to\infty$,

current_manifest_record.statement: Assume AC. Observe $Y=\theta+Z$ with fixed truth $\theta\in\mathbb R$, $Z\sim N(0,1)$, and proper prior $\theta\sim N(0,1)$. Let $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ and $\Phi(y)=\int_{-\infty}^y\phi(x)\,dx$, let $z>0$ be the unique number satisfying $\Phi(z)=0.975$, and put $r=z/\sqrt2$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space and, for each integer $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal E_n=((\mathsf Y_n,\mathcal Y_n),(P_{\theta,n})_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment. Let $\Pi_{0,n}$ be a proper prior on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and let $y\mapsto\Pi_n(\cdot\mid y)$ be a supplied posterior probability kernel under the associated prior-predictive law. For $0<\gamma<1$, a data-indexed set rule $C_n:\mathsf Y_n\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$ is a posterior credible set at level $1-\gamma$ if its membership graph $\{(y,\theta):\theta\in C_n(y)\}$ is in $\mathcal Y_n\otimes\mathcal T$ and $\Pi_n(C_n(y)\mid y)\ge1-\gamma$ for every $y$ in its declared data domain. At a fixed truth $\theta\in\Theta$, its frequentist coverage is $c_n(\theta):=P_{\theta,n}\{y:\theta\in C_n(y)\}$. For a truth class $\mathcal T_n\subseteq\Theta$, the rule is asymptotically honest at level $1-\gamma$ on $\mathcal T_n$ if $\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}c_n(\theta)\ge1-\gamma$, and it is asymptotically exactly calibrated there if $\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}|c_n(\theta)-(1-\gamma)|\to0$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length,
Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

Its density φ is positive and symmetric and integrates to one, so Φ is continuous and strictly increasing, with Φ(0)=1/2 and Φ(y)→1 as y→∞. Choose B>0 with Φ(B)>0.975. By [F3] on [0,B], there is a unique z>0 with Φ(z)=0.975.

The prior density times likelihood is proportional to $\exp\{-\tfrac12[\theta^2+(Y-\theta)^2]\}=\exp\{-(\theta-Y/2)^2\}$ times a factor independent of $\theta$. Normalization gives posterior law $N(Y/2,1/2)$.
Under the fixed truth $\theta_*=2r+1$, write $Y=\theta_*+Z$. The event $\theta_*\in I(Y)$ is equivalent to $|Z-\theta_*|\le2r$, hence to $1\le Z\le4r+1$.

The interval membership graph is $\{(Y,\theta):|\theta-Y/2|\le r\}$, the inverse image of the closed interval $[-r,r]$ under a continuous map. It is closed, hence Borel, so the sampling membership event is measurable.
Under that posterior, $(\theta-Y/2)/\sqrt{1/2}$ is standard normal. The interval radius $r=z/\sqrt2$ therefore gives posterior mass $\Phi(z)-\Phi(-z)=0.975-0.025=0.95$ for every observed $Y$.
Since the standard normal density is positive and symmetric, $P(1\le Z\le4r+1)<P(Z\ge0)=1/2<0.95$. Thus the interval has posterior mass $0.95$ but frequentist coverage below $0.95$ at $\theta_*$.

current_manifest_record.title: Prior-preserving Crank–Nicolson sampler
current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let
$\mu_0$ be a centered Borel Gaussian probability measure on $H$, let
$D\subseteq H$ be Borel with $\mu_0(D)=1$, and let
$\Phi_D:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be Borel. Assume the evidence
$$
Z:=\int_D e^{-\Phi_D(u)}\,\mu_0(du)
$$
satisfies $0<Z<\infty$. Extend the potential to all of $H$ by setting
$\bar\Phi(u)=\Phi_D(u)$ for $u\in D$ and $\bar\Phi(u)=+\infty$ for
$u\notin D$, and define the target probability
$\mu(du)=Z^{-1}e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}\mu_0(du)$. For a scale $\beta\in[0,1]$,
write $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$. At state $u\in H$, draw $\xi\sim\mu_0$
independently and propose $v=\rho u+\beta\xi$. Set the acceptance probability
to $0$ if either $\bar\Phi(u)$ or $\bar\Phi(v)$ is $+\infty$, and otherwise set
$$
\alpha(u,v)=\min\{1,\exp(\bar\Phi(u)-\bar\Phi(v))\}.
$$
Draw an independent uniform random variable on $[0,1]$ and move to $v$ if it
is at most $\alpha(u,v)$; otherwise remain at $u$. The resulting one-step
transition rule is the prior-preserving Crank–Nicolson, or pCN, rule
$P_\beta$. States with infinite potential are absorbing under this total
definition; they have $\mu$-measure zero.

current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space and let
$\mu_0$ be a centered Borel Gaussian probability measure on $H$. Let $U$ and
$\xi$ be independent random elements with law $\mu_0$. For
$\beta\in[0,1]$, set $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$ and
$V=\rho U+\beta\xi$. The joint Borel law of $(U,V)$ on $H\times H$ is
unchanged by the coordinate swap $(u,v)\mapsto(v,u)$.

Draw an independent uniform random variable on $[0,1]$ and move to $v$ if it
is at most $\alpha(u,v)$; otherwise remain at $u$. The resulting one-step
transition rule is the prior-preserving Crank–Nicolson, or pCN, rule
$P_\beta$. States with infinite potential are absorbing under this total
definition; they have $\mu$-measure zero.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ (Dense, nowhere dense and codense subsets of a topological space, and the criterion by basic open sets, Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a
nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

**No choice principle is used.** The backward direction is where an appeal to
choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.

Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a
sequence in $H$ whose range $\{x_n : n\in\mathbb N\}$ is dense in $H$
([[def-dense-top]]), and let

$$L_0:=\varnothing,\qquad L_{n+1}:=L_n\cup\Bigl\{\tfrac{v_n}{\|v_n\|}\Bigr\}\ \text{ if }\ v_n:=x_n-\sum_{e\in L_n}\langle x_n,e\rangle e\ne0, \qquad L_{n+1}:=L_n\ \text{ otherwise}.$$

Then $L:=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}L_n$ is a finite or countably infinite orthonormal
set whose closed linear span is $H$; that is, $L$ is an orthonormal basis of $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
it is obtained from the given sequence by Gram–Schmidt elimination. The
enumeration of $L$ is the canonical one by the stage at which an element
appears, and no choice principle is used.

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ (The real numbers) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Let $A$ be at most countable ([[def-countable]]) and let $B \subseteq A$. Then
$B$ is at most countable.

The proof establishes the sharper statement about subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ from
which this follows: **a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is finite if it is
bounded above, and countably infinite if it is not.**

**No choice principle is used.** This is the point of the lemma rather than a
footnote to it. The enumeration of an unbounded $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is built
by always taking the *least* element of $S$ above the previous one, and the least
element of a nonempty set of naturals is canonical
([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]): it is determined by $S$, not selected from it.
Replacing "least" by "some" would turn the construction into an appeal to
dependent choice.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ (Order on the reals). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Ordered field):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric (Nonnegativity of a metric is a consequence of the other axioms, not an axiom) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear (Isometry, isometric embedding, and the subspace metric on a subset): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ (Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is Topologically, uniformly and Lipschitz equivalent metrics on a set.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open and closed sets
as in [[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]]. Then:

1. **Balls are open.** $B(x,r)$ is open, for every $x \in X$ and every $r > 0$.
2. **Arbitrary unions.** If $\mathcal{U}$ is any collection of open subsets of
   $X$, then $\bigcup \mathcal{U}$ is open.
3. **Finite intersections.** If $n \ge 1$ and $U_0, \dots, U_{n-1}$ are open,
   then $U_0 \cap \dots \cap U_{n-1}$ is open.
4. **Closed balls are closed.** $\bar B(x,r)$ is closed, for every $x \in X$ and
   every $r > 0$.

Together with the fact that $\emptyset$ and $X$ are open, recorded already in
[[def-metric-topology]], claims 2 and 3 say that $\mathcal{T}_d$ has exactly the
closure properties that the word *topology* names.

Let $X$ be a normed space over the scalar field $\mathbb{K}$, where
$\mathbb{K}\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, using [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] over $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] over $\mathbb C$. The
**dual space** of $X$ is

$$X^*:=\mathcal{B}(X,\mathbb{K}),$$

the space of bounded linear functionals on $X$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]).

Each $f \in X^*$ is in particular a linear functional in the algebraic sense,
so $X^*$ is a subspace of the algebraic dual from
[[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]].

The **dual norm** on $X^*$ is the operator norm:

$$\|f\|_{X^*}:=\|f\| =\sup\{|f(x)|:\|x\| \le 1\}.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let $B$ be a real
separable Banach space with its norm Borel sigma-algebra. A map
$W:\Omega\to B$ is a **centered Borel Gaussian random element** if it is
Borel-measurable and, for every $\ell\in B^*$, the real random variable
$\ell(W)$ has a centered (possibly zero-variance) normal law. Its law is the
Borel probability $\mu=P\circ W^{-1}$. When the word *tight* is used, it means
that for every $\delta>0$ there is a norm-compact $K\subseteq B$ with
$\mu(K)>1-\delta$.

This definition concerns a random element in $B$. A Gaussian process on an
arbitrary index set with only a cylinder-space law does not satisfy it unless
a Borel $B$-valued realization is separately constructed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random
element in a real separable Banach space $B$. There is a constant $a>0$ such
that
$$E\exp(a\|W\|^2)<\infty.$$
In particular, $E\|W\|^2<\infty$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
Independent sigma-algebras and independent events.

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from The sigma-algebra generated by a function.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

For real $a,b,t$, $\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)$. For a finite mutually independent family $(X_j)_{j=1}^n$ of real random variables, $\varphi_{\sum_jX_j}(t)=\prod_j\varphi_{X_j}(t)$. The empty sum has characteristic function one.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume AC. Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with equal characteristic functions are equal. In particular a real random variable has a real-valued characteristic function if and only if its law is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space with a
finite or countable complete orthonormal basis $(e_j)_{j\in J}$. For each finite
$F\subseteq J$, define the coordinate map
$\pi_F:H\to\mathbb R^F$ by
$\pi_F(x)=(\langle x,e_j\rangle)_{j\in F}$. If $\nu$ and $\nu'$ are Borel
probability measures on $H$ and
$\nu(\pi_F^{-1}(B))=\nu'(\pi_F^{-1}(B))$ for every finite $F\subseteq J$ and
every Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^F$, then $\nu=\nu'$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

A topological space $X$ is **second countable** when its topology has a basis $\mathcal B$ that is at most countable (Basis and subbasis for a topology, and the topology generated by a family of sets, Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable). Thus every open set is a union of members of one at most countable family $\mathcal B$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
Measurable rectangles in a product of measurable spaces.

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $X,Y$ be second-countable topological spaces and give $X\times Y$ the
product topology. Then
$$\mathcal B(X\times Y)=\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y).$$

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

derivations.claim: By [F2], take a finite or countable complete orthonormal basis $(e_j)$ of $H$. Give $H\times H$ the inner product $\langle(u,v),(x,y)\rangle_\times=\langle u,x\rangle+\langle v,y\rangle$. Its induced norm is $\sqrt{\|u\|^2+\|v\|^2}$. It is complete because a Cauchy sequence has Cauchy coordinate sequences in $H$, whose limits in $H$ give its product limit. Thus this is a Hilbert space. The family $(e_j,0),(0,e_j)$ is orthonormal, and any vector orthogonal to every listed vector has both components orthogonal to every $e_j$, hence both components are zero by completeness; it is a complete orthonormal basis. Let $D\subseteq H$ be countable and dense. The balls $B(d,s)$ with $d\in D$ and positive rational $s$ form a countable base for $H$: for $x\in U$ open, choose $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subseteq U$, then $d\in D$ with $\|d-x\|<r/3$ and rational $s$ with $\|d-x\|<s<r-\|d-x\|$. Thus $H$ is second-countable. Then $D\times D$ is countable by [F2] and dense, since each coordinate of a pair can be approximated within $\varepsilon/2$ to make the product norm error less than $\varepsilon$. Balls with centers in $D\times D$ and positive rational radii form a countable base: for $z$ in an open set choose $r>0$ with $B(z,r)$ contained there, then a center $d$ with $\|d-z\|<r/3$ and rational $s$ with $\|d-z\|<s<r-\|d-z\|$ give $z\in B(d,s)\subseteq B(z,r)$. Thus $H\times H$ is second-countable, and [F10] identifies its Borel sigma-algebra with the product Borel sigma-algebra. Since $U$ and $\xi$ are Borel random elements, the pair $(U,\xi)$ is measurable into the product sigma-algebra: the preimage of each measurable rectangle is the intersection of the two coordinate preimages, and rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra. Continuous addition and scalar multiplication then make $(U,V)$ and $(V,U)$ Borel random elements of $H\times H$. Their Borel laws are therefore defined.

Fix a finite list of continuous linear functionals on $H\times H$. Each has the form $(u,v)\mapsto\ell(u)+m(v)$, because its restrictions to the two coordinate subspaces sum to the functional. Any real linear combination of the listed projections is another such functional. Under $(U,V)$ that combination is $(\ell+\rho m)(U)+\beta m(\xi)$; under $(V,U)$ it is $(\rho\ell+m)(U)+\beta\ell(\xi)$. By [F3], the two summands in each display are centered normal, and [F5] makes them independent; [F6] makes their sum normal, including a zero coefficient. Hence every finite projection vector under either pair is multivariate normal by the projection definition in [F7], with zero mean.

Define the symmetric covariance form $\Gamma(\ell,m)=\mathbb E[\ell(U)m(U)]$. These products are integrable: [F4] gives finite second moments of $\|U\|$, boundedness of $\ell,m$ gives finite second moments of their evaluations, and $|ab|\le(a^2+b^2)/2$. The same argument applies to evaluations of $\xi$. For functionals $(\ell,m)$ and $(\ell',m')$, the projection under $(U,V)$ is $(\ell+\rho m)(U)+\beta m(\xi)$. Independence and centering make its mixed covariance terms zero by [F9], so its covariance with the corresponding projection for $(\ell',m')$ is $$\Gamma(\ell,\ell')+\rho\Gamma(\ell,m')+\rho\Gamma(m,\ell')+\Gamma(m,m'),$$ using $\rho^2+\beta^2=1$. Under $(V,U)$ the projections are $(\rho\ell+m)(U)+\beta\ell(\xi)$ and $(\rho\ell'+m')(U)+\beta\ell'(\xi)$; expansion gives the same expression because $\Gamma$ is symmetric. Therefore the finite projection vectors from step 2.1 have equal covariance matrices and zero means.

By [F7], the finite projection laws in step 3.1 are equal, in particular the finite coordinate laws for the product basis from step 1.1. That step also shows that $H\times H$ is a separable Hilbert space. By [A1], Countable Choice follows from AC; the coordinate-law result [F8] therefore identifies the two Borel probability laws. Hence $\operatorname{Law}(U,V)=\operatorname{Law}(V,U)$.
Step 4.1 is the claimed invariance of the joint law under coordinate swap, for every $\beta\in[0,1]$, including the identity proposal at $\beta=0$ and the independent-reference proposal at $\beta=1$.

current_manifest_record.title: The pCN accept-reject kernel preserves the posterior
current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the inputs of the prior-preserving
Crank–Nicolson algorithm: a separable real Hilbert space $H$, centered Borel
Gaussian reference probability $\mu_0$, full-mass Borel domain $D$, Borel
potential $\Phi_D:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]$, positive finite evidence $Z$, and
scale $\beta\in[0,1]$. Let $\mu$ be the normalized target on $H$ obtained by
extending $\Phi_D$ by $+\infty$ off $D$, and let $P_\beta$ be the algorithm's
accept-reject transition. Then $P_\beta$ is reversible with respect to $\mu$:
its joint flow
$$\Lambda_\beta(C):=\int_H P_\beta(u,C_u)\,\mu(du),\qquad C_u:=\{v\in H:(u,v)\in C\},$$
is unchanged by $(u,v)\mapsto(v,u)$ for every Borel
$C\subseteq H\times H$. Consequently, $\mu$ is invariant:
$$\int_H P_\beta(u,A)\,\mu(du)=\mu(A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal B(H)).$$
This conclusion gives invariance only; it does not assert uniqueness,
convergence, mixing, an effective-sample-size bound, mesh-independent cost,
or correctness of an approximate forward solver.
current_manifest_record.axiom_use: AC is inherited from the pCN Gaussian-reference algorithm. The symmetric-flow argument uses no further choice principle.
