citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let
$\mu_0$ be a centered Borel Gaussian probability measure on $H$, let
$D\subseteq H$ be Borel with $\mu_0(D)=1$, and let
$\Phi_D:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be Borel. Assume the evidence
$$
Z:=\int_D e^{-\Phi_D(u)}\,\mu_0(du)
$$
satisfies $0<Z<\infty$. Extend the potential to all of $H$ by setting
$\bar\Phi(u)=\Phi_D(u)$ for $u\in D$ and $\bar\Phi(u)=+\infty$ for
$u\notin D$, and define the target probability
$\mu(du)=Z^{-1}e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}\mu_0(du)$. For a scale $\beta\in[0,1]$,
write $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$. At state $u\in H$, draw $\xi\sim\mu_0$
independently and propose $v=\rho u+\beta\xi$. Set the acceptance probability
to $0$ if either $\bar\Phi(u)$ or $\bar\Phi(v)$ is $+\infty$, and otherwise set
$$
\alpha(u,v)=\min\{1,\exp(\bar\Phi(u)-\bar\Phi(v))\}.
$$
Draw an independent uniform random variable on $[0,1]$ and move to $v$ if it
is at most $\alpha(u,v)$; otherwise remain at $u$. The resulting one-step
transition rule is the prior-preserving Crank–Nicolson, or pCN, rule
$P_\beta$. States with infinite potential are absorbing under this total
definition; they have $\mu$-measure zero.

Under the inputs and instructions of the prior-preserving Crank–Nicolson
algorithm, for every $\beta\in[0,1]$ its proposal rule is a Borel probability
kernel and its accept-reject transition $P_\beta$ is a Borel probability
kernel on $H$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let
$\mu_0$ be a centered Borel Gaussian probability measure on $H$, let
$D\subseteq H$ be Borel with $\mu_0(D)=1$, and let
$\Phi_D:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be Borel. Assume the evidence
$$
Z:=\int_D e^{-\Phi_D(u)}\,\mu_0(du)
$$
satisfies $0<Z<\infty$. Extend the potential to all of $H$ by setting
$\bar\Phi(u)=\Phi_D(u)$ for $u\in D$ and $\bar\Phi(u)=+\infty$ for
$u\notin D$, and define the target probability
$\mu(du)=Z^{-1}e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}\mu_0(du)$. For a scale $\beta\in[0,1]$,
write $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$. At state $u\in H$, draw $\xi\sim\mu_0$
independently and propose $v=\rho u+\beta\xi$. Set the acceptance probability
to $0$ if either $\bar\Phi(u)$ or $\bar\Phi(v)$ is $+\infty$, and otherwise set
$$
\alpha(u,v)=\min\{1,\exp(\bar\Phi(u)-\bar\Phi(v))\}.
$$
Draw an independent uniform random variable on $[0,1]$ and move to $v$ if it
is at most $\alpha(u,v)$; otherwise remain at $u$. The resulting one-step
transition rule is the prior-preserving Crank–Nicolson, or pCN, rule
$P_\beta$. States with infinite potential are absorbing under this total
definition; they have $\mu$-measure zero.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space and let
$\mu_0$ be a centered Borel Gaussian probability measure on $H$. Let $U$ and
$\xi$ be independent random elements with law $\mu_0$. For
$\beta\in[0,1]$, set $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$ and
$V=\rho U+\beta\xi$. The joint Borel law of $(U,V)$ on $H\times H$ is
unchanged by the coordinate swap $(u,v)\mapsto(v,u)$.

Let $X,Y$ be second-countable topological spaces and give $X\times Y$ the
product topology. Then
$$\mathcal B(X\times Y)=\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y).$$

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   The product measure of two sigma-finite measure spaces is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. Then the following are
equivalent:

1. the family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent;
2. for every natural number $n\ge1$, every choice of distinct indices
   $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}\in I$, and every choice of measurable sets
   $B_k\in\Sigma_{i_k}$,
   $$\mathbb P\bigl(X_{i_0}\in B_0,\dots,X_{i_{n-1}}\in B_{n-1}\bigr)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(X_{i_k}\in B_k).$$

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
Independent sigma-algebras and independent events.

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from The sigma-algebra generated by a function.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
Measurable rectangles in a product of measurable spaces.

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a measurable space, let $P$ be a probability
kernel on it, meaning that $P(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure for each $x$
and $x\mapsto P(x,A)$ is measurable for each $A\in\mathcal X$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure, that is a countably additive measure of total mass one
([[def-probability-measure]]). The product sigma-algebra
$\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$ is generated by measurable rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The joint
flow measure of $(\pi,P)$ is the probability measure $\Lambda_{\pi,P}$ on
$(\mathsf X\times\mathsf X,\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X)$ given, for each
$C\in\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$, by

$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}(C):=\int_{\mathsf X}P(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x:=\{y\in\mathsf X:(x,y)\in C\}.$$

Existence, countable additivity, and the nonnegative iterated-integral identity
for this measure follow from
[[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. Let $\tau(x,y):=(y,x)$ be
the coordinate-swap map. It is measurable because the preimage of a measurable
rectangle $A\times B$ is $B\times A$ and such rectangles generate the product
sigma-algebra. Define the transpose measure by
$\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}(C):=\Lambda_{\pi,P}(\tau^{-1}(C))$.

The kernel $P$ is **reversible with respect to $\pi$** when
$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}=\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}.$$
This definition uses equality of measures and requires no density, standard
Borel assumption, or prior assumption that $\pi$ is invariant.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a measurable space, $P$ a probability kernel
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) on it, and $\pi$ a probability
measure ([[def-probability-measure]]) on it. If $P$ is reversible with
respect to $\pi$ in the sense of
[[def-general-state-reversibility-by-symmetric-flow-measure]], then $\pi$ is
invariant for $P$: for every $A\in\mathcal X$,

$$\int_{\mathsf X}P(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A).$$

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ (Dense, nowhere dense and codense subsets of a topological space, and the criterion by basic open sets, Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

A topological space $X$ is **second countable** when its topology has a basis $\mathcal B$ that is at most countable (Basis and subbasis for a topology, and the topology generated by a family of sets, Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable). Thus every open set is a union of members of one at most countable family $\mathcal B$.

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ (The real numbers) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Let $A$ be at most countable ([[def-countable]]) and let $B \subseteq A$. Then
$B$ is at most countable.

The proof establishes the sharper statement about subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ from
which this follows: **a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is finite if it is
bounded above, and countably infinite if it is not.**

**No choice principle is used.** This is the point of the lemma rather than a
footnote to it. The enumeration of an unbounded $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is built
by always taking the *least* element of $S$ above the previous one, and the least
element of a nonempty set of naturals is canonical
([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]): it is determined by $S$, not selected from it.
Replacing "least" by "some" would turn the construction into an appeal to
dependent choice.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ whose induced-length metric is complete: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm (Banach space).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
Banach space defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ (Order on the reals). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Ordered field):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric (Nonnegativity of a metric is a consequence of the other axioms, not an axiom) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear (Isometry, isometric embedding, and the subspace metric on a subset): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ (Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is Topologically, uniformly and Lipschitz equivalent metrics on a set.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open and closed sets
as in [[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]]. Then:

1. **Balls are open.** $B(x,r)$ is open, for every $x \in X$ and every $r > 0$.
2. **Arbitrary unions.** If $\mathcal{U}$ is any collection of open subsets of
   $X$, then $\bigcup \mathcal{U}$ is open.
3. **Finite intersections.** If $n \ge 1$ and $U_0, \dots, U_{n-1}$ are open,
   then $U_0 \cap \dots \cap U_{n-1}$ is open.
4. **Closed balls are closed.** $\bar B(x,r)$ is closed, for every $x \in X$ and
   every $r > 0$.

Together with the fact that $\emptyset$ and $X$ are open, recorded already in
[[def-metric-topology]], claims 2 and 3 say that $\mathcal{T}_d$ has exactly the
closure properties that the word *topology* names.

Let $X,Y$ be second-countable topological spaces and give $X\times Y$ the
product topology. Then
$$\mathcal B(X\times Y)=\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y).$$

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

derivations.claim: AC is assumed as recorded in [A1]. By [F9], $H$ is second-countable and the Borel sigma-algebra of $H\times H$ is the product sigma-algebra. Put $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$ and let $\Lambda_0(du,dv)=\mu_0(du)Q_\beta(u,dv)$ be the joint flow of the reference probability and proposal kernel. It exists by [F4]. Take the product probability space $(H\times H,\mu_0\otimes\mu_0)$ and its coordinate random elements $U_0,\xi$; [F6] gives their independence and common law $\mu_0$. For every nonnegative product-Borel $h$, the iterated-integral identity in [F4] and [F1] give $$\int h\,d\Lambda_0=\int_H\int_H h(u,\rho u+\beta z)\,\mu_0(dz)\,\mu_0(du)=\mathbb E[h(U_0,\rho U_0+\beta\xi)],$$ where the proposal-row pushforward and the change-of-variables identity [F5] identify the flow integral with expectation under $U_0\sim\mu_0$, and the product joint law [F6] together with the measurable proposal map identifies that expectation with the displayed one. Thus $\Lambda_0$ is the law in [F3], so $\Lambda_0$ is symmetric.

Define $w(u)=e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}$ and $m(u,v)=\min\{w(u),w(v)\}$. For every $(u,v)$, if both potential values are finite, then $$w(u)\alpha(u,v)=e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}\min\{1,e^{\bar\Phi(u)-\bar\Phi(v)}\}=\min\{e^{-\bar\Phi(u)},e^{-\bar\Phi(v)}\}=m(u,v).$$ If either value is $+\infty$, the algorithm sets $\alpha(u,v)=0$ and $m(u,v)=0$, so the identity still holds. In particular, $m$ is a symmetric nonnegative Borel function.

Set $r(u)=1-a(u)\in[0,1]$. The diagonal map $d(u)=(u,u)$ is continuous from $H$ into the product topology on $H\times H$, so by [F10] it is Borel. Thus $u\mapsto\mathbf1_C(u,u)=\mathbf1_C(d(u))$ is measurable for every Borel $C\subseteq H\times H$. By the diagonal term in [F1] and the joint-flow formula [F4], the rejection part of the target joint flow has mass on $C$ $$\Lambda_{\rm rej}(C)=\int_H\mathbf1_C(u,u)r(u)\,\mu(du).$$ It is symmetric because $\tau(d(u))=d(u)$ for every $u$: for every Borel $C$, $\mathbf1_{\tau^{-1}C}(u,u)=\mathbf1_C(u,u)$.

For Borel $C\subseteq H\times H$, the accepted part of the target joint flow is $$\Lambda_{\rm acc}(C):=\int_H\int_H\mathbf1_C(u,v)\alpha(u,v)Q_\beta(u,dv)\,\mu(du)=Z^{-1}\int_{H\times H}\mathbf1_C(u,v)m(u,v)\,\Lambda_0(du,dv).$$ The equality follows from the target density in [F2], identity 1.2, and the iterated-integral formula [F4]. Since $\Lambda_0$ is symmetric by step 1.1 and $m(u,v)=m(v,u)$, this accepted measure is symmetric. Indeed, for $\tau(u,v)=(v,u)$, the change-of-variables identity [F5] gives $$\int\mathbf1_C(u,v)m(u,v)\,d\Lambda_0=\int\mathbf1_C(v,u)m(v,u)\,d\Lambda_0=\int\mathbf1_{\tau^{-1}C}(u,v)m(u,v)\,d\Lambda_0.$$ Equality for every Borel $C$ is symmetry under $\tau$.

By the decomposition of $P_\beta$ in [F1] and the joint-flow identity [F4], $\Lambda_\beta=\Lambda_{\rm acc}+\Lambda_{\rm rej}$. The accepted and rejection pieces are symmetric by steps 2.1 and 1.3, hence $\Lambda_\beta$ is symmetric. By [F7], $P_\beta$ is reversible with respect to $\mu$.

The hypotheses of [F8] hold: [F1] gives a probability kernel and the algorithm gives the probability measure $\mu$. Therefore [F8] yields $\int_H P_\beta(u,A)\,\mu(du)=\mu(A)$ for every Borel $A$. The proof uses only the symmetric-flow identity; it establishes no uniqueness or convergence claim.

current_manifest_record.title: Infinite-dimensional Gaussian random-walk reverse flow is singular
current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix $\beta\in(0,1]$. Let
$H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ with its complete coordinate basis positively indexed as $(e_j)_{j\ge1}$, where $e_j$ has its nonzero coordinate at $j-1$. Write $u_j=\langle u,e_j\rangle$ for coefficients in this basis throughout. Take
mutually independent standard normal variables $(X_j,Y_j)_{j\ge1}$ and set
$$U=\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-j/2}X_je_j,\qquad \xi=\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-j/2}Y_je_j.$$
These series converge almost surely in $H$ and define independent centered
Borel Gaussian random elements with the same law $\mu_0$. Define the Gaussian
random-walk proposal $V=U+\beta\xi$, its probability kernel
$$Q_\beta(u,B)=\mu_0(\{z\in H:u+\beta z\in B\}),$$
its forward flow $\eta(du,dv)=\mu_0(du)Q_\beta(u,dv)$, and its transpose
$\eta^\top(C)=\eta(\{(u,v):(v,u)\in C\})$. Then $\eta$ and $\eta^\top$ are
mutually singular: a Borel set $A_\beta\subseteq H\times H$ satisfies
$$\eta(A_\beta)=1,\qquad \eta^\top(A_\beta)=0.$$
For the same reference law and scale, the pCN proposal flow is symmetric.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. Every probability measure $\nu$
on $(S,\Sigma)$ is the common law of a countable independent family of
$S$-valued random elements.

Let $H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ with its canonical real inner product, and for each $j\in\mathbb N$ let $e_j$ be the sequence whose $j$th coordinate is $1$ and whose other coordinates are $0$. Then $(e_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H$. For every $x=(x_j)\in H$, the truncations $\sum_{j<N} x_je_j$ converge in $H$ to $x$ as $N\to\infty$ (the $N=0$ sum is empty and equals $0$), and $\|x\|_2^2=\sum_{j\in\mathbb N}|x_j|^2$.

Let $H_0$ and $H_1$ be separable real Hilbert spaces with a continuous inclusion $H_1\hookrightarrow H_0$. Let $(e_j)_{j\ge1}$ be an orthonormal basis of $H_0$ that is a complete orthogonal basis of $H_1$, write $w_j=\|e_j\|_{H_1}^2>0$, and set $f_j=e_j/\sqrt{w_j}$, so $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ is an orthonormal basis of $H_1$. Let $(\xi_j)_{j\ge1}$ be independent real random variables on one probability space with $\mathbb E\xi_j=0$ and $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$, and let $\lambda_j\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j<\infty$. Then
$$S_N=\sum_{j=1}^N\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,\xi_j e_j$$
converges almost surely in $H_1$ and in $L^2(\Omega;H_1)$ to an $H_1$-valued Borel-measurable random element $S$, with
$$\mathbb E\|S\|_{H_1}^2=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j.$$
These norm-convergence conclusions use no choice axiom beyond the supplied probability space and variables. For the following Gaussian conclusions, assume in addition that each $\xi_j$ has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. Under the Axiom of Choice and countable choice, $S$ is a centered Borel Gaussian random element in $H_1$. Its covariance map $C:H_1^*\to H_1$, transported to $H_1$ by the Hilbert-space Riesz identification, is diagonal in the basis $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_jw_j$, and these eigenvalues are summable. If $D$ is a Borel forward-map domain in $H_1$ and $\mathbb P(S\in D)=1$, then the law of $S$ is a prior on $D$. Under the Axiom of Choice there is $a>0$ such that
$$\mathbb E\exp\!\bigl(a\|S\|_{H_1}^2\bigr)<\infty.$$

Let $H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ with its canonical real inner product, and for each $j\in\mathbb N$ let $e_j$ be the sequence whose $j$th coordinate is $1$ and whose other coordinates are $0$. Then $(e_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H$. For every $x=(x_j)\in H$, the truncations $\sum_{j<N} x_je_j$ converge in $H$ to $x$ as $N\to\infty$ (the $N=0$ sum is empty and equals $0$), and $\|x\|_2^2=\sum_{j\in\mathbb N}|x_j|^2$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
Independent sigma-algebras and independent events.

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from The sigma-algebra generated by a function.

Let $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of sigma-algebras on a
probability space, and let $J_0,\dots,J_{m-1}\subseteq I$ be pairwise disjoint
index sets. For each $r<m$, define

$$\mathcal G_r:=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{i\in J_r}\mathcal F_i\right).$$

Then the sigma-algebras $\mathcal G_0,\dots,\mathcal G_{m-1}$ are independent.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma\ge0$, and a real random variable
$X$ with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$,
$$E[X]=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$

Assume AC and let $G\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ for $\sigma\ge0$. Then $\mathbb E[G^2]=\sigma^2$ and $\mathbb E[G^4]=3\sigma^4$; in particular the fourth moment is finite. For independent centered normal coordinates $G_j\sim N(0,\sigma_j^2)$, every finite linear combination of the variables $G_j^2$ has finite second moment.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in Law or distribution of a random element agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in Independent random elements. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.
IID square-integrable real variables satisfy $S_n/n\to\mathbb EX_1$ almost surely.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from A total pointwise product for extended-real-valued functions, and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
The positive and negative parts of a function. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ with its canonical real inner product, and for each $j\in\mathbb N$ let $e_j$ be the sequence whose $j$th coordinate is $1$ and whose other coordinates are $0$. Then $(e_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H$. For every $x=(x_j)\in H$, the truncations $\sum_{j<N} x_je_j$ converge in $H$ to $x$ as $N\to\infty$ (the $N=0$ sum is empty and equals $0$), and $\|x\|_2^2=\sum_{j\in\mathbb N}|x_j|^2$.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

Let $A$ be at most countable ([[def-countable]]) and let $B \subseteq A$. Then
$B$ is at most countable.

The proof establishes the sharper statement about subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ from
which this follows: **a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is finite if it is
bounded above, and countably infinite if it is not.**

**No choice principle is used.** This is the point of the lemma rather than a
footnote to it. The enumeration of an unbounded $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is built
by always taking the *least* element of $S$ above the previous one, and the least
element of a nonempty set of naturals is canonical
([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]): it is determined by $S$, not selected from it.
Replacing "least" by "some" would turn the construction into an appeal to
dependent choice.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a family of at most countable sets
([[def-countable]]) indexed by $\mathbb{N}$. Then

$$U = \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_n$$

is at most countable.

**The role of $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.** It is spent at exactly one step, step 3.1 below, where a surjection $\mathbb N\to A_n$ is selected simultaneously for each nonempty $A_n$. The individual countability hypotheses assert that these sets of surjections are nonempty; they specify no simultaneous selection.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ (The real numbers) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ (Dense, nowhere dense and codense subsets of a topological space, and the criterion by basic open sets, Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

A topological space $X$ is **second countable** when its topology has a basis $\mathcal B$ that is at most countable (Basis and subbasis for a topology, and the topology generated by a family of sets, Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable). Thus every open set is a union of members of one at most countable family $\mathcal B$.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ (Order on the reals). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Ordered field):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric (Nonnegativity of a metric is a consequence of the other axioms, not an axiom) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear (Isometry, isometric embedding, and the subspace metric on a subset): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ (Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is Topologically, uniformly and Lipschitz equivalent metrics on a set.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open and closed sets
as in [[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]]. Then:

1. **Balls are open.** $B(x,r)$ is open, for every $x \in X$ and every $r > 0$.
2. **Arbitrary unions.** If $\mathcal{U}$ is any collection of open subsets of
   $X$, then $\bigcup \mathcal{U}$ is open.
3. **Finite intersections.** If $n \ge 1$ and $U_0, \dots, U_{n-1}$ are open,
   then $U_0 \cap \dots \cap U_{n-1}$ is open.
4. **Closed balls are closed.** $\bar B(x,r)$ is closed, for every $x \in X$ and
   every $r > 0$.

Together with the fact that $\emptyset$ and $X$ are open, recorded already in
[[def-metric-topology]], claims 2 and 3 say that $\mathcal{T}_d$ has exactly the
closure properties that the word *topology* names.

Let $X,Y$ be second-countable topological spaces and give $X\times Y$ the
product topology. Then
$$\mathcal B(X\times Y)=\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y).$$

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space and let
$\mu_0$ be a centered Borel Gaussian probability measure on $H$. Let $U$ and
$\xi$ be independent random elements with law $\mu_0$. For
$\beta\in[0,1]$, set $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$ and
$V=\rho U+\beta\xi$. The joint Borel law of $(U,V)$ on $H\times H$ is
unchanged by the coordinate swap $(u,v)\mapsto(v,u)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most

In ZF,

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space with a
finite or countable complete orthonormal basis $(e_j)_{j\in J}$. For each finite
$F\subseteq J$, define the coordinate map
$\pi_F:H\to\mathbb R^F$ by
$\pi_F(x)=(\langle x,e_j\rangle)_{j\in F}$. If $\nu$ and $\nu'$ are Borel

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F1], take a countable independent sequence $(Z_n)_{n\ge1}$ with law $N(0,1)$ and put $X_j=Z_{2j-1}$, $Y_j=Z_{2j}$. Each subsequence is again IID standard normal. The odd and even coordinate sigma-algebras are independent by [F4]. Apply [F3] with $H_0=H_1=H$, $w_j=1$, and $\lambda_j=2^{-j}$ to each subsequence. Since $\sum_j2^{-j}=1$, both series converge almost surely in $H$ and define centered Borel Gaussian random elements. Their finite coordinate laws agree: by [F3], each finite coordinate vector is obtained by multiplying independent standard normals by the same coefficients $2^{-j/2}$, so each vector has the same product normal law by [F5] and [F9]. AC implies Countable Choice by [A1], so [F13] identifies their Borel laws. Each limit is measurable with respect to its own coordinate sigma-algebra: its partial sums are block-measurable, the event that they are Cauchy is a countable combination of measurable norm inequalities, and the limit, set to zero on the null complement, is therefore block-measurable. In detail, for a proper open $O\subset H$ with closed complement $C$, on the convergence event the preimage of $O$ is the condition $\liminf_N\operatorname{dist}(S_N,C)>0$; the distance function is 1-Lipschitz, and the zero value assigned off that event is included exactly when $0\in O$. This is a measurable condition on the block. The odd and even coordinate sigma-algebras are independent by [F4], hence $U$ and $\xi$ are independent. Denote their common law by $\mu_0$.

For $(u,v)\in H\times H$, set $$f_n(u,v):=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n2^j(v_j^2-u_j^2),\qquad A_\beta:=\left\{(u,v):f_n(u,v)\to\beta^2\right\}.$$ Each coordinate map is continuous since $|u_j-v_j|\le\|u-v\|_2$ by [F2]; finite arithmetic operations make $f_n$ Borel by [F10]. Explicitly, $$A_\beta=\bigcap_{k=1}^\infty\bigcup_{N=1}^\infty\bigcap_{n=N}^\infty\{|f_n-\beta^2|<1/k\},$$ so $A_\beta$ is Borel by [F10]. The limit criterion follows because for every $\varepsilon>0$ one can choose $k$ with $1/k<\varepsilon$.

For each $u\in H$, $Q_\beta(u,\cdot)$ is the pushforward of $\mu_0$ under the continuous map $z\mapsto u+\beta z$, hence is a probability measure. By [F11], $H$ is second-countable and the product Borel sigma-algebra is $\mathcal B(H)\otimes\mathcal B(H)$. For Borel $B\subseteq H$, addition and scalar multiplication make $(u,z)\mapsto u+\beta z$ continuous, so $(u,z)\mapsto\mathbf1_B(u+\beta z)$ is product-measurable. Integrating it against the constant kernel $u\mapsto\mu_0$ is measurable by [F11], so $Q_\beta$ is a probability kernel. Its joint flow $\eta$ exists by [F8]. By the product joint law [F9] and the proposal pushforward, $\eta$ is the law of $(U,U+\beta\xi)$.

For each $j$, define $$D_j:=2^j\bigl((U+\beta\xi)_j^2-U_j^2\bigr)=(X_j+\beta Y_j)^2-X_j^2=2\beta X_jY_j+\beta^2Y_j^2.$$ The pairs $(X_j,Y_j)$ are independent by grouping the independent coordinates, and have the same product standard-normal law by [F9]. Applying the same polynomial map to each pair therefore makes $(D_j)$ IID by [F4] and [F9]. By [F5]–[F6], $\mathbb E[X_jY_j]=\mathbb E[X_j]\mathbb E[Y_j]=0$, $\mathbb E[Y_j^2]=1$, and $$\mathbb E[D_j]=\beta^2.$$ They are square-integrable: using $(a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2$, $$\mathbb E[D_j^2]\le8\beta^2\mathbb E[X_j^2Y_j^2]+2\beta^4\mathbb E[Y_j^4]=8\beta^2+6\beta^4<\infty,$$ where independence gives $\mathbb E[X_j^2Y_j^2]=1$ and [F5] gives $\mathbb E[Y_j^4]=3$. By [F7], $$\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^nD_j\longrightarrow\beta^2\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

Under the forward flow $\eta$, the pair has the law of $(U,V)$ from step 2.1, and $f_n(U,V)=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^nD_j$. Step 2.2 therefore gives $\eta(A_\beta)=1$. Under the transpose $\eta^\top$, the pair has the law of $(V,U)$, and $f_n(V,U)=-f_n(U,V)\to-\beta^2$. Since $\beta>0$, $-\beta^2\ne\beta^2$, hence $\eta^\top(A_\beta)=0$.

Thus $A_\beta$ and its complement are disjoint Borel sets with $\eta(A_\beta)=1$ and $\eta^\top(A_\beta^c)=1$. This is mutual singularity of the two probability measures, and in particular neither is absolutely continuous with respect to the other. By [F12], the pCN reference proposal flow at this same scale equals its transpose.

Let $X,Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be open, and let $F:U\to Y$ be Fréchet differentiable at every point with a derivative map $F':U\to\mathcal B(X,Y)$ that is continuous in operator norm. This is the real-Hilbert forward-map convention. Assume Countable Choice, so every bounded derivative $F'(x)$ has the Hilbert adjoint $F'(x)^*:Y\to X$ characterized by $\langle F'(x)u,v\rangle_Y=\langle u,F'(x)^*v\rangle_X$.

An **admissible local instance** consists of an initial point $x_0\in U$, a radius $r>0$, an exact solution $x^\dagger\in\overline B_r(x_0):=\{x\in X:\|x-x_0\|_X\le r\}$ with exact datum $y=F(x^\dagger)$, a noise level $\delta\ge0$, noisy datum $y^\delta\in Y$ with $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$, a constant $0\le\eta<1/2$, a discrepancy parameter $\tau>2(1+\eta)/(1-2\eta)$, and a finite update budget $M\in\mathbb N_0$. The closed outer ball $\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$ is contained in $U$; $\|F'(x)\|\le1$ for every $x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$; and the uniform two-point tangential-cone inequality

$$
\|F(x)-F(\widetilde x)-F'(x)(x-\widetilde x)\|_Y\le\eta\|F(x)-F(\widetilde x)\|_Y
$$

holds for every $x,\widetilde x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$. This is the uniform family of the one-basepoint local tangential-cone inequality; the shared constant and pair domain are part of the admissibility hypothesis. The exact solution and the bounds are analysis data and need not be available to the computational loop.

**Inputs:** $F$, $x_0$, $y^\delta$, $\delta$, $\tau$, and $M$ from an admissible local instance.

**Output:** Either `stopped` with an index $k$, iterate $x_k^\delta$, and residual $\|y^\delta-F(x_k^\delta)\|_Y$, or `budget_exhausted` with the last iterate and its residual.

**Procedure:** Set $x_0^\delta:=x_0$. For $k=0,1,\ldots,M$, compute $r_k^\delta:=\|y^\delta-F(x_k^\delta)\|_Y$. If $r_k^\delta\le\tau\delta$, return `stopped` with $(k,x_k^\delta,r_k^\delta)$. If $k=M$, return `budget_exhausted` with $(k,x_k^\delta,r_k^\delta)$. Otherwise set

$$
x_{k+1}^\delta:=x_k^\delta+F'(x_k^\delta)^*(y^\delta-F(x_k^\delta))
$$

and continue at the next index. Each update is evaluated at a current point in $U$, where the derivative and its Hilbert adjoint are defined.

Let $X,Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be open, and let $F:U\to Y$ be Fréchet differentiable at $x\in U$. For $\delta>0$ such that the closed ball

$$\overline B_\delta(x):=\{x+h:h\in X,\ \|h\|_X\le\delta\}$$

is contained in $U$, the **local tangential cone condition at $x$ on radius $\delta$ with constant $\eta$** holds if $0\le\eta<1$ and

$$\|F(x+h)-F(x)-F'(x)h\|_Y\le\eta\,\|F(x+h)-F(x)\|_Y\qquad(\|h\|_X\le\delta).$$

Let $X,Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be open, and let $F:U\to Y$ be Fréchet differentiable at every point with $F':U\to\mathcal B(X,Y)$ continuous in operator norm. Fix $x_0\in U$ and $r>0$ such that $\overline B_{2r}(x_0)\subseteq U$, and suppose an exact solution $x^\dagger\in\overline B_r(x_0)$ satisfies $y=F(x^\dagger)$. Assume $\|F'(x)\|\le1$ for every $x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$ and that, for some $0\le\eta<1/2$,

$$
\|F(x)-F(\widetilde x)-F'(x)(x-\widetilde x)\|_Y\le\eta\|F(x)-F(\widetilde x)\|_Y
$$

for every $x,\widetilde x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$. This is a uniform two-point hypothesis with the derivative based at the first point. Assume Countable Choice so that the bounded derivatives have Hilbert adjoints. For $\delta\ge0$ and $y^\delta\in Y$ with $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$, set $x_0^\delta=x_0$ and define the ideal Landweber sequence by

$$
x_{n+1}^\delta=x_n^\delta+F'(x_n^\delta)^*(y^\delta-F(x_n^\delta)).
$$

Let $\tau>2(1+\eta)/(1-2\eta)$. For $\delta>0$, let $N(\delta,y^\delta)$ denote the first $n\in\mathbb N_0$ with $\|y^\delta-F(x_n^\delta)\|_Y\le\tau\delta$, if it exists. Put $d_0=\|x_0-x^\dagger\|_X$ and $c_\tau=1-2\eta-2(1+\eta)/\tau>0$. Then the following hold.

1. For every update before the first discrepancy stop, writing $R_n^\delta=\|y^\delta-F(x_n^\delta)\|_Y$, the squared-error estimate is

   $$
   \|x_{n+1}^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X^2-\|x_n^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X^2\le R_n^\delta\bigl(2(1+\eta)\delta-(1-2\eta)R_n^\delta\bigr).
   $$

   In particular, the iterates are Fejér monotone relative to $x^\dagger$ up to the stop: their distance to $x^\dagger$ does not increase. Here Fejér monotonicity means exactly this nonincrease of distance to the stated solution.

2. If $\delta>0$, the first discrepancy index exists and

   $$
   N(\delta,y^\delta)<C\delta^{-2},\qquad C:=1+\frac{d_0^2}{c_\tau\tau^2}.
   $$

   A run of the finite-budget algorithm with budget $M\ge N(\delta,y^\delta)$ returns `stopped` at this first index; if $M<N(\delta,y^\delta)$, it returns `budget_exhausted` at $M$.

3. For exact data ($\delta=0$ and $y^\delta=y$), the ideal sequence is defined for every $n$, satisfies

   $$
   (1-2\eta)\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\|F(x_n)-y\|_Y^2\le d_0^2,
   $$

   and converges strongly to some $\bar x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$ with $F(\bar x)=y$. No finite stopping index is claimed in the exact-data case.

4. For noisy data ($\delta>0$), the ideal stopped iterates converge uniformly over the admissible noise ball to that same exact-data limit:

   $$
   \lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\ \sup_{\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta}\|x_{N(\delta,y^\delta)}^\delta-\bar x\|_X=0.
   $$

   For finite-budget runs this conclusion concerns outputs only when their budgets reach the first discrepancy indices. The theorem asserts neither a convergence rate nor that $\bar x$ is an $x_0$-minimum-norm solution.

derivations.claim: For every $x,h\in\mathbb R$, $F(x+h)-F(x)-2xh=h^2$, so $F$ is Fréchet differentiable with $F'(x)h=2xh$. Thus $F(1)=0=y$ is an exact solution and $F'(x_0)=F'(0)=0$. The Landweber update in [F1] gives $x_1=0$; induction gives $x_n=0$ and residual $|y-F(x_n)|=1$ for every $n$. The exact-data iterates therefore do not converge to a solution.

For any proposed local radius $\delta>0$, choose $h=\delta/2>0$. At $x_0=0$, $F(h)-F(0)=h^2$ and $F'(0)h=0$, so [F2] would require $h^2\le\eta h^2$. Since $h^2>0$, this forces $\eta\ge1$. Thus no local TCC ball at this initial point has a constant $\eta<1/2$, violating the theorem's retained local hypothesis [F3].

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $\Omega=B_1(0)\subset\mathbb R^3$, fix $0<\rho<1$ and $0<m<1<M$, and let $E$ be the closed real subspace of $L^\infty(\Omega)$ consisting of functions vanishing almost everywhere outside $B_\rho(0)$. Set $\mathcal A=\{a\in E:\operatorname*{ess\,inf}(1+a)>m,\ \operatorname*{ess\,sup}(1+a)<M\}$ and $\sigma=1+a$. Choose an orthonormal spherical-harmonic basis $Y_{\ell k}$ of mean-zero $L^2(S^2)$, with $\ell\ge1$ and $1\le k\le2\ell+1$. For each basis current there is a unique weak solution $u_{\sigma,\ell k}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with boundary mean zero such that
$$\int_\Omega\sigma\nabla u_{\sigma,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla v}=\int_{S^2}Y_{\ell k}\overline{\operatorname{Tr}v}\qquad(v\in H^1(\Omega)).$$
The centered sequence
$$G(a):=\big(\operatorname{Tr}(u_{\sigma,\ell k}-u_{1,\ell k})\big)_{\ell,k}$$
belongs to $Y=\ell^2(L^2(S^2))$. The map $G:\mathcal A\to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable, and both $G$ and $G'$ are Lipschitz on $\mathcal A$, with constants depending only on $m,M,\rho$ and the ball. Its derivative in direction $h\in E$ is the trace sequence of the unique boundary-mean-zero solutions
$$\int_\Omega\sigma\nabla v_{h,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla w}=-\int_\Omega h\nabla u_{\sigma,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla w}.$$
The uncentered sequence $(\operatorname{Tr}u_{1,\ell k})_{\ell,k}$ does not belong to $Y$. Thus absolute voltage data in this convention lie in an affine translate of $Y$, whereas data differences belong to $Y$. All complex spaces here may be regarded as real Banach spaces when taking derivatives with respect to real conductivities.
