Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Use $\mathcal H_\ell$ from [[def-spherical-harmonic-partial-wave-conventions]]. For every $\ell\ge0$, $\dim_\mathbb C\mathcal H_\ell=2\ell+1$; the spaces $\mathcal H_\ell$ are pairwise orthogonal in $L^2(S^2,d\sigma;\mathbb C)$ and their algebraic sum is dense there. Thus they give a complete orthogonal spherical-harmonic expansion. For any orthonormal basis $Y_{\ell 1},\ldots,Y_{\ell,2\ell+1}$ of $\mathcal H_\ell$, the basis-independent reproducing kernel
$$Z_\ell(\omega,\eta):=\sum_{m=1}^{2\ell+1}Y_{\ell m}(\omega)\overline{Y_{\ell m}(\eta)}$$
satisfies $Z_\ell(\omega,\omega)=(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)$. In particular,
$$|g(\omega)|\le\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}}\,\|g\|_{L^2(S^2)}\qquad(g\in\mathcal H_\ell).$$
For fixed $\eta$, rotational invariance makes $Z_\ell(\omega,\eta)$ a degree-$\ell$ zonal polynomial of $\omega\cdot\eta$; normalizing $P_\ell(1)=1$ gives the usual addition identity $Z_\ell(\omega,\eta)=\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}P_\ell(\omega\cdot\eta)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
nonempty bounded connected extension domain, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then there is
$C=C(\Omega,p)$ such that every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ satisfies
$$\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad u_\Omega:=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u(x)\,dx.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded connected open set whose boundary is covered by finitely many $C^1$ graph charts. Give $H^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ its Sobolev norm, let $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ be the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and let $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ have the finite-chart Slobodeckij norm. Define $\mathcal D(\Omega):=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with its quotient norm. The trace induces a bounded linear bijection $\overline T:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with bounded inverse, so these two norms are equivalent under the induced identification. The induced map after quotienting by constants is also a bounded linear bijection $\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb K\mathbf1\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)/\mathbb K$, with equivalent quotient norms. A continuous linear functional on $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ descends to the constant quotient exactly when it annihilates constants, and its descended functional has the quotient dual norm.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p<\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then the set of restrictions
to $\Omega$ of functions in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ is dense in
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|\varphi|_\Omega-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$.

The exponent range is $1\le p<\infty$; the result asserts no density in the
$W^{k,\infty}$ norm, and it does not hold on arbitrary open sets, as the
companion examples page shows.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $\Omega=B_1\subset\mathbb R^3$, and let $\sigma_j=1+a_j$ be positive real conductivities with $a_j$ supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$, $\|a_j\|_{H^s}\le A$, $5/2<s<7/2$, $0<\rho<1$, and $m\le\sigma_j\le M$, for fixed positive bounds. Put $g_j=\sqrt{\sigma_j}$, $q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$, $Q=q_1-q_2$, and $N=\|Q\|_{H^{-1/2}(\mathbb R^3)}$. Let $\mathscr N_j$ be the boundary-mean-zero Neumann-to-Dirichlet map for $\sigma_j$ on $L^2_0(S^2)$, and define the actual data difference by the centered voltage sequences
$$\delta=\left(\sum_{\ell\ge1}\sum_{k=1}^{2\ell+1}\|(\mathscr N_1-\mathscr N_2)Y_{\ell k}\|_{L^2(S^2)}^2\right)^{1/2}.$$
This quantity is finite. If $U_j=e^{i\zeta_j\cdot x}(1+r_j)$ are the solutions from the positive-Sobolev CGO lemma, then
$$\int_\Omega Q U_1U_2\,dx=\int_{S^2}f_1(\mathscr N_2-\mathscr N_1)f_2\,dS,\qquad f_j=\partial_\nu U_j\big|_{S^2},$$
and the fluxes $f_j$ have mean zero. The boundary pairing is bilinear, without complex conjugation. In particular, there are $C,T>0$ depending only on the fixed class such that for $t\ge T$ and $|\xi|\le t$ one can choose null phases with $\zeta_1+\zeta_2=-\xi$, $|\zeta_j|=\sqrt2t$, and obtain the rigorous estimate
$$|\widehat Q(\xi)|\le C\delta e^{Ct}+C\langle\xi\rangle^{1/2}t^{-1}N.$$
The factor $\langle\xi\rangle^{1/2}$ is part of this conclusion; this lemma does not assert the sharper stability estimate that would follow from dropping it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $\Omega=B_1(0)\subset\mathbb R^3$, fix $0<\rho<1$ and $0<m<1<M$, and let $E$ be the closed real subspace of $L^\infty(\Omega)$ consisting of functions vanishing almost everywhere outside $B_\rho(0)$. Set $\mathcal A=\{a\in E:\operatorname*{ess\,inf}(1+a)>m,\ \operatorname*{ess\,sup}(1+a)<M\}$ and $\sigma=1+a$. Choose an orthonormal spherical-harmonic basis $Y_{\ell k}$ of mean-zero $L^2(S^2)$, with $\ell\ge1$ and $1\le k\le2\ell+1$. For each basis current there is a unique weak solution $u_{\sigma,\ell k}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with boundary mean zero such that
$$\int_\Omega\sigma\nabla u_{\sigma,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla v}=\int_{S^2}Y_{\ell k}\overline{\operatorname{Tr}v}\qquad(v\in H^1(\Omega)).$$
The centered sequence
$$G(a):=\big(\operatorname{Tr}(u_{\sigma,\ell k}-u_{1,\ell k})\big)_{\ell,k}$$
belongs to $Y=\ell^2(L^2(S^2))$. The map $G:\mathcal A\to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable, and both $G$ and $G'$ are Lipschitz on $\mathcal A$, with constants depending only on $m,M,\rho$ and the ball. Its derivative in direction $h\in E$ is the trace sequence of the unique boundary-mean-zero solutions
$$\int_\Omega\sigma\nabla v_{h,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla w}=-\int_\Omega h\nabla u_{\sigma,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla w}.$$
The uncentered sequence $(\operatorname{Tr}u_{1,\ell k})_{\ell,k}$ does not belong to $Y$. Thus absolute voltage data in this convention lie in an affine translate of $Y$, whereas data differences belong to $Y$. All complex spaces here may be regarded as real Banach spaces when taking derivatives with respect to real conductivities.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $5/2<s<7/2$, $0<\rho<1$, $0<m<1<M$ and $A>0$. Suppose $\sigma_j=1+a_j$ on $\mathbb R^3$, where $a_j$ is real, supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$, $\|a_j\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^3)}\le A$, and $m\le\sigma_j\le M$, for $j=1,2$. $$q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$$
belong to $H^{s-2}(\mathbb R^3)$, have support in $\overline{B_\rho}$, and have norms bounded in terms of $s,\rho,m,M,A$. Moreover,
$$\|\sigma_1-\sigma_2\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^3)}\le C\|q_1-q_2\|_{H^{-1}(\mathbb R^3)},$$
with the same dependence. In particular the right side may be replaced by $C\|q_1-q_2\|_{H^{-1/2}}$ when that stronger norm is used. The Fourier and intrinsic norms for collared variations are those of the collared Sobolev source-functional lemma.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$ and

set $K_0\subset\Omega$. Let $E_0u$ denote the extension of a representative of

by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: The energy argument in [F1] applies to every mean-zero $f\in L^2(S^2)$: the functional $v\mapsto\int f\overline{\operatorname{Tr}v}$ is bounded on the boundary-mean-zero $H^1$ subspace by [F4], and its uniformly coercive conductivity form has a unique solution with norm at most $C\|f\|_2$. This defines a bounded map $\mathscr N_j:L^2_0\to L^2_0$. Its centered sequence columns are those in [F1], so their difference has finite squared sum. For a finite current expansion $f=\sum c_{\ell k}Y_{\ell k}$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|(\mathscr N_1-\mathscr N_2)f\|_2\le\delta(\sum|c_{\ell k}|^2)^{1/2}$. Density and boundedness extend this to every $f\in L^2_0$. Finally the bilinear symmetry $\int f\mathscr N_jh=\int h\mathscr N_jf$ follows by testing the two weak equations against one another, using real coefficients and complex bilinear extension.

Put $u_j=U_j/g_j$. The weak Liouville identity gives $\operatorname{div}(\sigma_j
abla u_j)=0$: expand $\sigma_j
abla(U_j/g_j)=g_j
abla U_j-U_j
abla g_j$, whose divergence is $g_j\Delta U_j-U_j\Delta g_j=0$. Products are legitimate by [F2]–[F3]; one may also verify the equality first on smooth approximations and pass in distributions. Since $g_j=1$ on a full collar of $S^2$, the boundary normal flux of $u_j$ is exactly $f_j=\partial_
u U_j$. It belongs to $L^2$ because $U_j\in H^2(B_2)$ and [F4] applies to each first derivative. The divergence theorem [F5] gives the Green identity for smooth approximants; density [F6] and trace continuity [F4] pass it to the $H^2$ CGO solutions on $B_1$. On the collar $U_j$ is harmonic and the coefficient is identically one. Taking the test function one shows $\int f_j=0$. Thus $\operatorname{Tr}u_j=\mathscr N_j f_j+c_j$ for a constant $c_j$.

Subtract the two bilinear Schrödinger Green identities [F5]–[F6], testing the $j=1$ equation against $U_2$ and the $j=2$ equation against $U_1$. Their gradient terms cancel, giving $\int Q U_1U_2=\int_{S^2}(f_1\operatorname{Tr}U_2-f_2\operatorname{Tr}U_1)$. Since $U_j=u_j$ on the boundary, step 2.1 identifies these traces with $\mathscr N_jf_j+c_j$. The constant terms disappear because the fluxes have mean zero; the symmetry from step 1.1 gives exactly the displayed centered NtD identity. All volume terms are integrable since $Q\in L^2$ and $U_j\in H^2(B_2)\subset L^\infty(B_1)$; boundedness follows, for example, by weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz after multiplication by an interior cutoff.

If $|\zeta_j|=\sqrt2t$, [F3] and differentiation of the exponential give $\|U_j\|_{H^2(B_1)}\le Ce^{Ct}t^3$ for $t\ge T$. The trace bound on first derivatives then gives $\|f_j\|_2\le Ce^{Ct}$, increasing $C$ to absorb the polynomial. The operator-norm bound in step 1.1 and Cauchy–Schwarz in the bilinear boundary pairing yield $|\int Q U_1U_2|\le C\delta e^{Ct}$.

For smooth compactly supported $w$ put $[w]^2_{1/2}:=\iint|w(x)-w(y)|^2|x-y|^{-4}\,dx\,dy$. Translation, Plancherel and Tonelli [F7] give $$[w]^2_{1/2}=\int|\widehat w(\xi)|^2\left(\int\frac{|e^{i\xi\cdot h}-1|^2}{|h|^4}\,dh\right)d\xi=c_3\int|\xi||\widehat w(\xi)|^2d\xi,$$ where rotation and dilation give the inner integral, and $0<c_3<\infty$ follows from $|e^{iu}-1|\le\min\{2,|u|\}$. Thus $\|w\|_{H^{1/2}}^2\asymp\|w\|_2^2+[w]^2_{1/2}$. Restrict each $H^2(B_2)$ remainder to $B_1$ and use [F6] to approximate it there by ambient smooth functions; multiplication by a cutoff supported in $B_1$ and [F8] extend the products to $H^2(\mathbb R^3)$, so the norm comparison extends to these cutoff remainders. For bounded compactly supported factors the identity $f(x)g(x)-f(y)g(y)=f(x)(g(x)-g(y))+g(y)(f(x)-f(y))$ then yields $\|fg\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C(\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_{H^{1/2}}+\|g\|_\infty\|f\|_{H^{1/2}})$. For $\xi\ne0$, choose real orthonormal $d_1,d_2$ perpendicular to $\xi$ and set $\zeta_1=-\xi/2+\sqrt{t^2-|\xi|^2/4}\,d_2+itd_1$, $\zeta_2=-\xi/2-\sqrt{t^2-|\xi|^2/4}\,d_2-itd_1$; for $\xi=0$ choose any orthonormal pair. Direct expansion gives $\zeta_j\cdot\zeta_j=0$, $\zeta_1+\zeta_2=-\xi$ and $|\zeta_j|=\sqrt2t$. Hence $U_1U_2=e^{-i\xi\cdot x}(1+r_1+r_2+r_1r_2)$. Choose cutoffs $\chi,\eta\in C_c^\infty(B_1)$ with $\chi=1$ on $B_\rho$ and $\eta=1$ on $\operatorname{supp}\chi$. Applying the product estimate to $\chi r_j$ and $\eta r_j$, and [F3], gives $\|\chi(r_1+r_2+r_1r_2)\|_{H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^3)}\le C/t$. Fourier translation and $\langle\eta+\xi\rangle\le\sqrt2\langle\eta\rangle\langle\xi\rangle$ then give $\|e^{-i\xi\cdot x}\chi(r_1+r_2+r_1r_2)\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\langle\xi\rangle^{1/2}/t$.

Extract the Fourier coefficient of $Q$ from the exact product identity in step 5.1. Its remainder is precisely the signed pairing of $Q$ with $e^{-i\xi\cdot x}\chi(r_1+r_2+r_1r_2)$, not with the unmodulated remainder. Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz bounds its absolute value by $CN\langle\xi\rangle^{1/2}/t$. Combine this with step 4.1 and absorb the fixed unitary Fourier factor $(2\pi)^{-3/2}$ into $C$. This proves the stated estimate with its modulation factor retained.

current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Fix $5/2<s<7/2$, $0<\rho<1$, $0<m<1<M$ and $A>0$. Suppose $\sigma_j=1+a_j$ on $\mathbb R^3$, where $a_j$ is real, supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$, $\|a_j\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^3)}\le A$, and $m\le\sigma_j\le M$, for $j=1,2$. Then $g_j=\sqrt{\sigma_j}$ and $\log g_j$ belong to $C^1$, with $g_j-1,\log g_j\in H^s(\mathbb R^3)$ supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$ and uniformly bounded in $H^s$ and $C^1$. The real Liouville potentials
$$q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$$
belong to $H^{s-2}(\mathbb R^3)$, have support in $\overline{B_\rho}$, and have norms bounded in terms of $s,\rho,m,M,A$. Moreover,
$$\|\sigma_1-\sigma_2\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^3)}\le C\|q_1-q_2\|_{H^{-1}(\mathbb R^3)},$$
with the same dependence. In particular the right side may be replaced by $C\|q_1-q_2\|_{H^{-1/2}}$ when that stronger norm is used. The Fourier and intrinsic norms for collared variations are those of the collared Sobolev source-functional lemma.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice. Put $\Omega=B_1(0)\subset\mathbb R^3$, fix $0<\rho<1$, and let $5/2<s<7/2$ and $s<t<2s-1$. Use the following precise intrinsic Hilbert norm on $H^s(\Omega)$. If $s=m+\theta$ with integer $m\ge0$ and $0<\theta<1$, set
$$\|v\|_{s,\Omega}^2=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\|D^\alpha v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\sum_{|\alpha|=m}\int_{\Omega\times\Omega}\frac{|D^\alpha v(x)-D^\alpha v(y)|^2}{|x-y|^{3+2\theta}}\,dx\,dy.$$
For integer $s=3$ use just the derivative sum with $m=3$. Denote the corresponding real inner product by $(\cdot,\cdot)_{s,\Omega}$. On $\mathbb R^3$ use the unitary Fourier transform and $\|f\|_{H^r}^2=\int\langle\xi\rangle^{2r}|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi$. Let $B^r_{2,\infty}(\mathbb R^3)$ have norm $\sup_{j\ge0}2^{jr}\|\mathbf1_{A_j}\widehat f\|_2$, where $A_0=\{|\xi|<2\}$ and $A_j=\{2^j\le|\xi|<2^{j+1}\}$ for $j\ge1$; the restriction space on $\Omega$ consists of restrictions of members of this whole-space Besov space.

Let $\sigma^\dagger\in H^s(\Omega)\cap B^t_{2,\infty}(\Omega)$ be real and equal to $1$ almost everywhere on $\Omega\setminus B_\rho$. Then there is $C>0$, depending on $\sigma^\dagger,s,t,\rho$, such that for every real $\sigma\in H^s(\Omega)$ also equal to $1$ there and every integer $J\ge0$,
$$-(\sigma^\dagger,\sigma-\sigma^\dagger)_{s,\Omega}\le C2^{J(2s-t-1)}\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{H^1(\Omega)}+C2^{-J(t-s)}\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{s,\Omega}.$$
Consequently, suppose on a specified admissible sublevel a forward map $G$ satisfies $\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C_0\omega(\|G(\sigma)-G(\sigma^\dagger)\|)$ with $\omega(0)=0$ and $0\le\omega\le1$. For the exact regularizer $R(\sigma)=\frac12\|\sigma\|_{s,\Omega}^2$, its exact Bregman distance is $D_R(\sigma,\sigma^\dagger)=\frac12\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{s,\Omega}^2$, and
$$-(\sigma^\dagger,\sigma-\sigma^\dagger)_{s,\Omega}\le\frac34D_R(\sigma,\sigma^\dagger)+C_1\omega(\|G(\sigma)-G(\sigma^\dagger)\|)^{2(t-s)/(t-1)}.$$
In particular, an $H^1$ stability modulus of order $[\log(1/u)]^{-(s-3/2)}$ yields a VSC source term of order $[\log(1/u)]^{-\nu}$ with $\nu=(t-s)(2s-3)/(t-1)$. The conditional stability estimate is a hypothesis here, not a conclusion.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Suppose
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ vanishes almost everywhere outside a compact
set $K_0\subset\Omega$. Let $E_0u$ denote the extension of a representative of
$u$ by zero to $\mathbb R^n$, and for $|\alpha|\le k$ let
$E_0(D^\alpha u)$ denote the extension by zero of the corresponding
derivative representative. Then
$$E_0u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad D^\alpha(E_0u)=E_0(D^\alpha u)\quad\text{almost everywhere, }|\alpha|\le k,$$
and every $L^p$ component norm is preserved:
$$\|E_0(D^\alpha u)\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|E_0u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},$$
so that $\|E_0u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$. The case
$k=0$ is included, and complex scalars are handled by the same bilinear
pairing.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

An **$L^1$ approximate identity** on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a family
$(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ of functions in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$, where

$$\|K_\varepsilon\|_1:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}|K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx,$$

such that:

1. $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} K_\varepsilon(x)\,dx = 1$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$;
2. there is $M < \infty$ with $\|K_\varepsilon\|_1 \le M$ for every
   $\varepsilon > 0$;
3. for every $\delta > 0$,
   $$ \int_{|x|>\delta} |K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+). $$

This is the general notion used later for both compactly supported mollifiers
and the Gaussian family.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ be nonnegative with
$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$.
For $\varepsilon>0$ put $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$
and
$$\Omega_\varepsilon=\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^n\setminus\Omega)>\varepsilon\},\qquad\Omega_\varepsilon=\mathbb R^n\ \text{when }\Omega=\mathbb R^n .$$
Then $\rho_\varepsilon*u$ is defined and smooth on $\Omega_\varepsilon$, and
for every multi-index $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le k$,
$$D^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*u)=\rho_\varepsilon*(D^\alpha u)\qquad\text{on }\Omega_\varepsilon,$$
as pointwise smooth functions for the constructed representatives and as
almost-everywhere classes. Here $D^\alpha u$ is extended by zero off $\Omega$
in the convolution.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|a\|_\infty+\|\nabla a\|_\infty\le C_s\|a\|_{H^s}$ because $\int(1+|\xi|^2)^{-s}(1+|\xi|)^2d\xi<\infty$ for $s>5/2$. The Fourier integrals for $a$ and its first derivatives converge absolutely and are continuous by dominated convergence, so these bounds hold for a $C^1$ representative. We shall also use $\|fg\|_{H^b}\le C\|f\|_{H^r}\|g\|_{H^b}$ when $r>3/2$ and $0\le b\le r$. Here is a direct justification: split Fourier space into dyadic annuli, use $\|f_j\|_\infty\le C2^{3j/2}\|f_j\|_2$ for low-high products, and $\|Q_j(f_kg_k)\|_2\le C2^{3j/2}\|f_k\|_2\|g_k\|_2$ when comparable high shells $k$ produce a shell $j\le k+C$. The low-high sum is bounded by $\|f\|_{H^r}\|g\|_{H^b}$ since $r>3/2$. For high-low products, sum the low $g$ blocks with bound $C2^{j(3/2-b)}\|g\|_{H^b}$ if $b<3/2$, a square-root logarithmic factor if $b=3/2$, or $C\|g\|_{H^b}$ if $b>3/2$; the excess $r-3/2>0$ makes the resulting geometric sum converge. For high-high products, weighted summation over $k\ge j-C$ has geometric kernel $2^{-(k-j)(r+b)}$ and excess factor $2^{j(3/2-r)}$; Cauchy–Schwarz for the input shell sequences completes the bound. The estimates are first proved for Fourier truncations and then passed to their norm limits.

For $0<\theta<1$, multiplication by a bounded $C^1$ function $h$ is bounded on $H^\theta$. Indeed $|h(x)f(x)-h(y)f(y)|^2\le2\|h\|_\infty^2|f(x)-f(y)|^2+2|f(y)|^2|h(x)-h(y)|^2$. In the last term use $|h(x)-h(y)|\le\min\{2\|h\|_\infty,\|\nabla h\|_\infty|x-y|\}$; integrating the kernel $|x-y|^{-3-2\theta}$ near and far from the diagonal gives a finite constant times $\|f\|_2^2$. Apply [F2] to get the Fourier Sobolev bound. For $\theta=0$ this is just the $L^2$ multiplier bound.

If $F$ is any smooth scalar function on a neighborhood of $[m,M]$, then $F(1+a)-F(1)$ belongs to $H^s$ with a uniform bound over this class. To verify the fractional highest derivative directly, write $s=k+\theta$ with $k=2$ or $3$ and $0\le\theta<1$. For $k=2$, the chain rule gives terms $F'(\sigma)D^2a$ and $F''(\sigma)Da\,Da$. The first term is in $H^\theta$ by step 2.1, since $F'(\sigma)$ is bounded $C^1$ uniformly; for the second, $Da\in H^{s-1}$ with $s-1>3/2$, so the algebra bound in step 1.1 and then step 2.1 apply. For $k=3$, the terms are $F'(\sigma)D^3a$, $F''(\sigma)D^2a\,Da$, and $F'''(\sigma)(Da)^3$. Here $Da\in H^{s-1}$ is a multiplier on $H^{s-2}$ by step 1.1, so $D^2a\,Da\in H^{s-2}\subset H^\theta$; the remaining products follow from the same algebra and step 2.1. Lower derivatives have the corresponding easier estimates; the function itself has an $L^2$ bound by the mean value theorem and vanishes wherever $a=0$. These calculations may first be made for smooth approximations: convolve $a$ with a nonnegative mollifier, which preserves $m\le1+a\le M$ and uniform $H^s$ and $C^1$ bounds, and then use convergence in lower Sobolev orders and weak compactness in the Hilbert $H^s$ space to identify the asserted weak derivatives and bound. A bounded sequence in this separable Fourier Hilbert space has a weakly convergent subsequence by diagonal convergence of its countable Fourier coordinates and the norm bound; hence only Countable Choice is used.

Apply step 3.1 to $F(t)=\sqrt t$, $\frac12\log t$, and $t^{-1/2}$ to obtain the stated regularity and support of $g_j-1$, $\log g_j$, and $g_j^{-1}-1$. To bound $q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$ in $H^{s-2}$, for $s<3$ use step 2.1 with $\theta=s-2\in(1/2,1)$ and the uniform $C^1$ norm of $g_j^{-1}$; for $s\ge3$ use the multiplier bound in step 1.1 with $r=s$ and $b=s-2$. Split $g_j^{-1}=1+(g_j^{-1}-1)$ for that whole-space bound. The support statement follows from $g_j=1$ outside the collar ball and from the local definition of weak derivatives.

Put $w=\log g_1-\log g_2$, $H=g_1g_2$ and $Q=q_1-q_2$. Since $H
abla w=g_2
abla g_1-g_1
abla g_2$, distributional differentiation gives $\operatorname{div}(H
abla w)=g_2\Delta g_1-g_1\Delta g_2=HQ$. The equality follows first for smooth positive approximations and then in distributions using step 4.1 and the Sobolev products from steps 1.1–2.1; all terms also have their ordinary weak-product interpretation because $g_j$ are $C^1$ and $\Delta g_j\in L^2$. The functions $w$ and its gradient vanish outside $\overline{B_ho}$. By [F3], extend $w$ by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. Choose a nonnegative unit-mass smooth mollifier from [F4]. For small $\varepsilon$, its convolution with the zero extension is supported in $B_2$; by [F5], the mollifications converge to $w$ in $H^1$. Thus the distributional identity may be tested against $w$: $Q\in H^{-1}$ and multiplication by the bounded $C^1$ function $H$ is bounded on $H^1$. It gives $\int H|
abla w|^2=-\langle Q,Hwangle$.

A compactly supported $H^1$ function in $B_\rho\subset(-2,2)^3$ obeys $\|w\|_2\le4\|\partial_1w\|_2$: for a smooth approximation supported in the same larger cube, write $w(x_1,x')=\int_{-2}^{x_1}\partial_1w(t,x')dt$, apply Cauchy–Schwarz, and integrate in $x_1,x'$; passing to $H^1$ limits gives the inequality. Since $H\ge m$, step 5.1 and the Fourier dual bound yield $m\|\nabla w\|_2^2\le\|Q\|_{H^{-1}}\|Hw\|_{H^1}\le C\|Q\|_{H^{-1}}\|w\|_{H^1}$. Poincaré in the first sentence then implies $\|w\|_{H^1}\le C\|Q\|_{H^{-1}}$, dividing by its norm if nonzero. Finally $\sigma_1-\sigma_2=\sigma_2(e^{2w}-1)$; the uniform bounds for $w$, $\sigma_2$ and $\nabla\sigma_2$, the mean value theorem, and the ordinary weak product rule give $\|\sigma_1-\sigma_2\|_{H^1}\le C\|w\|_{H^1}$. Also $\|Q\|_{H^{-1}}\le\|Q\|_{H^{-1/2}}$ by the Fourier weights. This proves all recovery claims.

references.locator: Theorem 6.12; the present proof treats the intrinsic quadratic Sobolev pairing directly

current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Put $\Omega=B_1(0)\subset\mathbb R^3$, fix $0<\rho<1$, and let $5/2<s<7/2$ and $s<t<2s-1$. Use the following precise intrinsic Hilbert norm on $H^s(\Omega)$. If $s=m+\theta$ with integer $m\ge0$ and $0<\theta<1$, set
$$\|v\|_{s,\Omega}^2=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\|D^\alpha v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\sum_{|\alpha|=m}\int_{\Omega\times\Omega}\frac{|D^\alpha v(x)-D^\alpha v(y)|^2}{|x-y|^{3+2\theta}}\,dx\,dy.$$
For integer $s=3$ use just the derivative sum with $m=3$. Denote the corresponding real inner product by $(\cdot,\cdot)_{s,\Omega}$. On $\mathbb R^3$ use the unitary Fourier transform and $\|f\|_{H^r}^2=\int\langle\xi\rangle^{2r}|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi$. Let $B^r_{2,\infty}(\mathbb R^3)$ have norm $\sup_{j\ge0}2^{jr}\|\mathbf1_{A_j}\widehat f\|_2$, where $A_0=\{|\xi|<2\}$ and $A_j=\{2^j\le|\xi|<2^{j+1}\}$ for $j\ge1$; the restriction space on $\Omega$ consists of restrictions of members of this whole-space Besov space.

Let $\sigma^\dagger\in H^s(\Omega)\cap B^t_{2,\infty}(\Omega)$ be real and equal to $1$ almost everywhere on $\Omega\setminus B_\rho$. Then there is $C>0$, depending on $\sigma^\dagger,s,t,\rho$, such that for every real $\sigma\in H^s(\Omega)$ also equal to $1$ there and every integer $J\ge0$,
$$-(\sigma^\dagger,\sigma-\sigma^\dagger)_{s,\Omega}\le C2^{J(2s-t-1)}\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{H^1(\Omega)}+C2^{-J(t-s)}\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{s,\Omega}.$$
Consequently, suppose on a specified admissible sublevel a forward map $G$ satisfies $\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C_0\omega(\|G(\sigma)-G(\sigma^\dagger)\|)$ with $\omega(0)=0$ and $0\le\omega\le1$. For the exact regularizer $R(\sigma)=\frac12\|\sigma\|_{s,\Omega}^2$, its exact Bregman distance is $D_R(\sigma,\sigma^\dagger)=\frac12\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{s,\Omega}^2$, and
$$-(\sigma^\dagger,\sigma-\sigma^\dagger)_{s,\Omega}\le\frac34D_R(\sigma,\sigma^\dagger)+C_1\omega(\|G(\sigma)-G(\sigma^\dagger)\|)^{2(t-s)/(t-1)}.$$
In particular, an $H^1$ stability modulus of order $[\log(1/u)]^{-(s-3/2)}$ yields a VSC source term of order $[\log(1/u)]^{-\nu}$ with $\nu=(t-s)(2s-3)/(t-1)$. The conditional stability estimate is a hypothesis here, not a conclusion.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$ and
$s\in\mathbb R$, and let $H^s(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential
space with the exact norm
$$\|U\|_{H^s}=\bigl\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal F(E_sU)\bigr\|_2$$
of [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-fractional-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]],
where $\langle\xi\rangle=(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$. Fix the partition of
[[def-inhomogeneous-dyadic-frequency-partition]] and let $\Delta_jU$ be the
tempered distributions obtained by the multipliers $\varphi_j$. Then for every
$U\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$, $U$ lies in the image of the canonical
embedding $E_s$ (and is identified with its preimage in $H^s$) if and only if
$$\sum_{j\ge0}2^{2js}\|\Delta_jU\|_{L^2}^2<\infty,$$
where $\|\Delta_jU\|_{L^2}$ denotes the $L^2$ norm of the unique $L^2$ function
representing the tempered distribution $\Delta_jU$ when such a function exists
and is set equal to $+\infty$ otherwise (the convention is needed only for the
converse direction; for $U$ in the image of $E_s$ every $\Delta_jU$ is a
regular $L^2$ distribution, as the proof records), and in that case
$$c_{n,s,\psi}\|U\|_{H^s}^2\le\sum_{j\ge0}2^{2js}\|\Delta_jU\|_{L^2}^2\le C_{n,s,\psi}\|U\|_{H^s}^2$$
with constants depending only on $n,s$ and the partition. The low-frequency
block carries the weight $2^{0}=1$, and the series converges absolutely.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $1 \le p,q,r \le \infty$ satisfy

$$ \frac1r = \frac1p + \frac1q - 1. $$

If $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $g \in L^q(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then the
convolution $f*g$ is defined almost everywhere and satisfies

$$ \|f*g\|_r \le \|f\|_p\|g\|_q. $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: We record explicitly the smooth-multiplication bound for the stated Besov convention. Write $Q_j=\mathbf1_{A_j}(D)$. For $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, $Q_j\chi Q_k$ has Fourier kernel $(2\pi)^{-3/2}\mathbf1_{A_j}(\xi)\widehat\chi(\xi-\eta)\mathbf1_{A_k}(\eta)$. If $|j-k|\le2$, Young's convolution inequality [F3] bounds its $L^2$ operator norm by a constant times $\|\widehat\chi\|_1$. If $|j-k|>2$, then $|\xi-\eta|\ge c2^{\max(j,k)}$ on these supports. Repeated integration by parts in the Fourier integral of $\chi$ gives $|\widehat\chi(\zeta)|\le C_N(1+|\zeta|)^{-N}$. Cauchy–Schwarz in the two frequency variables therefore bounds the operator norm by $C_N2^{-N\max(j,k)}2^{3(j+k)/2}$. For any real $r$, multiply these bounds by $2^{jr-kr}$ and sum over $k$. Choosing $N>2|r|+8$ makes both off-diagonal geometric sums uniformly bounded in $j$, while the near-diagonal sum has at most five terms. Hence $\|\chi f\|_{B^r_{2,\infty}}\le C_{r,\chi}\|f\|_{B^r_{2,\infty}}$. These calculations first apply to finite block sums; the same estimates give their convergence in distributions, since a Schwartz test has faster-than-polynomial Fourier decay.

The sharp annular definition agrees, up to constants, with any usual smooth inhomogeneous dyadic definition at $p=2$. Indeed a sharp annulus meets at most a fixed number of the smooth supports at neighboring scales. On that annulus, the identity $\sum\varphi_j=1$ and Cauchy–Schwarz give its $L^2$ norm at most the sum of those finitely many smooth-block $L^2$ norms; conversely each smooth symbol has magnitude at most one and support in finitely many sharp annuli. The weights $2^{jr}$ differ by only a constant at neighboring scales. The low blocks also meet only finitely many supports. This proves both Besov norm comparisons. For Hilbert Sobolev norms, [F1] gives directly $\|f\|_{H^r}^2\asymp\sum_j2^{2jr}\|Q_jf\|_2^2$, consistently with [F2].

Choose $\chi_0\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ equal to one near $\overline{B_\rho}$, and choose $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ equal to one near $\overline\Omega$. Let $\widetilde\sigma^\dagger$ be one whole-space $B^t_{2,\infty}$ extension, whose existence is part of the restriction-space hypothesis. The compactly supported distribution $f^\dagger:=\chi_0(\widetilde\sigma^\dagger-1)$ is in $B^t_{2,\infty}(\mathbb R^3)$ by step 1.1 (the constant term multiplied by $\chi_0$ is smooth). It equals $\sigma^\dagger-1$ on $\Omega$ and vanishes outside $\overline{B_\rho}$, since the conductivity equals one in the collar. Thus $v^\dagger=\eta+f^\dagger$ is a compactly supported $B^t_{2,\infty}$ extension of $\sigma^\dagger$. In particular $v^\dagger\in H^s(\mathbb R^3)$: the squared block sum is bounded by a constant times $\sum_j2^{-2j(t-s)}<\infty$.

For $e=\sigma-\sigma^\dagger$, let $e_0$ be its zero extension. Its support lies in $\overline{B_\rho}$. Zero extension creates no boundary derivatives because $e$ vanishes on an open collar: local distributional tests near $\partial\Omega$ see zero, and interior tests give exactly the zero extensions of the weak derivatives. For $s=m+\theta$ noninteger, the whole-space top-order difference integral equals the integral over $\Omega^2$ plus $2\int_\Omega|D^\alpha e(x)|^2\int_{\mathbb R^3\setminus\Omega}|x-y|^{-3-2\theta}dy\,dx$. Where $D^\alpha e$ can be nonzero, the inner integral is bounded by $\int_{|z|\ge1-\rho}|z|^{-3-2\theta}dz<\infty$. The whole-space difference norm is therefore bounded by $C\|e\|_{s,\Omega}$, and the integer case is immediate. For $g\in L^2$, [F1] and Tonelli [F4] give $\int\int|g(x+h)-g(x)|^2|h|^{-3-2\theta}dx\,dh=\int|\widehat g(\xi)|^2\int|e^{i\xi\cdot h}-1|^2|h|^{-3-2\theta}dh\,d\xi$. The inner integral equals $c_\theta|\xi|^{2\theta}$ by rotation and dilation; $0<c_\theta<\infty$ follows by the bounds $|e^{iu}-1|\le\min\{2,|u|\}$. Summing derivative multipliers shows that this whole-space difference norm is equivalent to $\|e_0\|_{H^s}$. Thus $\|e_0\|_{H^s}\le C\|e\|_{s,\Omega}$, while exactly $\|e_0\|_{H^1}=\|e\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$.

Let $B_s(v,w)$ be the whole-space intrinsic bilinear form associated with the derivative and difference norm in step 3.2. Its Fourier multiplier $p_s(\xi)$ equals $\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\xi^{2\alpha}+c_\theta\sum_{|\alpha|=m}\xi^{2\alpha}|\xi|^{2\theta}$ in the noninteger case, and just the first polynomial in the integer case. Thus $|p_s(\xi)|\le C\langle\xi\rangle^{2s}$, and $P_0:=p_s(D)v^\dagger$ belongs to $B^{t-2s}_{2,\infty}$ by the annular multiplier bound and step 3.1. Its distributional pairing with $e_0$ is $B_s(v^\dagger,e_0)$. The pairing is defined by convergent Fourier blocks: high blocks have the product bound $C2^{-j(t-s)}\|e_0\|_{H^s}$, a summable sequence. This also justifies the bilinear identity by truncation and limits, without assuming classical derivatives of order $2s$.

In the integer case the whole-space and domain pairings are identical, since every derivative of $e_0$ is supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$; take $P=P_0$. For noninteger $s=m+\theta$, their difference is $$B_s(v^\dagger,e_0)-(\sigma^\dagger,e)_{s,\Omega}=2\sum_{|\alpha|=m}\int_\Omega D^\alpha e(x)\big(A(x)D^\alpha v^\dagger(x)-b_\alpha(x)\big)dx,$$ where $A(x)=\int_{\Omega^c}|x-y|^{-3-2\theta}dy$ and $b_\alpha(x)=\int_{\Omega^c}D^\alpha\eta(y)|x-y|^{-3-2\theta}dy$. To obtain the formula, split each whole-space double integral into $\Omega^2$, $\Omega\times\Omega^c$ and its transpose; $D^\alpha e_0$ is zero outside and $v^\dagger=\eta$ there. On any fixed neighborhood of $\overline{B_\rho}$ compact in $\Omega$, every derivative of $A,b_\alpha$ is bounded, by differentiating the separated kernel and using its integrable tail. Choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ equal to one on that neighborhood. The domain pairing is therefore the pairing of $e_0$ with $$P=P_0-2\sum_{|\alpha|=m}(-1)^mD^\alpha\big(\chi A D^\alpha v^\dagger-\chi b_\alpha\big).$$ By step 1.1, its correction terms lie in $B^{t-2m}_{2,\infty}$: differentiation lowers the block regularity by the derivative order, multiplication by the smooth compact coefficient preserves it, and $\chi b_\alpha$ is smooth and compactly supported. Since $2m\le2s$, they also lie in $B^{t-2s}_{2,\infty}$. Hence $P\in B^{t-2s}_{2,\infty}$ in every case, and $\langle P,e_0\rangle=(\sigma^\dagger,e)_{s,\Omega}$. This treats the exact domain penalty pairing rather than replacing its norm by an equivalent one.

Put $d=t-s>0$ and $a=2s-t-1>0$. Let $P_{\le J}=\sum_{j\le J}Q_jP$. By step 5.1 and the Hilbert block norm formula, $\|P_{\le J}\|_{H^{-1}}^2\le C\sum_{j\le J}2^{2j(2s-t-1)}\le C2^{2Ja}$. Similarly $\|P-P_{\le J}\|_{H^{-s}}^2\le C\sum_{j>J}2^{2j(s-t)}\le C2^{-2Jd}$. Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz and step 3.2 now give $|\langle P,e_0\rangle|\le C2^{Ja}\|e\|_{H^1(\Omega)}+C2^{-Jd}\|e\|_{s,\Omega}$, the first claimed estimate.

Expansion of the quadratic form gives exactly $D_R(\sigma,\sigma^\dagger)=\|e\|_{s,\Omega}^2/2$. Set $W=\omega(\|G(\sigma)-G(\sigma^\dagger)\|)$. The conditional stability hypothesis and $uv\le3u^2/8+2v^2/3$ applied to the high-frequency term in step 6.1 yield $-(\sigma^\dagger,e)_{s,\Omega}\le3\|e\|_{s,\Omega}^2/8+C(2^{Ja}W+2^{-2Jd})$. If $W=0$, stability gives $e=0$. For $0<W\le1$, take the integer $J\ge0$ with $2^{-J(a+2d)}\ge W>2^{-(J+1)(a+2d)}$. Then $2^{-2Jd}\le2^{2d}W^{2d/(a+2d)}$ and $2^{Ja}W\le W^{2d/(a+2d)}$. Since $a+2d=t-1$, this proves the asserted source inequality with coefficient $3/4$ on the exact Bregman distance. Substitution of the stated logarithmic stability exponent gives $\nu=2(s-3/2)(t-s)/(t-1)$ by multiplying exponents.

references.locator: Theorem 3 and Remark 1; the additional endpoint noise condition is derived from the scalar estimate here

current_manifest_record.statement:
Fix $p,
u,a,C_*,C>0$ and let $\psi$ be a continuous nondecreasing concave source index with $\psi(0)=0$. Suppose its conjugate $H(q)=\sup_{t\ge0}(\psi(t)-qt)$ satisfies $H(q)\le C(\log q)^{-
u}$ for all sufficiently large $q$. Let $\delta\downarrow0$ be a nominal parameter, and put $L_\delta=\log(1/\delta)$. Suppose nonnegative errors satisfy
$$S_\delta+a\alpha_\delta e_\delta\le d_\delta+\alpha_\delta\psi(C_*S_\delta),\qquad \alpha_\delta\asymp\delta^p,\qquad d_\delta=O(\delta^pL_\delta^{-
u}).$$
Then
$$e_\delta=O(L_\delta^{-
u}),\qquad S_\delta=O(\delta^pL_\delta^{-
u}).$$
For the joint objective estimate with $p\ge1$ and actual data noise $\varepsilon_\delta=\|y^\delta-y\|$, the hypothesis on $d_\delta$ is supplied by $2\varepsilon_\delta^p+\eta_\delta=O(\delta^pL_\delta^{-
u})$. This condition explicitly strengthens the usual nominal bound $\varepsilon_\delta\le\delta$, $\eta_\delta=O(\delta^p)$ at the endpoint. If $e_\delta= rac12\|u_\delta-u^\dagger\|^2$, the norm rate is $O(L_\delta^{-
u/2})$.

The universal assertion that $\alpha\asymp\delta^2$ yields a vanishing norm error for every deterministic noise family bounded by $\delta$ is false, even for an exact quadratic Tikhonov minimizer and a truth satisfying every nonnegative variational source inequality: on real $\ell^2$, take $Ke_j=j^{-1}e_j$, $x^\dagger=0$, $y^{\delta_j}=\delta_j e_j$, $\delta_j=1/j$, $\alpha_j=\delta_j^2$, and objective $\|Kx-y^{\delta_j}\|^2+ rac{\alpha_j}{2}\|x\|^2$. Its unique minimizer is $2e_j/3$. This counterexample refutes the universal abstract endpoint assertion; it makes no assertion that these data arise from an EIT conductivity map.

citations.quote:
Let $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, nondecreasing, concave, and satisfy $\psi(0)=0$. Extend $g=-\psi$ to $\mathbb R$ by $g(s)=+\infty$ for $s<0$, and define $H(q):=g^*(-q)=\sup_{s\ge0}(\psi(s)-qs)$ for $q>0$, assuming the displayed suprema below are finite. For $c_1,c_2,C_3,\alpha>0$ and $d,r,e\ge0$, if

$$c_1r+c_2\alpha e\le d+\alpha\psi(C_3r),$$

then

$$e\le\frac1{c_2}\left(\frac d\alpha+H\!\left(\frac{c_1}{C_3\alpha}\right)\right),\qquad r\le\frac2{c_1}\left(d+\alpha H\!\left(\frac{c_1}{2C_3\alpha}\right)\right).$$

derivations.claim:
Put $d_\delta^+:=\max\{d_\delta,0\}$. The scalar inequality remains true with $d_\delta^+$ on its right, and $d_\delta^+=O(\delta^pL_\delta^{-
u})$. Since $\alpha_\delta\asymp\delta^p$, one has $\log(1/(c\alpha_\delta))\sim pL_\delta$ for either fixed $c=C_*$ or $c=2C_*$. Thus both conjugate terms in [F1] are $O(L_\delta^{-
u})$, while $d_\delta^+/\alpha_\delta=O(L_\delta^{-
u})$. Substitution into [F1] proves both error estimates. If the joint approximate-minimum comparison is made with actual noise $\varepsilon_\delta$ and $p\ge1$, its comparison term is $d_\delta=2\varepsilon_\delta^p+\eta_\delta$; this follows by replacing the noise upper bound by its actual value in the triangle-power comparison. The explicitly stated effective noise hypothesis therefore suffices. The quadratic norm rate follows by taking square roots.

For the asserted counterexample, complete squares coordinatewise in $\|Kx-y^{\delta_j}\|^2+(\alpha_j/2)\|x\|^2$. Every coordinate $i\ne j$ has unique minimizer zero. The $j$th coordinate has unique minimizer $\frac{j^{-1}\delta_j}{j^{-2}+\alpha_j/2}=2/3$. All quadratic coefficients are positive and the penalty is strictly positive definite, so this point is the unique global minimizer on $\ell^2$. Its norm error is $2/3$ for every $j$. At truth zero the regularizer subgradient is zero, so the variational source left side is zero and any nonnegative source index satisfies the inequality. Also $\|y^{\delta_j}-Kx^\dagger\|=\delta_j$, so the ordinary deterministic noise bound holds exactly. This proves the false universal endpoint assertion fails and explains the need for an explicit additional noise condition in step 1.1.

current_manifest_record.title: Uniform density and Hausdorff convergence of TV level-set boundaries
current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $A:L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)\to L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ be bounded and real-linear, let $f=Au^\dagger$, and suppose $u^\dagger$ is a minimum-TV exact solution with a source certificate $p^\dagger$. For $\alpha_n>0$ tending to zero and noises $w_n\in L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$, assume $\|A^*\|\|w_n\|_2/\alpha_n\le\eta$ and let $u_n$ be supplied global minimizers of $\frac12\|Au-(f+w_n)\|_2^2+\alpha_n TV(u)$. Define $p_n=(f+w_n-Au_n)/\alpha_n$ and $v_n=A^*p_n$. Use $TV_2$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ for full-space TV; on a nonempty bounded Lipschitz domain use zero-extension Dirichlet TV, and on a nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz domain use relative Neumann TV. For bounded-domain geometry use the ambient zero-extended level sets and their topological boundaries in $\mathbb R^2$.

For full-space or Dirichlet TV, assume $\eta<2\sqrt\pi$; in the bounded Dirichlet case also assume $\Omega$ has global obstacle curvature $\kappa_\Omega\in L^1(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ with $\kappa_\Omega\ge g$ almost everywhere outside $\Omega$ for some real-valued $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^2\setminus\Omega;\mathbb R)$. For Neumann TV, let $C_\Omega$ be a constant from the BV Sobolev–Poincaré inequality $\|u-u_\Omega\|_2\le C_\Omega TV(u;\Omega)$ and assume $\eta<1/C_\Omega$.

For almost every nonzero $t$, the level set $E_n(t)$ has finite measure and perimeter, minimizes the branch-specific perimeter minus $\int_{E}\operatorname{sgn}(t)v_n$ under compactly supported perturbations, and satisfies $P(E_n(t))=\operatorname{sgn}(t)\int_{E_n(t)}v_n$. There are constants $c>0$ and $r_0>0$, independent of $n$ and almost every such $t$, such that for every $x\in\partial E_n(t)$ and $0<r<r_0$,
$$|B(x,r)\cap E_n(t)|\ge c|B(x,r)|,\qquad |B(x,r)\setminus E_n(t)|\ge c|B(x,r)|.$$
In the full-space branch all these level sets are contained in one common ball; in the bounded branches they lie in $\overline\Omega$. The same density and support conclusions are asserted for any selected minimum-TV exact limit that carries the inherited source certificate, using zero noise. Whenever the corresponding level sets converge in measure, their canonical boundaries converge in Hausdorff distance.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, and let $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be one of the full-space, Dirichlet, or Neumann TV functionals. Assume that $R$ is proper, convex, lower semicontinuous, and positively one-homogeneous, and that $u^\dagger$ is a minimum-$R$ exact solution of $Au=f$ with a dual source certificate $p^\dagger\in Y$, so $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$. Define $K:=\{p\in Y:A^*p\in\partial R(0)\}$ and $D_{\alpha,w}(p):=\langle f+w,p\rangle_Y-\frac{\alpha}{2}\|p\|_Y^2$ for $\alpha>0$ and $w\in Y$.

For each $\alpha>0$ and $w\in Y$, $D_{\alpha,w}$ has a unique maximizer $p_{\alpha,w}=\operatorname{Proj}_K((f+w)/\alpha)$. If $u_{\alpha,w}$ is any supplied global minimizer of $u\mapsto\frac12\|Au-(f+w)\|_Y^2+\alpha R(u)$, then $p_{\alpha,w}=(f+w-Au_{\alpha,w})/\alpha$, $A^*p_{\alpha,w}\in\partial R(u_{\alpha,w})$, and $A^*p_{\alpha,w}\in\partial R(0)$. For every such supplied minimizer, the correctly normalized primal-dual value identity is

$$\min_u\{\tfrac12\|Au-(f+w)\|_Y^2+\alpha R(u)\}=\alpha D_{\alpha,w}(p_{\alpha,w}).$$

Let $P_0:=\{p\in K:\langle f,p\rangle_Y=R(u^\dagger)\}$ and let $p_0$ be its unique minimum-norm element. For every sequence $\alpha_n>0$ with $\alpha_n\to0$, $p_{\alpha_n,0}\to p_0$ strongly in $Y$ and $A^*p_{\alpha_n,0}\to A^*p_0$ strongly in $X$. For every $\alpha>0$ and $w\in Y$,

$$\|p_{\alpha,w}-p_{\alpha,0}\|_Y\le\frac{\|w\|_Y}{\alpha},\qquad \|A^*p_{\alpha,w}-A^*p_{\alpha,0}\|_X\le\frac{\|A^*\|\,\|w\|_Y}{\alpha}.$$

Moreover, for any $R_0>R(u^\dagger)$ the certificate yields a variational source condition on $\{u:R(u)\le R_0\}$ with exponent $2$, coefficient $\beta=0$, and index function $\psi(s)=(1+\|p^\dagger\|_Y)\sqrt{s}$. Consequently, if $\delta_n\downarrow0$, $\|w_n\|_Y\le\delta_n$, $\alpha_n\asymp\delta_n$, and exact global minimizers $u_n$ are supplied, then the variational-source rate theorem gives

$$D_R^{A^*p^\dagger}(u_n,u^\dagger)=O(\delta_n),\qquad \|Au_n-(f+w_n)\|_Y=O(\delta_n).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, or let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain. Set $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ for a measure space $(\Sigma,\mu)$, using the real integral inner products; under Countable Choice these are real Hilbert spaces. Let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, and let $A^*:Y\to X$ be its Hilbert adjoint, characterized by $\langle Au,p\rangle_Y=\langle u,A^*p\rangle_X$. Define $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ as follows. If $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, take $R(u)=TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$, the supremum of $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi$ over smooth compactly supported vector fields of Euclidean norm at most one. For bounded $\Omega$, either take Neumann TV, $R(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$ when $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise, or Dirichlet TV, $R(u)=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)$ when the zero extension $\widetilde u$ belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^2)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise. Thus the bounded-domain choices count, respectively, only the interior derivative or also the jump of the zero extension across the boundary. In the full-space case finite $R$ does not require global $L^1$ integrability.

Identify each $q\in X$ with the continuous linear functional $h\mapsto\langle q,h\rangle_X$ by the real Hilbert-space Riesz representation. For exact data $f=Au^\dagger$, a **minimum-TV exact solution** is a point $u^\dagger\in X$ satisfying $Au^\dagger=f$ and $R(u^\dagger)\le R(u)$ for every $u\in X$ with $Au=f$. A vector $p^\dagger\in Y$ is a **dual source certificate** for $u^\dagger$ if $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$, where $\partial R$ is the convex subdifferential on the real Banach space $X$. The **TV source condition** at $u^\dagger$ is that such a certificate exists; it does not assert uniqueness of the truth or of the certificate. For a chosen certificate, the associated Bregman distance is

$$D_R^{A^*p^\dagger}(u,u^\dagger):=R(u)-R(u^\dagger)-\langle A^*p^\dagger,u-u^\dagger\rangle_X,$$

for $u\in\operatorname{dom}R$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$, with functions identified when they agree almost everywhere. For full-space TV, use $u$ itself. For a bounded-domain Dirichlet or Neumann problem, use the zero extension $\widetilde u$ only to define the geometric level sets; this does not change the selected regularizer, and for each nonzero level the resulting set lies inside $\Omega$. For $t>0$, the positive $t$-level class is the measurable-set class of $E_t^+(u):=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:u(x)>t\}$; for $t<0$, the negative $t$-level class is the class of $E_t^-(u):=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:u(x)<t\}$. These classes do not depend on the representative of $u$. For any measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, its density-one representative is

$$E^{(1)}:=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{|E\cap B(x,r)|}{|B(x,r)|}=1\right\}.$$

This representative depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $E$. The canonical level set $U_u^{(t)}$ is $(E_t^+(u))^{(1)}$ when $t>0$ and $(E_t^-(u))^{(1)}$ when $t<0$. Its canonical boundary is the ordinary topological boundary $\partial U_u^{(t)}$ in $\mathbb R^2$. For two nonempty boundary sets, use the usual extended Hausdorff distance induced by Euclidean distance; set $d_H(\varnothing,\varnothing)=0$ and $d_H(E,F)=+\infty$ if exactly one set is empty. Hausdorff convergence uses this convention and is invariant under changes to a function on a null set.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)<\infty$. For $t>0$ set $E_t^+=\{x:u(x)>t\}$, and for $t<0$ set $E_t^-=\{x:u(x)<t\}$. Each set has finite area, almost every applicable level set has finite perimeter, and
$$TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)=\int_0^\infty P(E_t^+;\mathbb R^2)\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0P(E_t^-;\mathbb R^2)\,dt.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $u\in BV(\Omega)$, and for $t>0$ set $E_t^+:=\{x\in\Omega:u(x)>t\}$ while for $t<0$ set $E_t^-:=\{x\in\Omega:u(x)<t\}$. Then for almost every applicable $t$ these sets have finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$, and $$TV(u;\Omega)=\int_0^\infty P(E_t^+;\Omega)\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0P(E_t^-;\Omega)\,dt.$$

Let $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$ or let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain. Choose one of three perimeter functionals for measurable $E\subseteq\Omega$: full-space perimeter $P_R(E)=P(E;\mathbb R^2)$ when $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$; Neumann relative perimeter $P_N(E)=P(E;\Omega)$ on a bounded domain; or Dirichlet perimeter $P_D(E)=P(\widetilde E;\mathbb R^2)$, where $\widetilde E$ is $E$ extended by the empty set outside $\Omega$. Require finite measure and finite selected perimeter, and let $\kappa:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be Lebesgue-measurable with $\int_F|\kappa|<\infty$ for every set considered. The set $E$ has **variational curvature** $\kappa$ for the selected model if its selected perimeter minus $\int_E\kappa\,dx$ is no greater than the same quantity for every finite-measure finite-selected-perimeter competitor $F\subseteq\Omega$ whose symmetric difference $F\mathbin\triangle E$ has compact closure in $\Omega$. In the full-space model, this means compact closure in $\mathbb R^2$.

For bounded Dirichlet TV, a separate **obstacle curvature** condition on $\Omega$ means that $\Omega$, viewed as a finite-perimeter set in $\mathbb R^2$, minimizes $F\mapsto P(F;\mathbb R^2)-\int_F\kappa_\Omega\,dx$ over all finite-measure finite-perimeter $F\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ whose symmetric difference with $\Omega$ has compact closure in $\mathbb R^2$, where $\kappa_\Omega\in L^1(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Every Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ with finite area and finite perimeter satisfies
$$4\pi |E|\le P(E;\mathbb R^2)^2.$$

Assume Countable Choice. For every nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, there is a finite constant $C_\Omega>0$ such that every $u\in BV(\Omega)$ satisfies
$$\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega TV(u;\Omega),\qquad u_\Omega:=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u\,dx.$$

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. In addition, assuming Countable Choice, for any real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, with equality to $TV(u;\Omega)$; under the same assumption, an $L^1$ limit of real-valued BV functions with bounded liminf total variation belongs to $BV(\Omega)$ and satisfies the same lower-semicontinuity inequality.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Assume Countable Choice. In this lemma $\mathcal H^1$ means arclength, equivalently normalized one-dimensional Hausdorff measure. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open, let $E\subseteq U$ have finite measure and finite relative perimeter, and fix $x\in\mathbb R^2$. Put $\mu=|D\chi_E|$ on $U$. For almost every $r>0$, $\mu(\partial B(x,r))=0$ and, with $s_E(r)=\mathcal H^1(E^{(1)}\cap U\cap\partial B(x,r))$,
$$P(E\cap B(x,r);U)=\mu(U\cap B(x,r))+s_E(r),\qquad P(E\setminus B(x,r);U)=\mu(U\setminus\overline B(x,r))+s_E(r).$$
The volume $a(r)=|E\cap B(x,r)|$ is locally absolutely continuous with $a'(r)=s_E(r)$ almost everywhere. The analogous inside-cut formula holds for $(U\setminus E)\cap B(x,r)$, with the complementary sphere slice. When $U=\mathbb R^2$ this clause requires no finite area for the uncut complement. For finite-area $E$, the outside volume $|E\setminus B(x,r)|$ has derivative $-s_E(r)$ almost everywhere.

For a real-valued measurable field $k:U\to\mathbb R$, if $E$ globally minimizes $P(F;U)-\int_F k$ among the finite-measure finite-relative-perimeter sets in $U$, with all displayed integrals finite, then for almost every $r$,
$$P(E\cap B;U)\le2s_E(r)+\int_{E\cap B}k,\qquad P((U\setminus E)\cap B;U)\le2s_{U\setminus E}(r)-\int_{(U\setminus E)\cap B}k.$$
For $U=\mathbb R^2$ one also has $P(E\setminus B)\le2s_E(r)+\int_{E\setminus B}k$. Here $B=B(x,r)$; the competitors may touch the boundary of $U$.

Full-space finite-measure finite-perimeter sets satisfy $P(F\cap G)+P(F\cup G)\le P(F)+P(G)$. Consequently, suppose bounded $\Omega$ has the global obstacle curvature $\kappa_\Omega$ and $\kappa_\Omega\ge g$ outside $\Omega$, with $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^2\setminus\Omega;\mathbb R)$. If $E\subseteq\Omega$ globally minimizes $P(F)-\int_F k$ among $F\subseteq\Omega$, then it minimizes against all full-space competitors with bounded symmetric difference for the extended field $k\chi_\Omega+g\chi_{\Omega^c}$. In particular all bounded-ball removal and filling comparisons above apply to this extended field.

Assume Countable Choice. Suppose $z_n\to z_\infty$ in $L^2(U;\mathbb R)$ and $v_n=z_n+e_n$ with real-valued $e_n\in L^2(U;\mathbb R)$ satisfying $\|e_n\|_2\le\eta$. Include $v_\infty=z_\infty$ with zero perturbation if desired. For each index, either sign $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$, and any finite-measure finite-selected-perimeter set $E\subseteq U$ globally minimizing the selected perimeter minus $\int_E\sigma v_n$, use its ambient density-one representative $E^{(1)}$ and ambient boundary. The selected branch is full-space perimeter on $U=\mathbb R^2$; zero-extension Dirichlet perimeter on bounded Lipschitz $U=\Omega$ with the obstacle curvature and exterior lower bound $g\in L^2(\Omega^c;\mathbb R)$; or relative Neumann perimeter on bounded connected Lipschitz $U=\Omega$ with specified $C_\Omega$ satisfying $\|u-u_\Omega\|_2\le C_\Omega TV(u;\Omega)$.

If $\eta<2\sqrt\pi$ in the full-space and Dirichlet branches, or $\eta<1/C_\Omega$ in the Neumann branch, there exist $c,r_0>0$, independent of the index, sign and minimizing set, such that
$$|E\cap B(x,r)|\ge c\pi r^2,\qquad |B(x,r)\setminus E|\ge c\pi r^2\quad(x\in\partial E^{(1)},\ 0<r<r_0).$$
All the full-space representatives and their boundaries lie in one common closed ball; in bounded branches they lie in $\overline\Omega$. The full-space sets also have uniform area and perimeter bounds. These conclusions include the limiting field and the empty set. They require no connected-component or Jordan decomposition of finite-perimeter sets.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open and let $TV_2(\cdot;\Omega)$ be the extended distributional total variation on $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. It is proper, convex, lower semicontinuous in the $L^2$ norm, and positively one-homogeneous for nonnegative scalars. For every $u\in BV(\Omega)\cap L^2(\Omega)$, it agrees with spatial TV: $TV_2(u;\Omega)=TV(u;\Omega)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Here $\mathcal H^m$ on a boundary denotes normalized Hausdorff measure: the repository's unnormalised $m$-dimensional Hausdorff measure divided by $c_m=H^m((0,1]^m)$ for $m\ge1$, and counting measure for $m=0$. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, meaning a bounded open set whose boundary has a finite cover by coordinate neighborhoods in which it is the graph of a Lipschitz function and $\Omega$ lies on one side of the graph. There is a unique bounded linear trace operator $T:BV(\Omega)\to L^1(\partial\Omega,\mathcal H^{n-1})$ such that for every $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $\phi\in C_c^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^n)$, $$\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\phi\,dx=-\int_\Omega\phi\cdot dDu+\int_{\partial\Omega}Tu\,\phi\cdot\nu\,d\mathcal H^{n-1},$$ where $\nu$ is the outward unit normal defined almost everywhere on $\partial\Omega$. The zero extension $\widetilde u$ belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^n)$ and satisfies $$TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^n)=TV(u;\Omega)+\|Tu\|_{L^1(\partial\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\bigl(\|u\|_{L^1(\Omega)}+TV(u;\Omega)\bigr)$$ for a finite constant $C_\Omega$ depending only on the domain. The same conclusions hold in dimension one for a bounded open set with a finite one-sided graph cover, with the two one-sided endpoint traces and counting measure on its finite boundary.

$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: The TV functional is proper, convex, lower semicontinuous and positively one-homogeneous by [F12]. On a bounded domain $L^2\subset L^1$, so the relative functional agrees with that test-field functional by [F8]; the Dirichlet version is its composition with the linear isometric zero-extension map into full-space $L^2$. Thus the hypotheses of [F1] hold. Comparison of each objective with its finite value at zero also gives finite TV at a supplied minimizer. Put $z_n=v_{\alpha_n,0}=A^*p_{\alpha_n,0}$. By [F1], $z_n\to v_0=A^*p_0$ strongly in $L^2(\Omega)$ and $v_n=z_n+e_n$ with $\|e_n\|_2\le\eta$. Thus the exact-field sequence, its limit and the noisy fields have precisely the coefficient decomposition required by [F10]. In particular their uniform small-measure moduli and, in full space, exact-field tail moduli follow from strong convergence, as proved there, without an assumed uniform integrability of the noisy perturbations.

For each supplied minimizer, [F1] and positive one-homogeneity imply $R(u_n)=\langle v_n,u_n\rangle$ and $v_n\in\partial R(0)$. The selected TV is even, since its test-field class is symmetric and zero extension is linear. Applying its inequality to both $\chi_F$ and $-\chi_F$ gives $P_*(F)\ge\sigma\int_Fv_n$ for either sign $\sigma$, for every finite-area finite-selected-perimeter competitor; $P_*$ denotes the selected branch perimeter throughout this proof. Indeed these indicators belong to $L^2$ and their selected TV is exactly $P_*$ by [F8] and the boundary conventions. In full space every nonzero level has finite area by $|\{|u_n|>|t|\}|\le\|u_n\|_2^2/t^2$. Bounded-domain levels have finite area automatically. Coarea [F4] gives finite selected perimeter for almost every nonzero level. Relative-perimeter Neumann levels also have finite ambient perimeter by [F11]. Signed layer cake and Cauchy–Schwarz give an absolutely integrable level pairing: the integral over levels of $\int_{E_n(t)}|v_n|$ is $\int|u_n||v_n|\le\|u_n\|_2\|v_n\|_2$. Hence [F11] and coarea show that the integral of the nonnegative gaps $P_*(E_n(t))-\operatorname{sgn}(t)\int_{E_n(t)}v_n$ equals $R(u_n)-\langle v_n,u_n\rangle=0$. Each gap therefore vanishes almost everywhere. Their value zero is the global minimum of $P_*(F)-\operatorname{sgn}(t)\int_Fv_n$, since every competitor has nonnegative value. This proves the stated equality and even global branch minimization, which in particular implies compact-perturbation variational curvature [F5]. Taking the countable union of exceptional level sets makes this true simultaneously for all $n$.

The threshold and actual obstacle assumptions are exactly those of [F10]. Apply it to every calibrated set from step 1.2, with either level sign. It supplies one $c,r_0>0$ for both ambient density inequalities at every point of each canonical boundary, independently of the index and the nonexceptional level. In the Dirichlet branch the actual obstacle extension uses perimeter submodularity from [F10]; in the Neumann branch its proof uses relative cuts and the specified $C_\Omega$, and at points on $\partial\Omega$ it uses the uniform Lipschitz exterior area for the ambient complement. Thus no false relative-complement estimate is imposed on the valid case $E=\Omega$. In full space [F10] compares $E$ with actual radial cuts and proves finite-radius extinction of $|E\setminus B(0,r)|$, giving one common ball containing the density-one sets and their topological boundaries. Bounded-domain representatives and boundaries lie in $\overline\Omega$. These are the full density and support conclusions, rather than assumptions for the transfer below.

The limiting field calibrates every minimum-TV exact solution $u_0$ under consideration. More explicitly, the dual supplier [F1] defines $p_0\in\{p:A^*p\in\partial R(0),\ \langle f,p\rangle=R(u^\dagger)\}$. For any such exact minimum $Au_0=f$ and $R(u_0)=R(u^\dagger)$, one has $\langle v_0,u_0\rangle=\langle p_0,f\rangle=R(u_0)$, while $v_0\in\partial R(0)$. Its subgradient inequality is therefore also the inequality at $u_0$. Repeat step 1.2 with $u_0,v_0$; its almost-everywhere level sets are calibrated global minimizers. Adjoin the limiting exact field with perturbation zero in [F10]. The very same coefficient moduli and noise threshold used in step 2.1 then give the same uniform density and support conclusions for this limit. This includes any selected minimum-TV exact limit carrying the inherited certificate; it does not identify that solution with $u^\dagger$ without uniqueness.

Fix a nonzero nonexceptional level for which the corresponding sets converge in measure to such a canonical limit $E_0$. If $E_0=\varnothing$ and infinitely many $E_n$ are nonempty, their bounded common support makes each boundary nonempty: a boundaryless subset of connected $\mathbb R^2$ is clopen, and the only bounded clopen set is empty. Choose a boundary point and one fixed $0<r<r_0$; the density estimate gives $|E_n\triangle E_0|\ge c\pi r^2$, a contradiction. If $E_0$ is nonempty, it has positive measure by its density-one definition, so convergence rules out infinitely many empty $E_n$. The empty status therefore agrees eventually; two empty boundaries have Hausdorff distance zero. In the nonempty case, if $x_n\in\partial E_n$ stays at distance at least $\delta>0$ from $\partial E_0$, common compact support and [F9] give a subsequence $x_n\to x$. For $r<\min(r_0,\delta/4)$ the connected ball $B(x_n,r)$ misses $\partial E_0$ and is entirely in $E_0$ or entirely outside it. The two-sided density of $E_n$ forces symmetric difference at least $c\pi r^2$, again a contradiction. Conversely, if $y_n\in\partial E_0$ stays at distance at least $\delta$ from $\partial E_n$, take a convergent subsequence with limit $y\in\partial E_0$. A fixed smaller connected ball about $y$ misses every corresponding $\partial E_n$, so along a further subsequence its status is always full or always empty. Measure convergence makes $E_0$ full or empty almost everywhere on that ball. By the density-one definition it is then actually full or empty in a smaller ball, contradicting $y\in\partial E_0$. Both directed Hausdorff distances tend to zero, with all point and subsequence selections allowed by [A1].

current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ be real Hilbert spaces. Let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, let $f=Au^\dagger$, and assume $u^\dagger$ is an exact solution minimizing a proper, convex, lower semicontinuous, positively one-homogeneous TV functional $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ with a source certificate $p^\dagger\in Y$, so $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$. Use full-space $R=TV_2(\cdot;\mathbb R^2)$ if $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$; for a nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, use either Neumann $R(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$ or Dirichlet $R(u)=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)$ for the zero extension $\widetilde u$, assigning $+\infty$ outside the respective finite-variation domain. A bounded connected Lipschitz domain here is a nonempty bounded open set with a finite Lipschitz graph cover of its boundary, with the domain on one side of each graph, and with no separation into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets.

Let $\alpha_n>0$ tend to zero, let $w_n\in Y$, and suppose $\|A^*\|\,\|w_n\|_Y/\alpha_n\le\eta$ for some finite $\eta$. For each $n$, suppose a supplied global minimizer $u_n\in X$ minimizes
$$J_n(u)=\tfrac12\|Au-(f+w_n)\|_Y^2+\alpha_nR(u).$$
In the Neumann case, if $A\mathbf1_\Omega=0$, take $u_n$ after subtracting its mean $|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u_n$; this leaves $J_n$ unchanged. Then a subsequence converges weakly in $L^2(\Omega)$ and, in addition, strongly in $L^1(\Omega)$ when $\Omega$ is bounded or strongly in $L^1$ on every bounded ball when $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$. Its limit $u_0$ is an exact solution $Au_0=f$ minimizing $R$ among exact solutions, and $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u_0)$.
