citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, or let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain. Set $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ for a measure space $(\Sigma,\mu)$, using the real integral inner products; under Countable Choice these are real Hilbert spaces. Let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, and let $A^*:Y\to X$ be its Hilbert adjoint, characterized by $\langle Au,p\rangle_Y=\langle u,A^*p\rangle_X$. Define $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ as follows. If $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, take $R(u)=TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$, the supremum of $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi$ over smooth compactly supported vector fields of Euclidean norm at most one. For bounded $\Omega$, either take Neumann TV, $R(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$ when $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise, or Dirichlet TV, $R(u)=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)$ when the zero extension $\widetilde u$ belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^2)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise. Thus the bounded-domain choices count, respectively, only the interior derivative or also the jump of the zero extension across the boundary. In the full-space case finite $R$ does not require global $L^1$ integrability.

Identify each $q\in X$ with the continuous linear functional $h\mapsto\langle q,h\rangle_X$ by the real Hilbert-space Riesz representation. For exact data $f=Au^\dagger$, a **minimum-TV exact solution** is a point $u^\dagger\in X$ satisfying $Au^\dagger=f$ and $R(u^\dagger)\le R(u)$ for every $u\in X$ with $Au=f$. A vector $p^\dagger\in Y$ is a **dual source certificate** for $u^\dagger$ if $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$, where $\partial R$ is the convex subdifferential on the real Banach space $X$. The **TV source condition** at $u^\dagger$ is that such a certificate exists; it does not assert uniqueness of the truth or of the certificate. For a chosen certificate, the associated Bregman distance is

$$D_R^{A^*p^\dagger}(u,u^\dagger):=R(u)-R(u^\dagger)-\langle A^*p^\dagger,u-u^\dagger\rangle_X,$$

for $u\in\operatorname{dom}R$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, and let $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be one of the full-space, Dirichlet, or Neumann TV functionals. Assume that $R$ is proper, convex, lower semicontinuous, and positively one-homogeneous, and that $u^\dagger$ is a minimum-$R$ exact solution of $Au=f$ with a dual source certificate $p^\dagger\in Y$, so $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$. Define $K:=\{p\in Y:A^*p\in\partial R(0)\}$ and $D_{\alpha,w}(p):=\langle f+w,p\rangle_Y-\frac{\alpha}{2}\|p\|_Y^2$ for $\alpha>0$ and $w\in Y$.

For each $\alpha>0$ and $w\in Y$, $D_{\alpha,w}$ has a unique maximizer $p_{\alpha,w}=\operatorname{Proj}_K((f+w)/\alpha)$. If $u_{\alpha,w}$ is any supplied global minimizer of $u\mapsto\frac12\|Au-(f+w)\|_Y^2+\alpha R(u)$, then $p_{\alpha,w}=(f+w-Au_{\alpha,w})/\alpha$, $A^*p_{\alpha,w}\in\partial R(u_{\alpha,w})$, and $A^*p_{\alpha,w}\in\partial R(0)$. For every such supplied minimizer, the correctly normalized primal-dual value identity is

$$\min_u\{\tfrac12\|Au-(f+w)\|_Y^2+\alpha R(u)\}=\alpha D_{\alpha,w}(p_{\alpha,w}).$$

Let $P_0:=\{p\in K:\langle f,p\rangle_Y=R(u^\dagger)\}$ and let $p_0$ be its unique minimum-norm element. For every sequence $\alpha_n>0$ with $\alpha_n\to0$, $p_{\alpha_n,0}\to p_0$ strongly in $Y$ and $A^*p_{\alpha_n,0}\to A^*p_0$ strongly in $X$. For every $\alpha>0$ and $w\in Y$,

$$\|p_{\alpha,w}-p_{\alpha,0}\|_Y\le\frac{\|w\|_Y}{\alpha},\qquad \|A^*p_{\alpha,w}-A^*p_{\alpha,0}\|_X\le\frac{\|A^*\|\,\|w\|_Y}{\alpha}.$$

Moreover, for any $R_0>R(u^\dagger)$ the certificate yields a variational source condition on $\{u:R(u)\le R_0\}$ with exponent $2$, coefficient $\beta=0$, and index function $\psi(s)=(1+\|p^\dagger\|_Y)\sqrt{s}$. Consequently, if $\delta_n\downarrow0$, $\|w_n\|_Y\le\delta_n$, $\alpha_n\asymp\delta_n$, and exact global minimizers $u_n$ are supplied, then the variational-source rate theorem gives

$$D_R^{A^*p^\dagger}(u_n,u^\dagger)=O(\delta_n),\qquad \|Au_n-(f+w_n)\|_Y=O(\delta_n).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, meaning a bounded open set whose boundary has a finite cover by Lipschitz graph neighborhoods with $\Omega$ on one side of each graph. Total variation is lower semicontinuous under $L^1(\Omega)$ convergence of BV functions. Every sequence $(u_k)\subset BV(\Omega)$ satisfying $$\sup_k\bigl(\|u_k\|_{L^1(\Omega)}+TV(u_k;\Omega)\bigr)<\infty$$ has a subsequence converging in $L^1(\Omega)$ to a function in $BV(\Omega)$.
Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge2$. Every $u\in BV(\mathbb R^n)$ satisfies $$\|u\|_{L^{n/(n-1)}(\mathbb R^n)}\le TV(u;\mathbb R^n).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Every $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ with $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)<\infty$ satisfies
$$\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and connected. If $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ satisfies $\partial_i u=0$ as a distribution for every coordinate $i$, then there is a constant $c\in\mathbb R$ such that $u=c$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, meaning a bounded open set whose boundary has a finite cover by coordinate neighborhoods in which it is the graph of a Lipschitz function and $\Omega$ lies on one side of that graph. For $u\in BV(\Omega)$ define the Neumann total variation by $TV_N(u;\Omega):=|Du|(\Omega)$. Define its zero extension $\widetilde u\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)$ by $\widetilde u=u$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$ and $\widetilde u=0$ almost everywhere on $\mathbb R^n\setminus\Omega$. Define the Dirichlet total variation by $TV_D(u;\Omega):=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^n)$ when $\widetilde u\in BV(\mathbb R^n)$ and by $TV_D(u;\Omega):=+\infty$ otherwise. For $v\in BV(\mathbb R^n)$ define the full-space total variation by $TV_F(v):=TV(v;\mathbb R^n)$. Thus Neumann variation counts only the distributional derivative inside $\Omega$, while Dirichlet variation also counts any jump created by zero extension across $\partial\Omega$.

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. In addition, assuming Countable Choice, for any real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, with equality to $TV(u;\Omega)$; under the same assumption, an $L^1$ limit of real-valued BV functions with bounded liminf total variation belongs to $BV(\Omega)$ and satisfies the same lower-semicontinuity inequality.

Assume Countable Choice. If $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open, $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and $TV_2(u;\Omega)<\infty$, then each distributional derivative of $u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure. Their vector measure $Du$ has finite Radon variation and $|Du|(\Omega)=TV_2(u;\Omega)$.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ (The dual space X^* of a normed space and its dual norm). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

Assume Countable Choice. For every nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, there is a finite constant $C_\Omega>0$ such that every $u\in BV(\Omega)$ satisfies
$$\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega TV(u;\Omega),\qquad u_\Omega:=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u\,dx.$$

derivations.claim: If $\|A^*\|=0$, the adjoint identity implies $A=0$ and $f=0$. Since $0$ is exact, minimality gives $R(u^\dagger)=0$. The data term of $J_n$ is then constant, so every global minimizer has $R(u_n)=0$. In the full-space case [F6] makes $u_n$ constant and $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ forces it to be zero; in the Dirichlet case apply [F6] to its zero extension, which vanishes outside bounded $\Omega$, and again obtain zero; in the Neumann case [F6] makes it constant and the prescribed zero-mean choice makes it zero. Thus $u_0=0$ is an exact minimum-TV solution. Since $R\ge0$ and $R(0)=0$, $0\in\partial R(0)=\partial R(u_0)$, so $A^*p^\dagger=0\in\partial R(u_0)$ and the assertion holds. For the remainder assume $\|A^*\|>0$.

Put $p_n=(f+w_n-Au_n)/\alpha_n$. By [F2], $p_n=p_{\alpha_n,w_n}$ and $p_{\alpha_n,0}$ is bounded. The noise hypothesis gives $\|w_n\|_Y/\alpha_n\le\eta/\|A^*\|$, hence [F2] makes $(p_n)$ bounded and $\|w_n\|_Y\to0$. The identity $Au_n=f+w_n-\alpha_np_n$ therefore gives $Au_n\to f$ strongly in $Y$. Comparing the objective at $u_n$ and $u^\dagger$ gives $$\tfrac12\|Au_n-(f+w_n)\|_Y^2+\alpha_nR(u_n)\le\tfrac12\|w_n\|_Y^2+\alpha_nR(u^\dagger),$$ so $R(u_n)\le R(u^\dagger)+\|w_n\|_Y^2/(2\alpha_n)\le R(u^\dagger)+\eta^2\alpha_n/(2\|A^*\|^2)$. In particular the variations are bounded and $\limsup_nR(u_n)\le R(u^\dagger)$.

In the Neumann branch on bounded connected $\Omega$, write $m_n=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u_n$ and $v_n=u_n-m_n$. The Poincaré inequality [F14] gives $\|v_n\|_2\le C_\Omega TV(v_n;\Omega)=C_\Omega R(u_n)$, which is uniformly bounded by step 1.2.

If $A\mathbf1_\Omega=0$, subtracting $m_n$ leaves both $Au_n$ and Neumann TV unchanged, so we use the zero-mean minimizer specified in the Statement, which is uniformly bounded in $L^2$ by step 2.1. If $A\mathbf1_\Omega\ne0$, then [F1] and step 1.2 give bounded $\|Au_n\|_Y$ and $$|m_n|\,\|A\mathbf1_\Omega\|_Y=\|Au_n-Av_n\|_Y\le\|Au_n\|_Y+\|A\|\|v_n\|_2,$$ so the means, and therefore $\|u_n\|_2$, are bounded. In the full-space case [F5] gives $\|u_n\|_2\le R(u_n)$. In the Dirichlet case [F4] applied to $\widetilde u_n$ gives $\|u_n\|_2\le R(u_n)$. Thus in every branch the selected sequence is bounded in $L^2$.

If $\Omega$ is bounded, the $L^2$ bound gives an $L^1$ bound by [F11]; the interior variation is bounded by $R(u_n)$ in both boundary conventions [F7]. [F3] therefore supplies a subsequence converging strongly in $L^1(\Omega)$. If $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, restrict to each ball $B(0,m)$: the $L^1$ norms are bounded by $|B(0,m)|^{1/2}\sup_n\|u_n\|_2$, and [F9] bounds the variation there. Applying [F3] on each ball and taking a countable diagonal subsequence using [A1] gives convergence in $L^1$ on every bounded ball.

The resulting sequence is still bounded in the Hilbert space $L^2(\Omega)$. Its closed linear span is separable, since rational finite linear combinations of its terms are dense. Gram–Schmidt gives a finite or countable orthonormal family with dense span. Each coordinate sequence is bounded by [F11]; repeated use of [F10] and [A1] yields a subsubsequence on which every coordinate converges. Pythagoras applied to each finite orthogonal projection bounds the sums of squared limiting coordinates by the common squared norm bound, so these coordinates define a vector $u_0$ in the closed span. Approximation by finite linear combinations proves convergence of inner products against every vector in the span. For any $z\in L^2(\Omega)$, [F12] represents $x\mapsto\langle x,z\rangle$ restricted to that span by a vector in the span, so the convergence is weak in all of $L^2$. Testing against compactly supported smooth functions shows that this weak limit and the strong $L^1$ or local-$L^1$ limit from step 4.1 define the same distribution; injectivity [F13] makes them equal almost everywhere.

Weak convergence and boundedness of $A$ imply $Au_n\rightharpoonup Au_0$, while step 1.2 gives $Au_n\to f$ strongly; hence $Au_0=f$. In the full-space case, for every admissible test field $\varphi$, local $L^1$ convergence gives $\int u_0\operatorname{div}\varphi=\lim_n\int u_n\operatorname{div}\varphi\le\liminf_nR(u_n)$; taking the supremum gives $R(u_0)\le\liminf_nR(u_n)$. In the Neumann case the same lower semicontinuity follows from [F8] and strong $L^1(\Omega)$ convergence. In the Dirichlet case the zero extensions converge strongly in $L^1(\mathbb R^2)$, so [F8] gives the same inequality for their full-space TV. Thus $R(u_0)\le\liminf_nR(u_n)\le\limsup_nR(u_n)\le R(u^\dagger)$. Exactness and the minimum property of $u^\dagger$ force equality, so $u_0$ is a minimum-TV exact solution.

Let $\xi=A^*p^\dagger$. Since $Au_0=Au^\dagger=f$, the adjoint identity in [F1] gives $\langle\xi,u_0-u^\dagger\rangle_X=\langle p^\dagger,A(u_0-u^\dagger)\rangle_Y=0$. For every $v\in X$, the subgradient inequality at $u^\dagger$ therefore gives $$R(v)\ge R(u^\dagger)+\langle\xi,v-u^\dagger\rangle_X=R(u_0)+\langle\xi,v-u_0\rangle_X.$$ This is exactly $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u_0)$, as required.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $A:L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)\to L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ be bounded and real-linear, let $f=Au^\dagger$, and suppose $u^\dagger$ is a minimum-TV exact solution with a dual source certificate $p^\dagger$, meaning $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$. Use $R=TV_2$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ for full-space TV; for a nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz domain use either Dirichlet TV of the zero extension or Neumann TV relative to $\Omega$. Let $\alpha_n>0$ tend to zero, let $w_n\in L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\|A^*\|\|w_n\|_2/\alpha_n\le\eta$, and suppose a global minimizer $u_n$ is supplied for each functional
$$u\longmapsto\tfrac12\|Au-(f+w_n)\|_2^2+\alpha_nR(u).$$
For full-space or Dirichlet TV, assume $\eta<2\sqrt\pi$; for bounded Dirichlet TV also assume $\Omega$ has global obstacle curvature $\kappa_\Omega\in L^1(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ with $\kappa_\Omega\ge g$ almost everywhere outside $\Omega$ for some real-valued $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^2\setminus\Omega;\mathbb R)$. For Neumann TV, let $C_\Omega$ be a constant satisfying $\|u-u_\Omega\|_2\le C_\Omega TV(u;\Omega)$ on $BV(\Omega)$ and assume $\eta<1/C_\Omega$. In the Neumann case with $A\mathbf1_\Omega=0$, choose the minimizers after subtracting their means.

There is a subsequence $(u_{n_k})$ and a selected minimum-TV exact solution $u_0$ such that $Au_0=f$ and, for almost every nonzero $t$, the canonical level sets of $u_{n_k}$ converge in measure to the canonical level set of $u_0$, while their canonical ambient boundaries converge in Hausdorff distance. The limit $u_0$ need not equal the initially named truth $u^\dagger$ unless the minimum-TV exact solution is unique.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ be real Hilbert spaces. Let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, let $f=Au^\dagger$, and assume $u^\dagger$ is an exact solution minimizing a proper, convex, lower semicontinuous, positively one-homogeneous TV functional $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ with a source certificate $p^\dagger\in Y$, so $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$. Use full-space $R=TV_2(\cdot;\mathbb R^2)$ if $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$; for a nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, use either Neumann $R(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$ or Dirichlet $R(u)=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)$ for the zero extension $\widetilde u$, assigning $+\infty$ outside the respective finite-variation domain. A bounded connected Lipschitz domain here is a nonempty bounded open set with a finite Lipschitz graph cover of its boundary, with the domain on one side of each graph, and with no separation into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets.

Let $\alpha_n>0$ tend to zero, let $w_n\in Y$, and suppose $\|A^*\|\,\|w_n\|_Y/\alpha_n\le\eta$ for some finite $\eta$. For each $n$, suppose a supplied global minimizer $u_n\in X$ minimizes
$$J_n(u)=\tfrac12\|Au-(f+w_n)\|_Y^2+\alpha_nR(u).$$
In the Neumann case, if $A\mathbf1_\Omega=0$, take $u_n$ after subtracting its mean $|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u_n$; this leaves $J_n$ unchanged. Then a subsequence converges weakly in $L^2(\Omega)$ and, in addition, strongly in $L^1(\Omega)$ when $\Omega$ is bounded or strongly in $L^1$ on every bounded ball when $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$. Its limit $u_0$ is an exact solution $Au_0=f$ minimizing $R$ among exact solutions, and $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u_0)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$, with functions identified when they agree almost everywhere. For full-space TV, use $u$ itself. For a bounded-domain Dirichlet or Neumann problem, use the zero extension $\widetilde u$ only to define the geometric level sets; this does not change the selected regularizer, and for each nonzero level the resulting set lies inside $\Omega$. For $t>0$, the positive $t$-level class is the measurable-set class of $E_t^+(u):=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:u(x)>t\}$; for $t<0$, the negative $t$-level class is the class of $E_t^-(u):=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:u(x)<t\}$. These classes do not depend on the representative of $u$. For any measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, its density-one representative is

$$E^{(1)}:=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{|E\cap B(x,r)|}{|B(x,r)|}=1\right\}.$$

This representative depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $E$. The canonical level set $U_u^{(t)}$ is $(E_t^+(u))^{(1)}$ when $t>0$ and $(E_t^-(u))^{(1)}$ when $t<0$. Its canonical boundary is the ordinary topological boundary $\partial U_u^{(t)}$ in $\mathbb R^2$. For two nonempty boundary sets, use the usual extended Hausdorff distance induced by Euclidean distance; set $d_H(\varnothing,\varnothing)=0$ and $d_H(E,F)=+\infty$ if exactly one set is empty. Hausdorff convergence uses this convention and is invariant under changes to a function on a null set.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let
$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y
otin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and
$$\int f\,d\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}=\int_X I_f\,d\mu=\int_Y J_f\,d
u.$$
2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes 
u})$, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $A:L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)\to L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ be bounded and real-linear, let $f=Au^\dagger$, and suppose $u^\dagger$ is a minimum-TV exact solution with a source certificate $p^\dagger$. For $\alpha_n>0$ tending to zero and noises $w_n\in L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$, assume $\|A^*\|\|w_n\|_2/\alpha_n\le\eta$ and let $u_n$ be supplied global minimizers of $\frac12\|Au-(f+w_n)\|_2^2+\alpha_n TV(u)$. Define $p_n=(f+w_n-Au_n)/\alpha_n$ and $v_n=A^*p_n$. Use $TV_2$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ for full-space TV; on a nonempty bounded Lipschitz domain use zero-extension Dirichlet TV, and on a nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz domain use relative Neumann TV. For bounded-domain geometry use the ambient zero-extended level sets and their topological boundaries in $\mathbb R^2$.

For full-space or Dirichlet TV, assume $\eta<2\sqrt\pi$; in the bounded Dirichlet case also assume $\Omega$ has global obstacle curvature $\kappa_\Omega\in L^1(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ with $\kappa_\Omega\ge g$ almost everywhere outside $\Omega$ for some real-valued $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^2\setminus\Omega;\mathbb R)$. For Neumann TV, let $C_\Omega$ be a constant from the BV Sobolev–Poincaré inequality $\|u-u_\Omega\|_2\le C_\Omega TV(u;\Omega)$ and assume $\eta<1/C_\Omega$.

For almost every nonzero $t$, the level set $E_n(t)$ has finite measure and perimeter, minimizes the branch-specific perimeter minus $\int_{E}\operatorname{sgn}(t)v_n$ under compactly supported perturbations, and satisfies $P(E_n(t))=\operatorname{sgn}(t)\int_{E_n(t)}v_n$. There are constants $c>0$ and $r_0>0$, independent of $n$ and almost every such $t$, such that for every $x\in\partial E_n(t)$ and $0<r<r_0$,
$$|B(x,r)\cap E_n(t)|\ge c|B(x,r)|,\qquad |B(x,r)\setminus E_n(t)|\ge c|B(x,r)|.$$
In the full-space branch all these level sets are contained in one common ball; in the bounded branches they lie in $\overline\Omega$. The same density and support conclusions are asserted for any selected minimum-TV exact limit that carries the inherited source certificate, using zero noise. Whenever the corresponding level sets converge in measure, their canonical boundaries converge in Hausdorff distance.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to the supplied minimizers, retaining its subsequence, and call its limit $u_0$. Then $Au_0=f$, $R(u_0)$ is minimal among exact solutions, and $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u_0)$. In bounded domains the subsequence already converges strongly in $L^1(\Omega)$. In full space, [F5] supplies a common ball containing the regularized and limit level sets for almost every nonzero level. By [F2] and the positive and negative layer-cake identities, for each fixed $n$ the integral of $|u_n|$ outside that ball is the integral over levels of the measures of those level sets outside it; Tonelli [F3] makes this integral zero. The same argument applies to $u_0$, so local $L^1$ convergence from [F1] is global $L^1$ convergence.

By [F2], for each real-valued $u$ the positive and negative level sets use $\{u>t\}$ for $t>0$ and $\{u<t\}$ for $t<0$. They satisfy the pointwise layer-cake identity $$|u(x)-u_0(x)|=\int_0^\infty|\mathbf1_{\{u>t\}}-\mathbf1_{\{u_0>t\}}|\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0|\mathbf1_{\{u<t\}}-\mathbf1_{\{u_0<t\}}|\,dt.$$ Integrating and applying [F3] gives $$\|u_n-u_0\|_1=\int_0^\infty|E_n^+(t)\mathbin\triangle E_0^+(t)|\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0|E_n^-(t)\mathbin\triangle E_0^-(t)|\,dt.$$ The right side tends to zero by step 1.1.

Let $g_n(t)$ denote the symmetric-difference measure of the positive level sets for $t>0$ and of the negative level sets for $t<0$. Step 2.1 says $g_n\to0$ in $L^1(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\})$. Choose a further subsequence with $\sum_k\|g_{n_k}\|_1<\infty$; Tonelli implies $\sum_k g_{n_k}(t)<\infty$ for almost every nonzero $t$, hence the level sets converge in measure there.

Fix a nonzero level for which step 3.1 gives measure convergence. If the limit level set is empty and infinitely many regularized level sets are nonempty, [F5] gives compact common support, so each such set has a boundary point; choose one for each index using [A1]. Its two-sided density estimate at a fixed radius $r<r_0$ forces symmetric-difference measure at least $c\pi r^2$, contradicting convergence to the empty limit. If the limit set is nonempty, it has positive measure because it is a nonempty density-one representative; measure convergence therefore rules out infinitely many empty regularized sets. Hence empty status agrees eventually, and the empty boundaries have Hausdorff distance zero by [F2]. For the remaining nonempty sets, [F5] supplies the two-sided density and support bounds. If boundary points of $E_{n_k}(t)$ stayed a fixed distance from $\partial E_0(t)$, choose them using [A1]; bounded support and [F4] give a convergent subsequence. A ball around its limit lies on one side of $E_0(t)$, while the two-sided density bound forces a fixed positive symmetric-difference measure, contradicting step 3.1. Conversely, if a boundary point of $E_0(t)$ stayed a fixed distance from every $\partial E_{n_k}(t)$, choose these points using [A1]; compact support and [F4] give a subsequence converging to $y\in\partial E_0(t)$. A connected ball around $y$ misses those boundaries for all large $k$, so each $E_{n_k}(t)$ is either full or empty there. A subsequence with one fixed status and measure convergence would make $E_0(t)$ full or empty almost everywhere on a smaller ball, contradicting that $y$ lies on the boundary of its canonical density-one representative. Thus the canonical boundaries converge in Hausdorff distance. The limit is the selected solution from [F1]; if the exact minimum-TV solution is unique it equals $u^\dagger$, and otherwise no such identification is asserted.

current_manifest_record.statement:
Define $\eta(u)=0$ for $u\le0$ and $\eta(u)=e^{-1/u}$ for $u>0$, and put $f(x)=\eta(1-|x|^2)$ on $\mathbb R^2$. This is a nonzero, smooth, compactly supported radial phantom. Its Euclidean Radon transform is independent of $\theta$ and is
$$Rf(\theta,s)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int_{-\sqrt{1-s^2}}^{\sqrt{1-s^2}}\eta(1-s^2-t^2)\,dt,&|s|<1,\\[1.2ex]0,&|s|\ge1.\end{cases}$$

citations.quote:
Write $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth functions of compact support on the Euclidean plane. For $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, $n=1$ or $2$, use the compact-support Riemann Fourier transform
$$\widehat u(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}u(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx.$$
For $\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in S^1:=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x|=1\}$ put $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$. The line with normal $\theta$ and signed offset $s$ is $\{x\in\mathbb R^2:x\cdot\theta=s\}$. Its **Euclidean Radon transform** is
$$Rf(\theta,s):=\int_{\mathbb R}f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt,\qquad f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C),\ (\theta,s)\in S^1\times\mathbb R.$$
The line integral is a compact-support Riemann integral.
The full data set uses every oriented normal $\theta\in S^1$ and every $s\in\mathbb R$; the same unoriented line is represented by $(\theta,s)$ and $(-\theta,-s)$.
For a one-dimensional function $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, define
$$|D_s|h(s):=\int_{\mathbb R}2\pi|\sigma|\,\widehat h(\sigma)e^{2\pi i s\sigma}\,d\sigma.$$
For $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ define the Riesz potential notation used here by
$$|D|^{-1}f(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\frac{\widehat f(\xi)}{2\pi|\xi|}\,d\xi.$$
The quotient in the last integral is assigned value $0$ at $\xi=0$. These integrals are absolutely convergent on the stated classes: compact-support integration by parts gives rapid decay of $\widehat f$ and $\widehat h$, while $\widehat f$ is bounded near $0$ and $|\xi|^{-1}$ is locally integrable in two dimensions. Here the multiplier for $|D_s|$ is $2\pi|\sigma|$, corresponding to the $e^{-2\pi i s\sigma}$ Fourier convention.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

derivations.claim: For $u>0$, repeated differentiation gives $\eta^{(k)}(u)=P_k(1/u)e^{-1/u}$ for a polynomial $P_k$. For every integer $m\ge0$, $v^me^{-v}\to0$ as $v\to\infty$: if $v>0$, the exponential series gives $e^v\ge v^{m+1}/(m+1)!$. Hence each right derivative tends to $0$ at $u=0$, and the quotient $\eta^{(k)}(u)/u$ also tends to $0$ because it is again a polynomial in $1/u$ times $e^{-1/u}$. Induction on $k$ shows the zero extension is smooth on $\mathbb R$.
The composition $f(x)=\eta(1-|x|^2)$ is smooth and radial; it vanishes whenever $|x|\ge1$ and is positive at $x=0$. Thus it is nonzero and has compact support in the closed unit disk.

For every $\theta\in S^1$, orthogonality gives $|s\theta+t\theta^\perp|^2=s^2+t^2$, so [F1] yields $Rf(\theta,s)=\int_{\mathbb R}\eta(1-s^2-t^2)\,dt$. If $|s|\ge1$, then $1-s^2-t^2\le0$ for every $t$, so the line integral is $0$; if $|s|<1$, the integrand vanishes outside $|t|<\sqrt{1-s^2}$ and equals the exponential displayed in the Example inside that interval, with value $0$ at its endpoints because $\eta(0)=0$. It depends on $\theta$ only through the norm identity, so the sinogram is radial-data independent of orientation. The continuous compactly supported integrands are Riemann integrable by [F2].

current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mu$ be the polar surface measure on $S^1$, defined on Borel $E\subseteq S^1$ by
$$\mu(E):=2\lambda_2\bigl(\{r\theta:\theta\in E,\ 0<r\le1\}\bigr),$$
where $\lambda_2$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^2$. For continuous $g:S^1\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ for which the integral exists, define its **backprojection** by
$$R^*g(x):=\int_{S^1}g(\theta,x\cdot\theta)\,d\mu(\theta).$$
For every $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^2$, the normal-operator and filtered-backprojection identities hold:
$$R^*Rf(x)=4\pi|D|^{-1}f(x),\qquad f(x)=\frac1{4\pi}R^*|D_s|Rf(x),$$
with $|D|^{-1}$ and $|D_s|$ as defined for the compact-support Fourier convention in the Euclidean Radon transform definition.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Write $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth functions of compact support on the Euclidean plane. For $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, $n=1$ or $2$, use the compact-support Riemann Fourier transform
$$\widehat u(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}u(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx.$$
For $\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in S^1:=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x|=1\}$ put $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$. The line with normal $\theta$ and signed offset $s$ is $\{x\in\mathbb R^2:x\cdot\theta=s\}$. Its **Euclidean Radon transform** is
$$Rf(\theta,s):=\int_{\mathbb R}f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt,\qquad f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C),\ (\theta,s)\in S^1\times\mathbb R.$$
The line integral is a compact-support Riemann integral.
The full data set uses every oriented normal $\theta\in S^1$ and every $s\in\mathbb R$; the same unoriented line is represented by $(\theta,s)$ and $(-\theta,-s)$.
For a one-dimensional function $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, define
$$|D_s|h(s):=\int_{\mathbb R}2\pi|\sigma|\,\widehat h(\sigma)e^{2\pi i s\sigma}\,d\sigma.$$
For $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ define the Riesz potential notation used here by
$$|D|^{-1}f(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\frac{\widehat f(\xi)}{2\pi|\xi|}\,d\xi.$$
The quotient in the last integral is assigned value $0$ at $\xi=0$. These integrals are absolutely convergent on the stated classes: compact-support integration by parts gives rapid decay of $\widehat f$ and $\widehat h$, while $\widehat f$ is bounded near $0$ and $|\xi|^{-1}$ is locally integrable in two dimensions. Here the multiplier for $|D_s|$ is $2\pi|\sigma|$, corresponding to the $e^{-2\pi i s\sigma}$ Fourier convention.

For every $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$, every unit normal $\theta\in S^1$, and every $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, the compact-support Fourier transform of the line data in the offset variable equals the restriction of the two-dimensional Fourier transform to the line in frequency space with direction $\theta$:
$$\widehat{Rf}(\theta,\sigma)=\widehat f(\sigma\theta).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix $n \ge 1$
and write
$$S^{n-1}:=\{\omega \in \mathbb R^n : |\omega|=1\}.$$
Let
$$\Phi:\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow(0,\infty)\times S^{n-1},\qquad \Phi(x)=(|x|,x/|x|).$$
This map is continuous. If $E\subseteq S^{n-1}$ is Borel, then
$(0,1]\times E$ is Borel and
$$\{r\omega:\omega\in E,\ 0<r\le1\}=\Phi^{-1}((0,1]\times E)$$
is Borel in $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ by
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]], hence Borel in
$\mathbb R^n$ by [[thm-borel-sigma-algebra-of-a-subspace-is-the-trace]]. It is
therefore Lebesgue measurable by [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]].
Define
$$\sigma(E):=n\,\lambda_n(\{r\omega : \omega \in E,\ 0<r\le 1\}).$$

The next theorem proves that this is a Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ and that it
is exactly the surface measure needed for polar coordinates.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ (Linear map between vector spaces over the same field,
Every Euclidean linear map has a unique matrix and satisfies $\|Lh\|_2\le K\|h\|_2$ for some $K\ge0$).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Assume countable choice. The negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform is continuous $\mathcal F:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S$, and
$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $Q=\prod_{i=1}^n[a_i,b_i]$ with $n\ge1$ and $a_i<b_i$. If a bounded Borel real function $f$ on $Q$ is Riemann integrable, then it is Lebesgue integrable and the two integrals agree. The corresponding assertion for complex functions holds componentwise. In particular it applies to smooth compact test integrands and their bounded Borel zero extensions from compact Jordan regions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.

If $T$ preserves $\mu$ and $f:X\to[0,\infty]$ is measurable, then $\int f\circ T\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu$, allowing infinity. If $f$ is integrable real or complex valued, $f\circ T$ is integrable and the same equality holds. Conversely, for a measurable self-map, equality for every measurable indicator implies measure preservation.

Since $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$, it is a Schwartz function. Choose $R>0$ with $\operatorname{supp}f\subset B_R(0)$. For every $	heta\in S^1$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, the integrand $f(s	heta+t	heta^\perp)$ vanishes for $|t|>R$, because $|s	heta+t	heta^\perp|^2=s^2+t^2$. Thus the line integral is over the fixed interval $[-R,R]$. On every bounded $s$-interval, $(	heta,s,t)\mapsto f(s	heta+t	heta^\perp)$ is uniformly continuous on the compact parameter product with $S^1$ and $[-R,R]$, so its integral is jointly continuous in $(	heta,s)$. For fixed $	heta$, write $f=f_{\mathrm R}+if_{\mathrm I}$ and $F_
u(s,t)=f_
u(s	heta+t	heta^\perp)$ for $
u\in\{\mathrm R,\mathrm I\}$. The inner coordinate map is linear with constant derivative, so repeated use of [F12] gives $\partial_s^kF_

u(s	heta+t	heta^\perp)$ for every $k$. Apply [F11] on $[0,1]$ to each real function $u\mapsto\partial_s^kF_
u(s+uh,t)$: by [F12] its derivative is $h\,\partial_s^{k+1}F_
u(s+uh,t)$, which is continuous and Riemann integrable by [F13], including at the endpoints. Dividing the resulting identity by any nonzero $h$ gives the difference quotient as the $u$-integral of $\partial_s^{k+1}F_
u(s+uh,t)$. Uniform continuity on each compact $(s,t)$ rectangle makes this converge uniformly in $t\in[-R,R]$; integrating and recombining the two real components therefore gives $\partial_s^k Rf(	heta,s)=\int_{-R}^{R}(	heta\cdot
abla)^k f(s	heta+t	heta^\perp)\,dt$ for every $k\ge0$, with each derivative continuous. Also $Rf(	heta,s)=0$ for $|s|>R$, so $Rf(	heta,\cdot)\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ and is Schwartz. For every $x$, joint continuity makes $	heta\mapsto Rf(	heta,x\cdot	heta)$ continuous; [F4] makes $\mu$ finite, so the defining backprojection integral exists. By [F6] and [F7], the Lebesgue Fourier transforms of $f$ and $Rf(	heta,\cdot)$ are Schwartz and satisfy pointwise inversion; [F8] identifies them with the compact-support Riemann transforms in [F1]. Also $|\widehat f(\xi)|\le\int|f|$, and [F4] shows $|\xi|^{-1}\widehat f(\xi)$ is integrable near $0$; outside the unit disk it is dominated by the integrable Schwartz function $|\widehat f|$. Rapid decay of $\widehat f$ and finiteness of $\mu$ make the later signed-frequency integrals absolutely convergent.

Apply [F7] to $Rf(\theta,\cdot)$ at $s=x\cdot\theta$, then substitute the slice identity [F2] to get $Rf(\theta,x\cdot\theta)=\int_{\mathbb R}\widehat f(\sigma\theta)e^{2\pi i\sigma x\cdot\theta}\,d\sigma$. By [F4], $\mu$ is finite, and by [F14] Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$ is sigma-finite, so the measure spaces in [F9] are sigma-finite. The integrand is continuous; since $\widehat f$ is Schwartz, $|\widehat f(\sigma\theta)|\le C_N(1+|\sigma|)^{-N}$ uniformly in $\theta$, and choosing $N>1$ shows it is absolutely integrable on their product. Thus [F9] permits either order of integration and gives $R^*Rf(x)=\int_{S^1}\int_{\mathbb R}\widehat f(\sigma\theta)e^{2\pi i\sigma x\cdot\theta}\,d\sigma\,d\mu(\theta)$.

The polar definition [F3] and change of variables [F5] imply $\mu(-E)=\mu(E)$ for every Borel $E\subseteq S^1$, since the cone of $-E$ is the image under $-I$ of the cone of $E$ and $|\det(-I)|=1$. Thus $\theta\mapsto-\theta$ preserves $\mu$. The reflection $\sigma\mapsto-\sigma$ preserves Lebesgue measure by [F5] in dimension one. Both maps are Borel, so [F15] permits these substitutions in the integrable angular and frequency integrands. Split the $\sigma$-integral in step 2.1 at zero and use $r=-\sigma$ and $\theta\mapsto-\theta$ on its negative half to obtain twice the positive-half integral. Apply [F4] to $h(\xi)=\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}/|\xi|$, set to zero at $\xi=0$; for complex $h$, apply the nonnegative formula to positive and negative real and imaginary parts and use [F10]. Thus $R^*Rf(x)=2\int_{\mathbb R^2}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}|\xi|^{-1}d\lambda_2(\xi)=4\pi|D|^{-1}f(x)$.

By [F1] and [F2], $|D_s|Rf(\theta,s)=\int_{\mathbb R}2\pi|\sigma|\widehat f(\sigma\theta)e^{2\pi i s\sigma}\,d\sigma$. Schwartz decay gives a bound $|\widehat f(\sigma\theta)|\le C_N(1+|\sigma|)^{-N}$ uniform in $\theta$. On each compact parameter set $S^1\times[-A,A]$, the truncated integrals over bounded $\sigma$-intervals are continuous in $(\theta,s)$, while the displayed bound makes their tails uniformly tend to zero; hence the filtered data are jointly continuous. The same bound gives absolute convergence and boundedness, so finiteness of $\mu$ makes the backprojection integral exist. For fixed $x$, the product integrand $2\pi|\sigma|\widehat f(\sigma\theta)e^{2\pi i\sigma x\cdot\theta}$ is continuous and absolutely integrable by the same bound with $N>2$. Step 3.1 is the normal-operator identity, and dividing step 4.1 by $4\pi$ gives the filtered-backprojection identity. Both hold pointwise for every $x\in\mathbb R^2$.

current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact smooth Riemannian manifold of positive dimension with smooth boundary and $q$ a smooth real function. Set $H=L^2(M,dV_g)$, $V=H^1_0(M)$ and $c=1+\|q\|_\infty$. Then
$$b(u,v)=\int_M(\langle\nabla u,\nabla\bar v\rangle+(q+c)u\bar v)\,dV_g$$
is an equivalent Hilbert inner product on $V$. There are an $H$-orthonormal sequence $(e_j)$ complete in $H$ and positive numbers $\mu_j\to\infty$ such that $b(e_j,v)=\mu_j(e_j,v)_H$ for every $v\in V$, and
$$b(u,u)=\sum_j\mu_j|(u,e_j)_H|^2\qquad(u\in V).$$
For $A=-\Delta_g+q$, weak solutions $v\in V$ of $Av=f\in H^k(M)$ satisfy
$$\|v\|_{H^{k+2}(M)}\le C_k(\|f\|_{H^k(M)}+\|v\|_{L^2(M)}),\qquad k=0,1,\ldots.$$
Here integer Sobolev norms use any finite smooth atlas. For every nonnegative integer $a$, the inclusion $H^k(M)\to C^a(M)$ is bounded for all sufficiently large integers $k$.

citations.quote: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $C^2$
domain, $n\ge2$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $L,a$ be as in
[[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with ellipticity
constant $\theta$, bounds $M_a,M_b,M_c$ and $a^{ij}\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)$,
$b^i,c\in L^\infty(\Omega)$, and let $f\in L^2(\Omega)$. If
$u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of $Lu=f$ with zero boundary values
([[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]]), then
$u\in H^2(\Omega)$ and there is
$C=C(n,\Omega,\theta,M_a,M_b,M_c,\|Da^{ij}\|_\infty)$ with
$$\|u\|_{H^2(\Omega)}\le C\big(\|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\big).$$
The $L^2$ norm of $u$ on the right cannot be deleted without a hypothesis
excluding the homogeneous kernel, as the companion counterexample shows; the
theorem is stated for zero Dirichlet data, and nonzero compatible boundary
data are handled by an $H^2$ lifting, with an $L^2$ residual forcing,
before the theorem is applied.

u_{\mathrm{out}}$ be the outward unit normal. Write $
abla_g u$ for the metric gradient, $\Delta_g u=\operatorname{div}_g
abla_g u$, $dV_g$ for Riemannian volume, and $dS_g$ for the induced boundary measure. The $C^1$ norms below are computed in any fixed finite smooth atlas of the indicated compact sets. For $u,v\in C^2([0,T]	imes M)$,
$$\int_Q ig((\partial_t^2-\Delta_g)u\,v-u(\partial_t^2-\Delta_g)v ig)\,dV_gdt =\int_\Sigma ig(u\,\partial_{
u_{\mathrm{out}}}v-v\,\partial_{
u_{\mathrm{out}}}u ig)\,dS_gdt +\int_M[\partial_tu\,v-u\,\partial_tv]_{t=0}^{t=T}\,dV_g.$$
For every $h\in C_c^\infty(\Sigma)$ there is a smooth lift $H$ on $[0,T]	imes M$ with $H|_\Sigma=h$, supported in a fixed boundary collar and zero near $t=0,T$, such that $\|H\|_{C^1([0,T]	imes M)}\le C\|h\|_{C^1(\Sigma)}$. For every $u\in C^1([0,T]	imes M)$ the classical normal trace obeys
$$\|\partial_{
u_{\mathrm{out}}}u\|_{L^2(\Sigma)}\le  ig(T\,\operatorname{area}_g(\partial M) ig)^{1/2}\|

derivations.claim: On each of finitely many relatively compact coordinate charts, metric eigenvalues and the volume density have positive lower and finite upper bounds. Thus the intrinsic $H^1$ norm is equivalent to the sum of coordinate $H^1$ norms of a fixed smooth partition of unity. A Cauchy sequence has $L^2$ limits for the localized functions and their first derivatives; testing against a smooth function and passing to the limit identifies the derivative limits as the weak derivatives of the function limit. This proves completeness; $V$, being a closure, is closed. Moreover $1\le q+c\le1+2\|q\|_\infty$, so $b$ and the $H^1$ inner product have equivalent norms. To prove density of $V$ in $H$, localize an $H$-function by a finite smooth partition. In an interior chart, extend each localized piece by zero and approximate it in $L^2$ by mollification. In a boundary half-chart, the localized piece is supported away from the chart sides; multiply it by a smooth cutoff that vanishes for $0\le x_n\le\delta$ and equals one for $x_n\ge2\delta$. The boundary face has $n$-dimensional volume zero. Given $\epsilon>0$, choose $R$ so large that $\int_{\{|u|^2>R\}}|u|^2\,dV_g<\epsilon/2$, by truncating the integrable function $|u|^2$. For the strip $S_\delta=\{0<x_n<2\delta\}$, $\int_{S_\delta}|u|^2\,dV_g\le\epsilon/2+R\,\operatorname{vol}_g(S_\delta)$, and $\operatorname{vol}_g(S_\delta)=O(\delta)$ because the coordinate density is bounded. Thus the $L^2$ error tends to zero as $\delta\downarrow0$. Each cut-off piece is supported away from the boundary and is then approximated by mollification. Summing the finite chart approximations proves that $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ is dense in $H$.

The inclusion $V\hookrightarrow H$ is compact without an arbitrary-index choice argument. Indeed, a localized $v\in V$ extends by zero across a flattened boundary: approximate in $H^1$ by localized interior smooth functions, extend those, and pass to the weak-derivative identities. All extensions have bounded support in a fixed coordinate box. On a cube $C$ of side $\delta$, successively average in its $n$ coordinate variables. The one-variable identity $f(s)-f(t)=\int_t^s f'(r)dr$ and Cauchy–Schwarz give $\|f-\operatorname{avg}_C f\|_{L^2(C)}\le n\delta\|Df\|_{L^2(C)}$ by telescoping those averages; density extends this to $H^1$. Replacement by the mean on each cube of a fixed finite grid is therefore a finite-rank approximation to each coordinate inclusion, with error $O(\delta)$ uniformly on the $H^1$ unit ball. Sum the finitely many coordinate reconstructions to approximate $V\hookrightarrow H$ in operator norm by finite-rank maps. A bounded finite-dimensional set has finite nets; choosing $\delta=2^{-k}$ makes the inclusion's image totally bounded, and completeness of $H$ makes its closure compact. Only countably many finite nets are involved.

In a coordinate chart $Av=f$ is $$-\partial_i(\rho g^{ij}\partial_jv)+\rho qv=\rho f,\qquad \rho=\sqrt{\det g}.$$ The principal matrix is smooth uniformly positive on each compact chart. Localize by a smooth cutoff; its commutator with $A$ has order one. For $n=1$, put $G=\rho g^{11}>0$ on a localized interval or half-interval and absorb the first-order cutoff commutator into an $L^2$ right side $f_\chi$, with $\|f_\chi\|_2\le C(\|f\|_2+\|v\|_{H^1})$. The weak equation is $-(Gv')'+\rho qv=f_\chi$, so $(Gv')'=\rho qv-f_\chi\in L^2$. Since $Gv'\in L^2$, this gives $Gv'\in H^1$, and smooth positivity of $G$ gives $v\in H^2$ with the local estimate $\|v\|_{H^2}\le C(\|f_\chi\|_2+\|v\|_{H^1})$. For $n\ge2$, in a boundary chart flatten to $x_n\ge0$ and localize away from the chart sides. The localization can be regarded as a zero-Dirichlet function on a bounded smooth domain agreeing with the half-space near its support and rounded elsewhere. Applying [F3] and the same interior estimate, then summing the finite cover, gives $\|v\|_{H^2}\le C(\|f\|_2+\|v\|_{H^1})$ in every dimension. Testing the equation with $v$ gives $\|v\|_{H^1}\le C(\|f\|_2+\|v\|_2)$ by absorbing the gradient term, so this is the stated $k=0$ estimate.

For $f\in H$, use [F1] to solve $b(Kf,v)=(f,v)_H$. The map $K:H\to V$ is bounded, and step 2.1 makes $K:H\to H$ compact. Symmetry gives $(Kf,h)_H=b(Kf,Kh)=(f,Kh)_H$, positivity gives $(Kf,f)_H=b(Kf,Kf)>0$ for $f\ne0$, and density of $V$ makes $K$ injective. Its range is dense since a vector orthogonal to the range lies in the kernel by self-adjointness. Apply [F2] to obtain positive eigenvalues $\kappa_j\to0$ and a complete $H$-orthonormal family; put $\mu_j=\kappa_j^{-1}$. Repeated finite multiplicities are included. The vectors $e_j/\sqrt{\mu_j}$ are $b$-orthonormal and complete in $V$: if $b(v,e_j)=0$ for every $j$, then $(v,e_j)_H=0$ for every $j$, hence $v=0$. Orthogonal projection and completeness therefore give the asserted $b$-Parseval identity and convergence of the spectral projections in $V$.

Here is the boundary induction for higher orders. For $n=1$, in each localized chart write $G=\rho g^{11}>0$ and $-(Gv')'+\rho qv=f_\chi$, where the cutoff commutator satisfies $f_\chi\in H^k$ and $\|f_\chi\|_{H^k}\le C_k(\|f\|_{H^k}+\|v\|_{H^{k+1}})$ whenever $f\in H^k$ and $v\in H^{k+1}$. Then $(Gv')'=\rho qv-f_\chi\in H^k$, so $Gv'\in H^{k+1}$ and smooth positivity of $G$ gives $v\in H^{k+2}$, with $\|v\|_{H^{k+2}}\le C_k(\|f\|_{H^k}+\|v\|_{H^{k+1}})$. This proves the one-dimensional induction, including its $k=0$ start. For $n\ge2$, suppose $f\in H^k$ and $v\in H^{k+1}$ is already known. In a flattened boundary chart apply a tangential derivative $D_{x'}^\alpha$, $|\alpha|=k$, to the localized equation. Its commutator with the second-order operator contains derivatives of $v$ of order at most $k+1$ with bounded smooth coefficients. The localized $D_{x'}^\alpha v$ has zero trace and lies in $H^1$; this follows first for tangential difference quotients, which preserve zero trace, and then by their $H^1$ limit. The $k=0$ local estimate of step 2.2 gives its $H^2$ bound in terms of $\|f\|_{H^k}+\|v\|_{H^{k+1}}$. If a derivative has total order $k+2$ and at least three normal factors, differentiate the equation $k$ times, isolating the term $\rho g^{nn}D_n^2v$. Divide by the positive coefficient $\rho g^{nn}$. Each other highest-order derivative has fewer normal factors because its two principal derivatives include a tangential derivative; all commutators have order at most $k+1$. Induction on the number of normal factors therefore bounds every derivative of order $k+2$. Interior patches allow derivatives in all directions. Difference quotients justify each differentiation before regularity is established; the bounds are uniform in their increments, and testing their weak limits identifies the claimed derivatives. Nested cutoffs and the finite cover give $\|v\|_{H^{k+2}}\le C_k(\|f\|_{H^k}+\|v\|_{H^{k+1}})$, and the previous induction level absorbs the last term into $C_k(\|f\|_{H^k}+\|v\|_2)$. This proves all asserted elliptic estimates.

For completeness the needed high-order embedding also has a finite-chart proof with this axiom base. In a half-chart extend across $x_n=0$ by $\sum_{j=1}^{k+1}a_jv(x',-jx_n)$ for $x_n<0$, where the finite Vandermonde system $\sum_j a_j(-j)^\ell=1$ for $0\le\ell\le k$ matches the derivatives at the interface. After a cutoff this is a bounded $H^k$ extension; the assertion follows first on smooth functions and then by the weak derivative identities and approximation. On a bounded support box, iterated one-dimensional integration gives $\|D^\alpha w\|_\infty\le C\|D_1\cdots D_nD^\alpha w\|_2$ for smooth compactly supported $w$. Apply this also to first derivatives of $D^\alpha w$ and to differences of mollifications. For $k\ge n+a+1$ these mollifications and all derivatives through order $a$ are uniformly Cauchy and their limits are continuous, with the asserted norm bound; passing to the coordinate segment integral identifies them as classical derivatives. Sum the finite chart extensions. This proves the embedding and completes the lemma.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a smooth spacetime manifold of dimension $m\ge2$ with a smooth positive density, and let $P=\sum_{|\alpha|\le2}a_\alpha(x)D^\alpha$ be a scalar second-order differential operator with smooth coefficients in local coordinates. In each local chart, use the microlocal convention $D_j:=(1/i)\partial_{x_j}=-i\partial_{x_j}$ and $D^\alpha:=D_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots D_m^{\alpha_m}$. Its principal symbol $p(x,\xi)=\sum_{|\alpha|=2}a_\alpha(x)\xi^\alpha$ is real and satisfies $dp\ne0$ on $\{p=0\}\subset T^*X\setminus0$. Equip $T^*X$ with its canonical cotangent symplectic form and define the Hamilton vector field by $\iota_{H_p}\omega_{\rm can}=dp$. A null bicharacteristic is a nonzero integral curve of $H_p$ contained in $\{p=0\}$. Let $\Gamma$ be a compact phase-space segment that is an injective immersion with no repeated phase points; assume its base projection is an immersion (the no-cusp condition) and that the segment is contained in the interior of $T^*X\setminus0$. For every integer $N\ge1$, there are complex smooth functions $u_\lambda$ formed from finitely many branch-local packets, each supported in a fixed tubular neighborhood of an embedded local branch of the base projection of $\Gamma$. Their longitudinal cutoffs equal one on the portion under observation and are supported in the chosen branch extensions. As $\lambda\to+\infty$, they have the following properties:

1. On each embedded local branch of the base projection, the phase has a formal transverse Taylor expansion solving the complex eikonal equation to every prescribed finite order; its transverse imaginary Hessian is positive definite and yields Gaussian decay away from that branch. At projected crossings the beam is the finite sum of the branch-local packets; a single phase on the crossing union is not required.
2. On each branch the amplitudes solve the transport hierarchy to the corresponding order and are realized by a Borel sum; the finitely many branch-local packets are patched and summed using their compatible jets.
3. Write $s$ for a fixed smooth parameter on the projected curve and fix its origin. There is a smooth positive transported density $w(s)ds$, normalized by $w(0)=1$, such that the measures $|u_\lambda|^2dV_X$ converge against compactly supported smooth tests away from endpoint neighborhoods to $\int a(\pi\Gamma(s))w(s)ds$. The weight is the one determined by the leading transport equation; a general operator with complex lower-order coefficients need not give constant $w$. For the real formally self-adjoint wave operator, with parameter equal to physical time along a unit-speed spatial ray and the wave phase normalized by $|\partial_t\phi|=1$, the transport gives $w=1$.
4. For every compact set $K$ disjoint from neighborhoods of the two projected endpoints, $\|Pu_\lambda\|_{L^2(K)}=O(\lambda^{-N})$ for each requested $N$, after carrying the expansions sufficiently far. The endpoint cutoff generally produces a residual near those endpoints. In particular, if the segment extends outside a compact measurement domain and its two endpoint neighborhoods are disjoint from that domain, the residual has the asserted order throughout that domain.

The cutoff in the ambient extension is one along the portion of the ray under observation and vanishes beyond the extended endpoints. A segment wholly in the spacetime interior does not have a globally negligible endpoint residual. Its tube can be supported away from the boundary and then has zero boundary trace; a wave beam entering and exiting a measurement domain instead has its actual smooth boundary trace there. In this wave specialization, if the extended beam is zero near the required initial or terminal time, the zero-boundary energy correction on the measurement cylinder gives an exact solution with the same boundary data and an $O(\lambda^{-N})$ energy error for any requested $N$. The claim concerns an embedded segment in phase space and permits projected self-intersections.

citations.quote: Let $X$ be a smooth manifold with an auxiliary smooth Riemannian metric, let $J=[a,b]$ be a compact interval, and let $\beta:J\to X$ be a smooth embedding with nonzero derivative. The normal fiber at $s$ is $N_s\beta=\{v\in T_{\beta(s)}X:g(v,\dot\beta(s))=0\}$. A **formal scalar jet along $\beta$** means a family of symmetric coordinate Taylor coefficients $T_{i,\alpha}(s)$ on a finite coordinate cover of a tubular neighborhood, smooth in $s\in J$, whose formal Taylor series transform on overlaps by the ordinary chain rule for a scalar function. Then there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $\beta(J)$ and, for either scalar field $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, an $F\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb K)$ whose transverse derivatives along $\beta$ realize every prescribed transverse coefficient $T_{i,\alpha}(s)$. The construction is uniform for a compact parameter family of such jets when all coefficient seminorms are uniformly bounded. The same assertion holds on a finite union $A$ of embedded compact segments provided the induced full ambient jets satisfy full Whitney compatibility on that compact union: in each coordinate chart, for every $k$ and $|\alpha|\le k$, the degree-$k$ Taylor polynomials $P_x^k$ satisfy $D^\alpha P_x^k(y)-D^\alpha P_y^k(y)=o(|x-y|^{k-|\alpha|})$ uniformly for $x,y\in A$ as $|x-y|\to0$. Tangential components of a full jet are obtained by differentiating the transverse coefficients along each segment and applying the coordinate chain rule. For parameter families on the same finite union, require these Whitney remainder moduli as well as all coefficient bounds to be uniform. The single-segment construction requires no choice axiom.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$ and let $p\in M$. Then there exist
$h>0$, an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, and a smooth map

$$ \Phi:(-h,h)\times U\to M $$

such that for every $q\in U$, the curve $t\mapsto \Phi(t,q)$ is the unique
integral curve of $X$ on $(-h,h)$ with initial value $\Phi(0,q)=q$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth Riemannian manifold with nonempty smooth boundary, let $T>0$, and let $q\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ be independent of time. Let $dV_g$ be Riemannian volume, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ be the scalar field, and set $L^2(M)=L^2(M,dV_g;\mathbb K)$. For complex scalars, the $L^2$ inner product is $(u,v)_{L^2}=\int_M u\overline v\,dV_g$, linear in its first argument; extend $g$ complex-bilinearly and set $|\nabla_gu|_g^2=\langle\nabla_gu,\nabla_g\overline u\rangle_g$. A weak coordinate derivative $D_iw$ is defined by $\int w\,\partial_i\psi=-\int D_iw\,\psi$ for every smooth compactly supported coordinate test $\psi$. Let $H^1(M;\mathbb K)$ be the space of $L^2(M;\mathbb K)$ functions whose weak coordinate first derivatives are locally $L^2$ in smooth charts and whose weak differential has finite metric $L^2$ norm; write $\nabla_gu$ for the metric dual of that weak differential. Give it norm
$$\|w\|_{H^1(M;\mathbb K)}^2=\int_M(|w|^2+|\nabla_gw|_g^2)\,dV_g,$$
and let $H_0^1(M;\mathbb K)$ be the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in this norm. For $u_0\in H_0^1(M;\mathbb K)$, $u_1\in L^2(M;\mathbb K)$, and $F\in L^1((0,T);L^2(M;\mathbb K))$, there is a unique energy solution of the homogeneous Dirichlet problem
$$u_{tt}-\Delta_gu+q(x)u=F,\qquad u|_{(0,T)\times\partial M}=0,\qquad (u(0),u_t(0))=(u_0,u_1),$$
where energy solution means
$$u\in C([0,T];H_0^1(M;\mathbb K))\cap C^1([0,T];L^2(M;\mathbb K)),$$
and, for every $\phi\in H_0^1(M;\mathbb K)$ and every real-valued $\zeta\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$, the weak equation is
$$\int_0^T(u(t),\phi)_{L^2}\zeta''(t)\,dt+\int_0^T\!\int_M\big(\langle\nabla_gu(t),\nabla_g\overline{\phi}\rangle_g+q\,u(t)\overline{\phi}\big)\zeta(t)\,dV_gdt=\int_0^T(F(t),\phi)_{L^2}\zeta(t)\,dt.$$
There is a constant $C=C(M,g,q,T)<\infty$ such that
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\big(\|u(t)\|_{H^1(M;\mathbb K)}+\|u_t(t)\|_{L^2(M;\mathbb K)}\big)\le C\big(\|u_0\|_{H^1(M;\mathbb K)}+\|u_1\|_{L^2(M;\mathbb K)}+\|F\|_{L^1((0,T);L^2(M;\mathbb K))}\big).$$
In particular, the solution $w$ with zero initial data satisfies the correction estimate
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\big(\|w(t)\|_{H^1(M;\mathbb K)}+\|w_t(t)\|_{L^2(M;\mathbb K)}\big)\le C\|F\|_{L^1((0,T);L^2(M;\mathbb K))}.$$
The corresponding assertion for prescribed terminal data follows by time reversal. For smooth Dirichlet data compactly supported away from the time endpoints, the boundary lifting in the Riemannian Green-and-lifting lemma reduces the problem to this homogeneous-boundary assertion.

derivations.claim: Write $\beta=\pi\circ\Gamma$ for the base curve. Cover its parameter interval by finitely many small overlapping intervals on which $\beta$ is embedded. In an ambient coordinate chart choose a coordinate $x_1$ whose derivative along $\beta$ is nonzero, and shrink the interval so $x_1\circ\beta$ is strictly monotone. Its inverse is continuous by monotonicity; the difference quotient gives derivative $1/(x_1\circ\beta)'$, and repeated differentiation gives smooth higher derivatives. The coordinate change $s=(x_1\circ\beta)^{-1}(x_1)$ and $y_j=x_j-x_j(\beta(s))$ has a triangular smooth inverse, so the branch is $y=0$ with its prescribed parameter $s$. Write $\xi(s)=(\xi_s(s),\xi_y(s))$ in these coordinates. Prescribe $\partial_y\phi(s,0)=\xi_y(s)$ and $\partial_s\phi(s,0)=\xi_s(s)$, integrating the latter from a chosen real initial phase value. These first jets are compatible with the eikonal equation because $p(s,0,\xi_s(s),\xi_y(s))=0$. The central covector has $p_{\xi_s}\ne0$ on a sufficiently small interval, since the Hamilton velocity in these coordinates is a nonzero multiple of $\partial_s$. Expand the formal equation $p(s,y,\partial_s\phi,\partial_y\phi)=0$ in transverse powers of $y$. At each degree the unknown coefficient satisfies a linear ODE in $s$ with nonzero leading coefficient $p_{\xi_s}$, so it is uniquely determined from its initial value; the coefficients depend smoothly on $s$. Its zeroth and first jet equations are exactly the given Hamilton curve (after its parameter change). Initialize the transverse Hessian by $H(0)=iI$ in the chosen transverse coordinates.

The quadratic jet equation is the matrix Riccati equation $$H'+D+BH+HB^T+HCH=0,$$ where $C,D$ are real symmetric and $B$ real, the corresponding blocks of the reduced Hamiltonian Hessian. Solve instead $Y'=B^TY+CZ$, $Z'=-DY-BZ$, $Y(0)=I$, $Z(0)=iI$. Direct differentiation gives $Y^TZ-Z^TY=0$ and $Y^*Z-Z^*Y=2iI$. If $Yv=0$ the second identity gives $0=2i|v|^2$, so $Y$ is invertible on the whole interval. Consequently $H=ZY^{-1}$ is symmetric, solves the Riccati equation, and $$\operatorname{Im}H=(Y^{-1})^*Y^{-1}>0.$$ Compactness gives uniform positive lower and finite upper bounds. At an overlap transform all jets by the coordinate chain rule, carry these initial data to the next chart, and use ODE uniqueness. Positivity is unchanged by real coordinate change and persists on the finite cover.

For transverse degree $k\ge3$, differentiating the reduced eikonal equation $k$ times gives a finite linear ODE for the degree-$k$ phase jet: its highest jet enters linearly, with coefficients determined by the Hessian and the first derivatives of the reduced Hamiltonian; the inhomogeneous terms involve only lower jets and derivatives of the symbol. This follows by the product rule: terms containing a highest derivative of $\phi$ can have only one such factor, and the coefficient of the transverse degree-$(k+1)$ jet is the transverse characteristic velocity $dy/ds$, which is zero on the central curve $y=0$. Choose zero initial transverse coefficients for degrees $k\ge3$ in the first chart, then solve successively for every degree using [F2]. On an overlap, transform the full jet by the coordinate chain rule before using ODE uniqueness, so the local jets agree. Apply [F1], or its explicit shrinking-cutoff series, to realize them. This yields a smooth phase with eikonal defect flat on each branch and $\operatorname{Im}\phi\ge c|y|^2$ after shrinking the transverse tube.

Define $T_\phi$ to be the coefficient of $h^{-1}$ in the exact conjugation identity $$P(e^{i\phi/h}a)=e^{i\phi/h}(h^{-2}p(x,d\phi)a+h^{-1}T_\phi a+Pa).$$ It is a first-order operator with derivative part $p_\xi(x,d\phi)\cdot D$, so its coefficient of $\partial_s$ on the ray is nonzero. Solve $T_\phi a_0=0$ and $T_\phi a_j=-Pa_{j-1}$ for $j\ge1$ to infinite transverse order. The central $a_0$ equation is a scalar homogeneous ODE with nonzero initial value, hence has nonvanishing exponential solution. For each successive transverse degree and amplitude index the differentiated equations are linear ODEs with already known right sides, by the same cancellation of derivatives along the curve as in step 3.1. Realize these jets by [F1]. The separate asymptotic series $a(x;h)\sim\sum_{j\ge0}h^ja_j(x)$ is realized by $\sum_jh^ja_j(x)\eta(h/\delta_j)$, where $\eta\in C_c^\infty([0,\infty))$ is one near zero and supported in $[0,1]$, and $\delta_j\downarrow0$ is chosen so its $C^k$ tails are summable for every fixed $k$ and have the required $h$ asymptotic bounds. Explicitly, for each $j$ make $\delta_j<2^{-j}$ and $\delta_j^{j/2}(1+\|a_j\|_{C^j})<2^{-j}$; for fixed $k,J$, terms $j\ge\max(k,2J+2)$ are then $O(h^J)$ in $C^k$. Only finitely many earlier terms remain. This proves the full transport and Borel realization.

On an embedded branch take $u_h=h^{-d/4}e^{i\phi/h}a(x;h)$ and a fixed transverse cutoff. For a flat defect $r$, Taylor's formula gives $|D^\alpha r|\le C_{k,\alpha}|y|^k$ for every $k$. Scaling $y=\sqrt h z$ and using $\operatorname{Im}\phi\ge c|y|^2$ shows $$\|h^{-d/4}|y|^ke^{-c|y|^2/h}\|_{L^2}\le C_kh^{k/2}.$$ Every application of $P$ loses at most two powers of $h$. Choose $k$ and the amplitude order large enough to dominate that loss and any requested $N$. Derivatives of the transverse cutoff are supported at fixed positive distance from the ray and are $O(h^\infty)$ by Gaussian decay. Thus the residual is $O(h^N)$ away from longitudinal endpoint cutoffs; at endpoints the commutator with a longitudinal cutoff remains, and no vanishing assertion is made there. This also proves uniform $L^2$ boundedness on each branch.

On each compact parameter interval choose finitely many smooth bump functions subordinate to the branch cover, positive on a smaller cover, and divide each by their sum. Such bumps follow from $\vartheta(t)=e^{-1/t}$ for $t>0$ and $0$ otherwise, by the same nested-interval formula used for a compactly supported cutoff. Patch using the compatible phase and amplitude jets constructed above. On overlaps of descriptions of the same branch, their phases and amplitudes differ by flat terms, so after multiplication by $h^{-d/4}e^{i\phi/h}$ their difference and any fixed number of derivatives are $O(h^N)$ for every $N$, by step 5.1. Derivatives of the partition cancel because its sum is one; the remaining flat differences have the same bound. For distinct parameter branches whose base tubes overlap, phase-space injectivity makes their central covectors distinct at every common base point. Shrink the finitely many overlap neighborhoods so that the gradient of the difference of their real phases is bounded away from zero. With $\theta=\operatorname{Re}(\phi_1-\phi_2)$, choose a smooth vector field $V$ there with $V\theta=1$ and integrate by parts in $e^{i\theta/h}$. Factoring out $e^{i\theta/h}$, the Gaussian scaling in step 5.1 gives an $O(1)$ normalized $L^1$ bound for the product amplitude; each transverse derivative costs at most $h^{-1/2}$ because $h^{-1}|y|=O(h^{-1/2})$ on $|y|=O(\sqrt h)$. Thus each integration contributes $h$ and costs at most $h^{-1/2}$, so after $k$ integrations the mixed term is $O(h^{k/2})$. Thus every mixed product tends to zero to arbitrary order. Away from overlaps ordinary Gaussian decay applies. Hence patching preserves the residual, positivity, and the sum of the branch mass limits, including at projected self-intersections.

Write the density in a branch as $\rho(s,y)|dsdy|$. For a smooth test function, set $y=\sqrt h z$. On each bounded $z$-set the rescaled integrand converges uniformly to the test value times $|a_0(s,0)|^2\rho(s,0)e^{-z^T\operatorname{Im}H(s)z}$. Since $\operatorname{Im}\phi\ge c|y|^2$ and the amplitudes are uniformly bounded, its absolute value is bounded by $Ce^{-2c|z|^2}$; the integral of this bound outside $|z|\le R$ tends to zero as $R\to\infty$, uniformly in $h$ and $s$. First integrate on $|z|\le R$, then let $R\to\infty$. The Gaussian integral gives $$|u_h|^2dV_X\ \longrightarrow\ w(s)ds,\qquad w(s)=\frac{\pi^{d/2}|a_0(s,0)|^2\rho(s,0)}{\sqrt{\det\operatorname{Im}H(s)}}.$$ This positive smooth function is fixed by the leading transport equation; choose the initial scalar amplitude to make $w(0)=1$. Coordinate changes preserve this expression as a density, and step 6.1 removes mixed terms. For a formally self-adjoint operator the leading transport equation and the Riccati determinant identity give $(p_{\xi_s}w)'=0$: this follows by multiplying $T_\phi a_0=0$ by $\bar a_0$, subtracting its conjugate, and using $\rho^{-1}\partial_j(\rho p_{\xi_j})$ for the real divergence term. For the real wave operator in physical-time coordinates the normalized central covector has $|\xi_t|=1$, hence $|p_{\xi_t}|=2$ is constant; its mass density is therefore constant and the chosen normalization gives $w=1$. Arbitrary complex lower-order terms instead enter the scalar amplitude ODE, giving precisely the transported weight above.

If the endpoint cutoff regions lie outside the measurement cylinder, step 5.1 gives $\|Pu_h\|_{L^2(Q)}=O(h^N)$ for every $N$. In the wave case assume also the approximate beam vanishes near the initial slice for a forward correction or terminal slice for a backward correction. Apply [F3] to $-Pu_h$ with zero boundary and the corresponding zero endpoint data. Its energy norm is $O(h^N)$, since $\|Pu_h\|_{L^1_tL^2_x}\le\sqrt T\|Pu_h\|_{L^2(Q)}$. Adding this correction gives an exact solution with the actual approximate boundary data and the same normalized wave ray limit; the product error is bounded by Cauchy–Schwarz and uniform $L^2$ bounds. This proves every claimed localization and correction assertion.
